PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
PROFOUND OBSERVER—Bread is a thing that all of us need. Honest Baker—Yes, and some of us

knead it badly. A YOUNG LADY, asked by a rich bachelor, "If not yourself, who would you rather be 2" replied. sweetly and modestly, "Yours truly." "JOHN, I wish it was as much the custom to sell wives as it is to sell horses." "Why so, Peter 2" "I'd cheat somebody shockingly before
night." A MERCENARY lover gave up his bride when her father presented a bill for the young woman's board during the four yeas they had been

-"engaged." - A LAWYER is like a restless man in bed. He lies first on the one side and then on the other. THE parents of a pair of twins named one Simul and the other Taneous, because they were born at

the same time. IN A CHEAP RESTACEANT.—" See here, waiter this steak is at least three weeks old." "Can't say, sir; I've only been here a fortnight." LADY (horses running away)—"Dear, dear, dear. hat will become of me 7" New Coachman (grimly) "Madam, it depends on your pat life. I'm all
right." "WHIT possesbes you, Irby dear, who have such an excellent husband, to make him angry so often ? " " Because he always brings me a present to make

peace again," A TEACHER having asked his class to write an essay on "The Results of Laziness," a certain bright youth handed in as his compoition a blank sheet of paper. • DOCTOR—" What is the matter with you?" Patient—" I find it very difficult to breathe with my lungs." Doctor—" My friend, you would find it still more difficult to breathe without your lungs." YOUNG LADY (distributing flowers to convicts) —"And when do you expect to come out, sir 7' Convict (inhaling the fragrance of a violet)—" It will be Di.,,cember of next year, miss, before I make

my dilna." A SPORTSMAN had with him a boy to carry the game-beg. Having missed five partridges in succession, the gunner cried, as he shot at the sixth bird: "There! I hit him! I saw the feathers fly! didn't they?" "Yes," replied the boy, dryly; "they/few—flew off with the bird ! " "Para, what do you intend to give me for a birthday present?" asked a young girl of her father, a magistrate. "Give you," said the magistrate, whose mind was evidently on something else— " give you? I'll give you six months." "I NEVER saw such a woman in all my life," said Bass; "you are never satisfied with anything." "People who know the man I took for a husband," replied Mrs. 8., "think, on the contrary, that I am easily satisfied." "I HAVE this evening been preaching to a con- gregation of idiots," said a conceited young parson. "Then what was the reason you always call them 'beloved brethren 2' " replied a strong-mizded lady. VESTRIS, the celebrated opera dancer, used to say with the most perfect sincerity, "I know only three men in Europe at the present day who are unique in their way—the Sing of Prussia, Voltaire, and my- self." "IF you haven't yet read that book you promised to," said a lady, severely, to her son, "you show a great lack of principle." "Oh, no, mamma," was the celm reply, "not lack of principle; only lack of interest." LOVER, passionately—" My sweet Mv darling I love you with all my heart! Be mine 1" Fair maiden—" Oh, William, this is no madden; I must have time--" Lover—" No, no I must have my answer now, for I have my eye on another girl." AIRS. BROWN—I roede that chalk-line on the floor to see if you had been drinking again, and I find that you have. Brown—Pshaw ? What's that to prove? Don't you know that a woman can't make a straight line? "Is that your dog ?" asked a passenger of a New York elevator boy. "No sir. It's my dog's chum." "How is that? Do dogs have their particular friends." "Oh, yes, sir, dog chum just like people. This is a black-and-tan, but my dog is a pug. When he was sick this one came to see him every day. They'll eat off the same bone," he added proudly, as he stopped at the fourth floor. MRS. SELFMADE—" Now, all the preparations for the housewarmie is complete, an' I can't think o' nothin' more to contribute to the enjoyment of them that's going to be present." Mr. Self made— " There's only one thing I would suggest. Nail up a sign in the parlour saying, Guests that use hair oil is requested not to lean their heads agin the wall paper." " TRAMP—" Thank you very much for the lunch, mum; but could you spare me a shilling or two?" Woman—" Mercy! What do you want with a shilling or two ? " Tramp—" Well, I don't want it for myself, mum. I'm just collecting a little money here and there, the same as the rest of the pro- fession, an when we get enough we're going to found a house for destitute tramps." COLMAN and Banister dining one day with Erskiee, the ex-chancellor, amongst other things observed that he had then about three thousand head of sheep. "I perceive," interrupted Colman, "that your Lordship has still an eye to the Wool- sack I" COUNTRYMAN to dentist—" I sha'n't pay nothin' extra for gas. Jest null her out if it does hurt." Dentist--" You are plucky, sir. Let me see the tooth." Countryman—" Orr, 'tain't me that's got the toothache—it's my wife! She'll be here in a minute." A LADY attended a funeral in a country church a short time ego, and after the singing of a hymn which was strieing, melodious, and appropriate, a rustic male friend who was seated beside her, remarked, with an air of intense local pride : "Beautiful hymn, isn't it? The corpse wrote it." "THAT'S a pretty dirty shirt you have on," said the sergeant at the Central Station to a prisoner who had just been registered. "Yes, it is; but it Isn't my fault. Your city is so dirty that a fellow can't wear a shirt hero over six weeks before some- body begins to complain of it." "SOME years ago," says Richardson in his "Anecdotes of Painting," a gentleman came to me to invite me to his house:—" I have," said he, " picture of Rubens, and it is a rare good one. There is little H— the other day came to see it, and says it is a copy. If any one says so again I'll break his head. Pray, Mr. Richardson, will you do me the favour to come, and give me .your real opinion of it?" MISS PRIMO: "Philosophers disagreee as to which period of life seems the longest to mankind. What ie your opieion, doctor?" Doctor (Medita- tively): "Well, it varies. In women, for instance, the longest, generally is between 29 and 30. I know in my wife's case ten years elapsed between her 29:h and 30th birthday." OMAHA TEACHER—" Yes, my children, remem- ber there is no human love equal to a mother's love." Little girl—"Wornens love their childrens better than their husbands, don't they?" "Very of tee." "Yes, indeed. When we gets the hiccoughs mamma gets very sorry and tries to cure 'eon but when papa gets the hiccoughs she gets mad." CULTURED DAME—"Just like a man! You grab the paper as soon as it arrives keep it all to yourself, and then blame me for not being informed on matters of public interest.' Husband—" Well, my dear, 11l read the paper aloud, if you wish. Let me Another Ocean Horror." "Oh, don't read that." "The Progress of the Campaign.'" "I don't care for politics." "'Science Solves a Problem.'" "I hate science." " Mrs. Tiptap's Party—Deecription of the Dresses.'" "Oh, read that —Philadelphia Record. "IHE wife for me," he said, "is the old-fashioned girl—the girl who makes a good housewife—who has been brought up to sew, and to cook, and to wash, and to iron—the kied of girl that they used to have before girls went in for fashionable flum- mery and accomplishments, and things." "Yes," said she, "I uucierstancl. Well, my idea of a hus- band is also of the old-fashioned sort. I want one who will shovel snow, put in coal, chop wood, put up stoves, dig garden beds, beat carpets— and do all thiugs that husbands used to before they went in for clubs, four-in-hands, and things." THE following toast was proposed at a firemen's dinner, and was received with great applause : "The ladies—their eyes kindle the only flame against which teens is no insurance."

div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."

Nearly one million of enumerators were employed in taking the Indian census. It has well been said that this simple fact brings home to the imagina- tion the vast population of Ilindostun even more directly than the estimated totals.

A great many stories have beea current during the last few days about the probable destination of Lord Powis's fortune, but I have the best authority for stating that he has left the whole of it to his nephew, Mr. George Herbert, now Earl of Powis, who married Lady Conyers's second daughter.

What would the shades of Ralei2h, Drake, Blake, Sir Cloudesley Shovel, Lord Nelson, and Commo- dore Trunnion think if they could peruse the adver- tisement of a firm of piano sellers, who announce that the Duke of Edinburgh has been supplied by them with a piano," for use in his Royal Highness's boudoir ? "

The Irish members intend to press on Mr. Balfour the duty of taking step: to carry out the recom- mendations of the Select Committee on the Irish Estates of the London Companies. These, it will be remembered, suggest that the revenues of the Irish estates shall be administered with some reference to the interests cf the localities in which they are situated.

" Enquiry" asks :—ls it the fact that where " big bags" of tigers have been obtained in India the animals have previously been heavily fed and drugged? I have it on good authority, and the story is current in India, that on some occasions the tigers in Nepaul were found so lazy or sleepy that it became necessary for the beaters to kick or spear them out in front of the guns.

Though the lion does not yet lie down with the lamb, he has been trained to peaceful tolerance of other animals. The summer novelty of the Crystal Palace is to be a show of trained wild beasts. In the language of the showman, the directors promise a sight of "lions, tigeis, cheetahs, pli.nthers, bears, and boarhounds. all living together as one happy family, and going through their astounding perform- ances in one huge cage."

"Atlas "writes in the" World " :—A paragraph appeared in these columns last week respecting his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, his alleged financial embarrassments, and their proposed liqui- dation. 1 am assured, on the highest possible autho- rity, that there is not the slightest foundation for the current rumours on which this paragraph was based, and I unhesitatingly express my regret that it should have appeared.

Recent experience in county elections has con- vinced Liberal canvassers that two reforms would add immensely to Liberal prospects of success. One is to close all public-houses on polling-day, and the other is to utilise every national school as a polling- booth. In one of the county divisions just con- tested beer was selling on the day of election at a penny a quart, and the polling places were so far apart that many labourers could not reach them.

A projected marriage is announced between Lady Constance Campbell, youngest daugb ter of the Duke of Argyll, and Mr. Charles Emmott, the son of a wealthy Lancashire cotton-spinner, who is familiarly known in Oldham district as" Bread-basket." This sobriquet has been attached to Mr. Emnictt, senior, —who, by the way, is a'Quaker—ever since a strike, during which he is stated to have declared that the men would very soon resume work "when the " bread-basket " was empty."

Farewell—a final farewell—was said to Mr. Sims Revees by the thousands present on Monday nigh t, at the Royal Albert Hall. Mr. henry Irving was the spokesman between the vast audience (among whom was the Prince of Wales) and the retiring singer. Few among Monday night's audience would recall the debut of the renowned tenor, who, now in his seventieth year, can look back to 1839 as the date of his first appearance. Since that time Mr. Sims Reeves has never been idle, and the record of his operatic career is full of life and interest.

A good story illustrative of the advanced state of education in the British Army of to-day was told by Sir George Chesney at a banquent in India. "A few days ago," he said, ." when .at a Calcutta dinner table, I observed a fine-looking young fellow at the end of the room, who, from his likeness, was evidently a son of the hostess, I asked her how he came to be there. The lady said that he had just 3orne out to India to seek his fortune. lie was not clever enough for the Army, she said, and so they were going to make a lawyer of him."

This was how the identity of Captain Verney with Wilson was discovered. The police had had their attention called for some time to the goings- on of the Captain. Miss Baskett in describing; Wilson had stated that he had a stiff leg. Discuss- ing the case amongst themselves, a policeman suddenly said, "I wonder if Wilson was Captain Verney." This was deemed possible, and a number of photographs with that of Captain Verney amongst them were given to her. She at once pointed to that of the Captain as Wilson.

Concerning the recent by-elections, here is what is vouched for as a true story. Mr. Gladstone and a Conservative member well known in Lancashire were having five minutes chat on Friday evening, chiefly about the Stowmarket election, and the Con- servative asked why Mr. Gladstone had not in- structed his friends to allow the Conservative to win, when a general election would probably have followed, giving the right hon. gentleman a chance of speedily becoming Prime Minister once more. " Good gracious," said Mr. Gladstone, affecting great concern, " I never thought of it. What an opportunity lost?'

Parliament men are still being stricken with influenza, but in diminishing numbers. Seven new cases only were reported on Wednesday, as com- pared with twelve on Tuesday and seventeen on Monday. Tin. symptoms, moreover, are said to be less severe. The new patients are Mr. Osborne Morgan (Denbighshire East), Mr. T. R. Buchanan (Edinburgh)' Sir henry Roscoe (Manchester South), Mr. R. Jasper More ;Shropshire), Mr. T. P. O'Connor (Scotland Division of Liverpool), Mr. R. A. Yer- burgh (Chester), and Mr. Burdett-Coutts (West- minster). These names being added to the pre- vious list brings the total of Parliament aufferers up to seventy-seven.

It is understood that the visit of the German Emperor to the Guildhall will be paid in the course of the second week in July, and that in order to admit of his Majesty's passage through the metro- poli%: being seen by the public the reception will take place in the afternoon. The ceremonial will consist of the presentation of the City's address in a magnificent gold casket and a stately dejeuner afterwards in the Guildhall. It is expected that the Emperor will be accompanied to the City by the Prince and Princess of Wales, and by other members of the Uoyal family. The Corporation have appointed a special committee to make ar- rangements for the reception of the German Em- peror, and it is nelieved that this will be one of the grandest entertainments ever given in the Guild hall.

Most of us think of Captain Marryatt only as the author of those delightful sea-stories, half farce, half romantic adventure, which have won the hearts of literally millions of boys. In Mr L'Estrange's " Recollections of Lady Belcher,"•just• published by Messrs. Hurst and Blackett, we find him in the new character of a philosopher on the subject of marriage. Captain Marryatt was a first cousin of Sir Edward Belcher, and so like him, al- though stouter, that the lady,on being introdueed to hirn,almost started. There is something startling too in the sample given of his long conversation with her with its short authoritative sentences, which read as if they must have been delivered through a speaking trumpet. "You have married (said the captain) one of the cleverest men in the navy. How sad you cannot go on comfortably together. You allow yourself to be dictated to by your mother and her friends. Well, if you cannot live together, part quietly and amicably. Look at my own case. There was incompatibility. I am, as you know, devoted to scribbling! We consequently agreed to live separately without any public controversy.or entertaining any feelings of resentment. She has the children, and sometimes they come to me.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 16, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 16, 1891.

various parts, and indulged themselves to their hearts' content. Other young men of elastic limbs got up " jigging " competitions in which the object seemed to be who could bold out the longest. The " music " tor these gyrations was furnished by the human whistler, by the flute, played by a very per- sistent individual, and by the accordion, manipu- lated, strange to gay, by a young woman. But the majority of the steerage passengers lay aimlessl3 along the decks all day long, the amorous portion of them getting as close as they could to their sweet- hearts, and such a " spooning " picnic they never , had before in their lives, nor are they ever likely to have again. The intermediate passengers were daily diverted by the affectionate proceedings of the emigrants, and would spend hours laughing at and chaffing the gushing couples as they lay entwined in each other's arms. The elderly people looked on without a word, and two old cronies afforded the 2nd cabin voyagers great amusement by the osten- tatious way in which they repeatedly spread them- selves on deck and proceeded to" count their beads." In such manner day succeeded day, varied only by the routine business of eating and sleeping.

div.head: ACROSS THE ATLANTIC.
div.p: ACROSS THE ATLANTIC.
SCENES IN THE STEERAGE.
BY "TOWNSMAN."

"Your letter of yesterday almost takes my breath away. What on earth has induced you to contem- plate a trip to Boston? I hope you are not going as a steerage passenger, on one of the 12 to 13 days boats, between the Mersey and Boston. It will kill you if you do!" So wrote a very particular friend —who has several times crossed the Atlantic Ocean, —just on the eve of my departure for Boston, and without stating any reason this regular Job's com- forter concluded a remarkable epistle by expressing his conviction that I should not go; but he was mis- taken. Having booked through. Mr. John Walker ' Examiner' °Jae, (local agent of the Cunard Line to Boston), I went and claimed my berth in the good ship Cephalonia. (Captain Seccombe), and, mirabile dictu,l still live!

div.head: OUR SHIP
div.p: OUR SHIP

Though not one of the swiftest, is a very good and serviceable seaboat. Built in Birkenhead in 1832,1 she has been in active service ever since, and, 1 believe, has never yet undergone repair. She is about 3,500 tons register, and licensed to carry aoout 1,200 passengers. The saloons are elegantly fitted, the intermediate quarters were all that could be desired, and the steerage, where it was my lot to be, was as gcod as can be found on any vessel sail- ing from the port of Liverpool. The ventilation throughout the ship is of the most ample and satis- factory character, and everything connected with ' the steamer was in as great a state of perfection as has yet been achieved.

div.head: PARTINGS.
div.p: THE PARTINGS.

It was about three o'clock on the afternoon of Thursday, April 16th, having received our saloon passengers, we left Old England behind us, and began to set our faces towards the Greet Land of Hope to many thousands of my fellow country- men. Shortly before we sailed, however, we went ' thro' the ceremony of passing the doctor, and mean- , while the many triends who had come to see us off and wish us" God Speed," were assembled on the tug to go ashore. Many eyes were dimmed at the partings, and not a few were unable to look their loved ones in the face as they gave expression to 1 the last words of farewell. But all were not alike. 1 One plucky little Yorkshire wife, going out with her little ones to join her husband in the States, as she saw her mother's eyes tilled with tears that she vainly tried.to withold, shouted across the space in- tervening between the two boats, "If they waant to knoa if we broke deawn, yo mann say, Noa,' we kept eaur pluck up!"

div.head: START.
div.p: THE START.

We were now fairly under weigh, and, passing New Brighton, the picture of misety, under the wintry weather, we slipped across to the deep on the Lancashire side of the Mersey, took a last peep at Bootle, and, rounding the North-West light-ship, sailed away for Ireland. "What's that, France ?" said a joker to a man that stood hy,as he pointed to the Welsh Coast. "No," replied the man, " it's Italy. I've been this way before!" and they both laughed at their own smartness. But the weather became dull, and presently dark. We turned in for tea, and then the moon arose, and we sat out in the moon- light until cold, and then went to bed. Our com- pany numbered about 350 persons, mostly English cotton operatives, bound for Providence, L iwrence, Manchester, and otl,er manufacturing centres in the New England States, with a sprinkling of North of Ireland men, who had come over by boat to join the Cunarder at Liverpool. When we awoke next morning, we were steaming quickly along the south coast of Ireland, and, breakfast over,we entered the harbour of Queenstown. We had heard a lot about the beauty of this town, and certainly as we looked upon it, bathed in the brightness of our April sun, it realised all our expectations, and we were fain to admit that it deserves the designation that it bears. As we had heard we were to ship about 800 Irish emigrants at Queenstown, we were all ex- pectations as to the kind of people they would prove.

div.head: IRISH EMIGRANTS.
div.p: IRISH EMIGRANTS.

" Ilolloa, here they come." said many, as boats containing plump lasses and bigger boxes were rapidly pulled towards us. The boats were made fast, lines were flung aboard, and then began a scramble to get on deck. It turned out these peo- ple were only hawkers, who had come out so far to meet us in order to get ahead of their rivals,and all our women-folk giggled mightily as they saw the smart way the Irish girls ran up the ship's sides. Boat after boat came alongside, and the pro- cess of hauling up the women became so frequent that those of us who assisted were becoming pretty expert with the lines. Presently a line, such as is used round orange boxes, was thrown aboard, and we, though doubting the propriety, began to haul, when snap went the cord, up went a shriek, and thud went &heavy woman to the bottom of the boat. However, she was more frightened than hurt, fortunately, and, having got a stouter line, we hauled her on deck, muttering maledictions upon us for letting her break the rope! All the hawkers being on board,they spread out their wares on deck, and for a couple of hours did a roaring trade in all sorts of goods. But now we were surrounded with tugs- containing the emigrants and their baggage, and it seemed as if we should fill the ship with boxes, let alone passengers. As the latter came on board they had to stand the searching gazes of the -Government doctor and a detective, and at length, all being satisfactorily concluded, we set our faces westward at a quarter past 12 on Friday noon,April 17th. The engines when started, ran for nine full days without a single stoppage, and then only for half-an-hour, until the completion of our voyage on the 10th day. The emigrants from Queenstown were all drawn apparently from the agricultural classes of the south of Ireland, and were as motley a gathering of people as you would car 3 to meet. They were of all ages and sizes, from the infant in arms to the aged couple going out to Boston to die in the bosom of their family which would be again united by their arrival. A striking peculiarity of the people was the strong physiognomical like- ness they bore towards each other. They were all tall, bony, men and women, with high cheek bones, sunken eyes, and very sharp chins, with scarcely a beauty amongst them. Another peculiarity was their clothing, which was different entirely to the rough home-spun material the Irish wear who visit Eng- land. Many of the girls wore garments of un- doubted English manufacture, and not a few those of the latest fashions. A large number of the girls bad the appearance of having been trained in homes of superior character—possibly they had been domestics to the neighbouring gentry. The bulk of the men had come direct from the clods of Connemara, and one finely built fellow, just as we were leaving the extreme south-west coast of Ire- land,where the rocks had been hewn by the mighty Atlantic into the resemblance of the outstretched finger of a man's hand, exclaimed "That was my home." No emotion seemed to fill his breast as he made the remark, for was he not going to a better country? A third peculiarity of the emigrants was that the girls of the party were about twice as numerous as the men. What theyovere going to do in America was a matter that puzzled many. I tried to solve the question myself by personal in- quiry, but was not very successful. " Phwhat am oi goin' to to do in Boston ? " said one girl I ad- dressed," Shure, an oi'm goin' to a.v a week's rist whin ei git to Boston ? " Most of them,however, are destined to work in the numerous mills on the eas- tern seaboard ; others go into service, and some few of them will help their relatives previously settled , here. As to the men, their occupation will be like that of one of their number, who, when asked by , the ticket collector his business, replied " Anny- think." Some of the " bhoys" had been in the States before and had done so well as to be able to take a three months' holiday home and then return with other relatives. One bright-faced young Irist.man so situated was pointed out to us. "Good mornin' "he nodded to the stewards as he stepped aboard, his face glowing like the western sun, "I know ye." " Holloa! Smiler," replied the stewards, "we remember you," Then, turning to me,a, steward continued" Re went out a year ago with what he stood in. He came back with us at Christmas, and I innocently asked him had he any baggage. "Sevin boxes and a valise! " he said.

div.head: AT SEA.
div.p: AT SEA.

We were now fairly at sea, and we knew it. No sooner had we reached the swell of the ocean than the vast majority of the passengers fell victims to Mark Twain's " Oh my" complaint, and for two days the ship was the scene of unutterable anguish. Monday morning, however, brought most of the sufferers on deck, and then a strange sight pre- sented itself. The people swarmed out of the hold like rabbits out of a.warren, until there was not a yard of spare standing room on the decks. Then the character ot the people became manifest. Reli- giously-inclined maidens took out their prayer books and read therein until tired; otherwise- inclined young men brought out packs of cards and began games of" nap," &c.; whilst Terpsichorean disciples formed select-companies for quadrilles in

div.head: BURIAL AT SEA.
div.p: BURIAL AT SEA.

On Tuesday an ominous silence prevailed through out the ship when it became known that one of our number had died in the early hours. It transpired that a poor Irish girl came on board at Queenstown in the last stage of consumption. She had been ten years previously in the States,and had returned to Irelant in the vain hops of recruiting her health. The Ship's doctor noticed her condition as she came on board, and as she had a sister and cousin with her he hacent the heart to refuse to take her. He thought she might benefit by the passage, but it was not to be. The interment took place the same day, shortly after crossing mid-ocean, and was a very sad affair. The passengers were haunted with the thought "supposing it had been any of ours that had died," and they did not at all like the idea of any of their loved ones being buried in the deep. Consequently much commiseration was felt and ex- pressed for the bereaved ones, and many attended the ceremony. Others could not bear the thought of a funeral at sea, and went below until it was all over. The ship's carpenter made a rough coffin, in which the body was placed, together with a num- ber of weights. At four o'clock the ship's bell began to toll, and six seamen carried the body, wrapped in the Union Jack, from the hospital to the lee side side of the ship. There it was swung over the side and suspended until the close of the service. The burial service was feelingly read by the purser Mr. A. Shea, and as he closed with the words commit- ting the body to the deep, the ropes were slipped, and the coffin sank immediately into the water and was seen no more. AS the poor sister of the deceased heard the coffin go she uttered a loud shriek, and rushed forward as if eager to grasp it, but it was useless. The sympathetic company !ingered a few minutes, and then the girl was led away to mourn in solitude the loss of her sister. The service was very reverently conducted, and many were visibly affected by the no el and unexpected event. STORM, ICE, AND FOG.

Meanwhile the wind was blowing hard, rain fell heavily, and the sea looked so angry that we were led to expect a rough time of it. Hitherto our course had been very calm and pleasant, so pleasant indeed that not a few were so astonished as to ex- press a wish to see a little storm "just to see what it was like." Their wish was gratitied, and in a manner that it took two days to get over. On Thursday the decks were beginning to again assume their normal crowded condition When it became intensely cold, and we sought warmth in bed. But we were, however, completely starved out, so Dwell , so that sleep vms impossible, and NirQ learned nat morning that the cold vital owing to an iceberg which we passed late on Thursday night, and which we had to go out of our course to avoid. To add to our discomfort we ran into a fog, on the Friday, and nearly all the day through the great fog horn was sounded, to the terror of the timid women. The weather on the American side of tha ocian was bitterly cold, and disappointed those of us who ex- pected a warmer atmosphere. Saturday morning broke beautifully clear and bright, but by noon it became dull and again threatened fog. Happily it held off, and pleasant weather continued to the end of the voyage.

div.head: OUR ARRIVAL.
div.p: OUR ARRIVAL.

It was expected that we should make the shore during the night of Saturday, and as a consequence a large number of the company were so restless that they would not go to bud. What was worse,though, was that those who were in bed could not sleep for the noise the excited ones made in passing up the companion way and in promenading the deck. At half-past three on Sunday morning I heard the engines stop, and, jumping up, found we had come to anchor in Massachussets Bay about four miles from Boston. By the time I had dressed, the sun lighted up the shores, and our first view of America was as pleasant as it could be,and my sleeping com- panion remarked that he was as glad to see the land lits ever Columbus was. The ship's complement was now alive, and the girls were busy making their toilets in the sunshine, and arraying themselves in their finery. The change in some of them was remarkable and as complete a transformation as the change from chrysalis to butterfly. It was hard to believe that they were the same people as had ' lounged on the decks for the previous nine days, ; and ones had a difficulty in identifying some of I them. At six o'clock the U.S. Government Medical Officer came on board, and the passengers filed past him. It seems the Americans are very strict as re- gards vaccination, and during the early part of the week Dr. J. T. McGiffen, the ship's medical officer, had been occupied in making an examination of the passengers in this respect, and had had to per- form the filthy practice of inoculation in 1(36 cases in two days. The Government inspection being con- cluded, and everything in readiness, the pilot gave the signal, and we proceeded slowly to the Cunard whart in East Boston,where the landing took place. Trio emigrants had here to pass the U.S. Commis- sioner of Immigration, who was very searching in his inquiries as to the prospects of young children and aged people. However, not a single passenger was rejected, and, as most of the Irish stepped ashore, they were greeted with the salutations of their friends, and conducted to their destinations.

div.head: SCENE ON THE WHARF
div.p: THE SCENE ON THE WHARF

was of the liveliest description. The Cephalonia was the first ship to land emigrants in Boston this year, and, as the large crowd of passengers had been announced in the papers, an immense con- course of people assembled to witness the landing. The baggage on being delivered in the wharf was eagerly seized upon, and men and women proceeded to undress and dress themselves publicly in their best attire in order to accompany their well-dressed relatives to the city. For hours the wharf pre- sented a most animated appearance, but at length the company separated and were quickly absorbed in the great population of Boston. THE SHIP'S DAILY RECORD
of steaming was as follows: April 17th 240 miles, 18th 320, 19th 350, 20th 320, 21st 319, 22nd 253, 23rd 306, 24th 300, 25th 338, 26th 209:—total 2,953.
NUMBER OF PASSENGERS &C.
We had 5 saloon, 91 intermediate, and 1.164 steer- age passengers, which, with 144 of a crew,made the ship's complement-1,404.
SHIP'S OFFICERS.

Only one desire seemed to animate the whole of the ship's officers, and that desire was the comfort of the passengers. Every officer on the boat, from the captain downwards, did his best to make the voyage pleasant to ail, and I never remember meet- ing with a more thoughtful and considerate lot of men. The stewards especially were a pleasant, happy lot of fellows always ready with a joke, and as attentive as it is posssible for men to he. My thanks are especially due to Dr. Giffen, Mr. Bryden, chief steward, and Mr. Shea, the purser, for infor- mation and amistance during the voyage.

div.head: TIM STRBRAGE PROVISION BILL.
div.p: TIM STRBRAGE PROVISION BILL.
The following quantities of the provisions con- sumed in the steerage only during the voyage were supplied by Mr. Bryden, the chief steward ;--
Tea Sugar ... , Barley Oatmeal
lbs. 153 Coffee 180• Peas 500 Rice ..... 550 Flour 60 barrels
Loaves 258 (8 lbs each) Butter BOO Beet (fresh) Mutton
Fresh pork BOO Living fish 10 cwt Fresh fish
Condensed milk, 300 quarts (would make five times quantity of milk). Marmalade 50 7lbs tins.

The food was of the best quality, and the only ob- jection that could be taken was to the rough and ready manner in which it was served. But when one remembers the class of steerage passengers as a rule, eren that objection vanishes. " You can't expect us, "said a steward," to seat these Irish people to tables with cloths on. They've never been used to it, and don't know what it means; when they come here they get plenty of good food, such as many of them never saw before," and I must confess to hearing men declare they had never lived so well before in their lives. The

wonder is how it is done. Allowing a "soy." for 10 days' food and lodginfr„ the C ompany carried its steerage passengers nearly 3,000 miles for less than a farthing a mile. Personally lam well satis- fied with the manner in which the Cunard Com- pany have treated me, and those contemplating emigration or a trip to the States cannot do better than commit themselves to the care of a Company who have always made a special feature of study- ling the comfort and safety of their passengers.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"Royal Edinburgh : her Saints, Kings, Prophets and loets," is the title of a most interesting work by Mrs. Oliphant, author of" Makers of Venice," &c. Edinburgh is one of the most picturesque and in- teresting cities in the world, and as Mrs. Oliphant has done justice to its extraordinary features and extraordinary history, it is a matter of course to say that the volume which she has produced is in its way unique. It is published by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., (price 10s. 6d.) and dedicated "To my old friend Alexander Macmillan." Part Ist deals with " Margaret of Scotland, Atheli ng—Queen and Saint;" part 2nd with the Stuarts of Scotland ; and we have "James Ist, poet and legislator ;" " James 2nd, with the fierpface ;" "James 3rd, the man of peace ;" "James 4th,knight-errant," and "James sth, the last of the heroic age." Part 3rd is devoted to the time of the prophets ; and chapter Ist describes the period "Under the Regent " ; chapter 2nd "Under Queen Mary." Then follows "The triumph and the end," and "The scholar of the Reformation." Part 4 deals with the modern city, Allan Ramsay being depicted as a "burgher poet," while we have I3urns as "The guest of Edinburgh" and Scott as "The Shakes- peare of Scotland.' Mts. Oliphant shows herself in every respect master of her subject; and her style hits the happy mean between the gossipy and the solid and instructive. No Englishman can read this book without being pleased with it, while to the Scotchman it must ever be delightful. The illus- trations are by Mr. George Reid, R.S.A. They are exceedingly numerous, and constitute a prime fea- ture of the work. Mr. Reid evidently knows Edin- burgh and its surroundings from top to bottom, and him illustrations are alike accurate, vigorous, and artistic. He seems to have a faculty for hitting off weird night effects, and strong contrasts of light And shade. Altogether it must be said of "Royal Edinburgh" that it has been royally treated both by author and artist.

'• The Poetical Works of Matthew Arnold," are now to be had in one volume,price 7s. Eid. They are published in handsome style by Messrs. Macmillan and Co., and com- prise over 500 pages. For frontispiece there is a highly finished and striking likeness of the poet. The late Matthew Arnold is not likely ever to become really popular as a poet, as his verse appeals in thought and expression to the cultured classes. He is tender, sincere, and highly intellectual, but he cannot be said to sing the joys and sorrows of the mass of mankind. His work- manship, too, is often unequal, for, like Jove, he some- times nods. Take, for instance, " A caution to poets," which is thus expressed When poets feel not that they make. A pleasure in creating : The world in its turn will not take Pleasure in contemplating. The thought here is undoubtedly strong and true, but it cannot be said that it is happily expressed, for the sense is not to be instantly apprehended. On the other hand, what could be finer in thought or expression, than this, from the "Lines written in Kensington Gardens ?" Calm Sour of all thltiViigslce it mine To feel amid thr3 city's jar, That there abicles a peace of thins Marl clkt not make and cannot mat, liatthew Arnold had undoubtedly a strong liympethy witk nature; and many of his desctiptiVe poems abound in charming lines. This one volume, containing all his poetical works, will doubtless be the means, as it deserves to be, of making him better known to his countrymen.

"The Pleasures of Life," by Sir John Lubbock, M.P., is complete now in two parts, published by Messrs. Mac- millan and Co., price 3s. 6d. The first part has had an extraordinary run, on account of the interesting grousid which was covered, and the admirable selections which it contaiaed from the best authors, ancient as well as modern. In a preface to the second part, the author re- 1 marks, referring to the first part :—" Not only has the book passed through twanty editions in less than three years, but the many letters which I have received have been most gratifying." There is no falling off in quality or treatment in the second part, while the subjects dealt with are of world-wide interest,such as ambition, wealth, health, love, art, poetry, music, the beauties of nature, religion, and the destiny of man. It would involve a large amount of labour, but it would add to the value of future editions of " The Pleasures of Life," if an index were given of the authors quoted and the subjects touched upon. The latest issue of" The Canterbury Poets," published by Mr. Walter Scott, is a shilling volume of American humorous verse. It is selected, and edited, with an in- troduction and motes, by Mr. James Barr, who has done his work as editor exceedingly well. American humour, as every reader knows, has quite a flavour of its own ; and nowhere is it more distinctly brought out than in the humorous poems of the best authors. Practically, all of them are laid under contribution, and, this being tho case, it is a matter of course to say that the little work may be said to sparkle with gems. The notes, it may be added, give, in most cases, a brief biographical account of American authors, and are therefore exceed- ingly valuable for reference purposes. We give, by way of a short specimen, a" mosquito triolet," by Mrs. Aria- tine Anderson.

He presented his bill, And I could not evade It; In valley, on hill, He presented his bill, With stinging ill will SO with blood, sir, I paid it : He presented his bill • And I could not evade It. In the "European Conversation Book" also published by Mr. Walter Scott, we have " German " for the use of English-speaking people in Germany. It is a model of admirable and thoughtful preparation. With this small pocket book to refer to, the intelligent English traveller will have no difficulty in "getting along." It contains, too, "Hints to Travellers" which cannot fail to be useful. The" Magazine of Art" for May is an admirable num- ber. It has for frontispiece a fine etching of George Wetherbee's painting, a picture entitled "Glad Spring." Mr. M. H. Spielmann leads off with an article on "me Royal Academy" as a feature of current art, the illus. tra:tions including reproductions of work by Sir John Gilbert, B. W. 'Leader, and John Collier, the last- named furnishing a portrait of Professor Huxley. " Berkeley Castle," by Percy Fitzg,erald, is profusely and charmingly illustrated, and the same may be said of the paper by Walter Shaw Sparrow on "The Holloway College Picture Gallery." Other illustrated papers include " The myth of the nightingale,,"" The International Shakespeare," " Hokusai," and "The French revival of etching." The contents of " The Cabinet Portrait Gallery," pub- lished by Messrs. Cassell and Co., include Mr. Henschell, Mrs. Henschell, and Sir Henry Roscoe. The photographs are of that high class which Messrs. W. and E. Downey never fail to produce, whilst the brief biographies are, as usual, pertinently and brightly written. " Cassell's Magazine "for May, in addition to the two current serials, contains tvvo complete stories, " On the Lake of Lucerne," and " Tracked : A mystery of the Sea." Amongst the miscellaneous illustrated papers we have the first of a series by Henry Frith, with the title of "Strange family histories,"" How wills are proved," " The teaching of cookery in Board Schools," "The garden in May," " What to wear in May," "The Gatherer," &c. "The Quiver "maintains its supremacy as an illus- trated magazine for Sunday and general reading. "The bride-elect "is the frontispiece for the current issue, and it is from a drawing by Mr. I.,Dieksee. There are several serials, besides complete stories ; and amongst the papers of special interest may be mentioned " Blind men at Jerusalem," "Heavy luggage," "Work in the Master's name,"" Sundays with the young," &c. " Little Folks " abounds as usual in stirring stories and lively bits of prose and verse, which are admirably calculated to suit all classes of young readers. The illu- strations improve every year, and are unsurpassed in this ' class of work Part 4 of Ca,ssell's "Storehouse of General Informa- tion 'is accompanied with a coloured map of the steam communication in the Atlantic Ocean. The letter "A " is still being dealt with,the reader being carried as far as the word aurelia. The illustrations are admirable, and there is every promise of the" Storehouse "being a valu- able cyclopoedia when it is completed. We have also to hand from Messrs. Cassell and Co. the current parts of "The Dor6 Gallery," "Science for All," "British Battles on Land and Sea," Figuier's "Popular Scientific Works," "Familiar Wild Flowers," "Natural History," "The World of Adventure," and the charming fine-art edition of "Robinson Crusoe." The "Ludgate Monthly," edited by Mr. Philip May, is a new magazine, price 3d., which is likely to•have a big run if sueweding numbers are equal to the first. The illustrations are good, and as the contributors include Rudvard Kipling, Florence Marryat, James Greenwood, - and F. E. Wetherley, it is almost unnecessary to say that the matter is excellent. The Spring Number of the " Gentlewoman " is an extraordinar3 production for sixpence--in quantity as well as quality. Many of the sketches and reproductions of photographs are very fine; and the topics dealt with are numerous and brightly written. There is, as usual, a good supply of plates of the latest fashions. Messrs. 'Griffith, Farran and Co., have issued in their admirable sixpenny series "The Three Commanders," by the late Mr. H. G. Kingston. The story is a dapital one—full of stirring adventure; and, as there are nearly 200 well-printed pages, it will be seen that thsre is plenty for the money.

div.head: PERCIVAL GORDON;
div.p: PERCIVAL GORDON;
OR, THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT.
Br SYLVANUS COBB.
CHAPTER XI.

WHAT OUR HEROINE FOUND IN THE CARDEN. A bright, balmy morning in early June, with nature in her loveliest garb ; the foliage of richest emerald tint, and luxuriant; the sweet perfume of garden flowers and orchard blossoms borne on the grateful, gentle zephyr ; the dewdrops gleaming upon every opening petal and drooping leaf; while the feathered songsters, as though sensible of the Good- ness which had created a world so beautiful, poured forth a melody divine. The Lady Caroline Archer, as she slowly and meditatively pursued her way alone, over the well, kept walks of a garden new and strange to her, felt in her heart that she had never known a morning so fair and beautiful. She had ridden over with her father on the after- noon of the previous day to attend the funeral of the aged Earl of Wenliain, anti had spent the night at the castle. On this lovely morning, finding none of the family stirring when she had performed her simple toilet, she thought she would enjoy a stroll in the garden. The window of her chamber over- looked the inviting inclosure, and the temptation was not to be resisted. She had only to slip out into the upper hail, descend the broad staircase, then turn about and proceed to a pair of glass doors that opened on to the veranda in the rear, the steps from which led down into the garden. The glass doors were secured upon the inside by a simple bolt, which she readily slipped, and then, with a thrill of bounding gladness, she stepped forth. Truly the Lady Caroline was beautiful. The charms of early childhood had been broadened, and deepened, and strengthened; the face had retained all its purity, and had taken on, besides, a richer lustre in the bloom of womanhood. The hair, now floating over her shouldels in gleaming, curling tresses, confined only by the light mantle of filmy gauze which she had thrown over her head, was the colour of burnished gold; and the eyes, like oriental sapphires, were full of liquid light, clear and truthful, eloquent when she smiled, and won- derfully eloquent in tears. As our lovely heroine pursued her way she had proposed to herself the curious problem of analyzing her feelings. She had acknowledged to herself that her emotions were strange. Well assured that the lord of Oxton would be stricken from the roll of the living before she returned home; here, at Wenham, for the purpose of paying the last tribute of public respect to the memory of another noble lord, with death casting its shadow upon her path in such a fashion, she ought to have been sad and mournful. But she did not feel so. Not a thought of mourn- fulness could she bring to mind. So all nature smiled, and the Maiden accepted her lightness of heart as a,gift from Heaven. She was repeating from memory the one hundredth and seventh psalm, when her sensitive ear caught the sound of other footsteps than her emit and on looking up she saw two men approaching her. One of them she recognized at a glance—her old friend and fellow-prisoner of the brigands' cavern, Genre,' Malsyell, now Earl of Wenham. His com- I pamtin,she did IRA itnev. was 6, the same height as the general, and full as strongly and com- pactly built, though the latter was now, with ad- vancing years, inclining to corpulency, while the former—much younger--stood straight as an arrow, without a grain of superfluous flash. "0 Ittehjt_,a thanks for this opportune meeting!" thought Caroline to herself. She could now ask Maxwell a question which she had shrank from asking during the brief half-hour she had spent in his company on the previous evening. Surely he could tell her of that other friend whom she had first met in the cavern of the wild Sierras. But he did not continue to approach. No sooner bad the twain discovered her than Maxwell, having spoken a few words to his companion, slipped away into a diverging path, and disappeared. The younger man stood for a brief space where the general had left him, and then, with a perceptible quiver of the whole frame, he came slowly towards her. He was young—not muoh older than herself, if any—and habited in a gentleman's garb, of superior quality and most exquisite fit. Upon his breast he wore a modest jewel of the Order of St. Julian, of Spain, suspended from a golden crown in which sparkled a diamond of exceeding brilliancy. The order, as well as the whole bearing of the man, bespoke the soldier. The citizen's garb had been donned for the funeral occasion. As he came nearer, so that she could clearly distinguish the milliner features, she told herself that he was the handsomest man she had ever seen. A little nearer, and he stopped. A wondrous tremor shook his frame; his frank, grey eyes grew moist, a great yearning warmed the hand- some face ; and presently be put forth his hands and whispered her name. It was but a whisper, uttered as though he feared to trust it to the outer world: "CAROLINE !" From the beautiful woman, as by magic, the years rolled away and were forgotten, and she was a shild again in the cavern of the Sierras. She was in the deadly grasp of a bloodthirsty brigand, and a bright-eyed, heroic boy set her free. She rode again over the Spanish highway, occupying the same saddle with her hero; she sat again in the vine-clad arbour at Salvaterra, her dimpled hand resting in her hero's grasp; and she beard him say to her-0, how well she remem- bered I—how many, many times she had repeated the words I—she heard him say "When lam a captain I will come and claim you fi.:r my own." And she, in the fullness of her heart, had solemnly promised that she would wait. And her hero was now before her, and she was still a child of that olden time. Only one thought possessed her—the thought of truth, of faith, of love, and of holy, happy trustfulness. Through all the years she had cherished that one object of her deep, fervent affection; her love had grown no less with the lapse of time, and now as she gazed upon her-hero in the wealth of his manhood, she know that love, warm and true, permeated every fibre of her being. She did not hesitate. With a low cry of ineffable joy she bounded forward and rested upon his bosom. His strong arms were around her, his lips were pressed reverently upon her pure, white brow, and a murmur of thanksgiving went up to the Giver of all Good. Then ho stepped back, still holding both her hands, and looked into her face. Infinite joy sparkled in the rich moisture of his eloquent eyes, and happiness was in every look. "Caroline, I am a captain, with a record bare to all the world. As chie! of General Maxwell's staff my position is an -honourable one. I have tried through all these years since I saw you last to do right, and. I may freely say to yo-u that a remembrance of my promise to yourself has been a mighty power in my favour. Do you remember what I promised in the little arbour of Salvaterra ?" She released her right hand from his grasp and carried it to his shoulder, where she rested it lovingly and confidently. Then she answered: "Yes, Percival, I remember. And I remember that I too, made a promise." "Aye," he cried, eagerly; "you promised that you would wait for me." "And here I am," she said, a happy smile breaking through the tears and lighting up every feature. It would seem that Percival had come, with the Instincts of a true soldier, prepared to see every approach clear before he offered to claim the prize. He again possessed himself of the lady's right hand, and looked earnestly, beseechingly into her face. "Dear lady—Caroline—pardon me for the liberty I take; but I must know on what ground I stand. If I was but a boy in that long-gone time when I told you, but a little girl, of my love be sure it was no boy's love I gave you, but the love of a heart grown old in trial and sorrow—a heart that was firm and true. ' And through all the years that have elapsed my love has never failed, but rather has it grown with my growth, and strengthened with my strength. Your image has been my constant companion -a- my guardian angel in temptation, and my one great joy when joy could, come from no other source. At Waterloo, I re- member well, when I had volunteered upon a mission of a danger—when death came so near to me that I thought full sure I must go down—in that moment two thoughts alone were present: First, the promise I had given the Duke of Wellington; the other, I spoke to myself aloud' Sweet Carrie I my own! Grod grant we may meet in heaven !" "And I was but a boy even then; but I may call myself a man now; and I have come, Carrie, as I promised. My heart is all your own •of its truth and devotion you shall judge; and I know, I know it now, that you love me in return." "0, Percival 1" "Hush, darling! 0 1 your own heart I can read; but how will it be with your father? I am told that you have been affianced—"

" Stop ! stop 1" the impetuous girl exclaimed,. taking away both her hands from her companion's grasp, and throwing her arms around his neck. "One word let me say, now, and for all time. My life I might give to my father, could it save him from a deadly calamity; but more than my life—my truth, my honour, my self-respect, and my life-long hope of comfort and joy, I will not give, even at a father's behest. Percy! my life! my love 1 I am yours, now and forevermore. I. think to lose you would kill me." With a murmur of blessivg, he bent and kissed her. Only death could part them, so far as he was concerned. And then Ca.rolitie told him bow Sir Edmund Cooper had persuaded her father into an arrange- ment by which she had been affianced to Matthew Egerton, the heir of the Earl of Oxton. She had not been consulted; nor, to the present time, had her father ever so much as told her that the Marriage would please him. "At all events," she said, "I have never agreed to it; but, on the contrary, I have declared that I would die before I would suffer such indignity and outrage. Matthew Egerton is a conceited rnan, and a coward. Percy ! 0, my own! lam • yours and yours alone 1 Yours forever, and for- - ever 1" He wound his arms around her, and drew her close, and their faith was then and there pledged in the first kiss of mutual love and devotion. Then, when they had become calm and tranquil, and their eyes had become clear and undimmed, she clung fondly to his arm, and they walked slowly on over the garden path, exchanging sweet confidence, until' they met the g.eneral. "Dear lady," he said, when the salutations of the morning had been exchanged, "were you offended because I did not tarry to introduce my friend ?" " Not in the least, General," she replied, with a light, joyous laugh. "I knew him very quickly." " By some Masonic sign, I suppose ?" "No," the noble, true-hearted girl quickly an- swered, the fervour of truth and trustfulness in every look and tone; "it was the sign of a stronger, holier bond than that of mere fraternity. His image bad never left my heart." "Lady Caroline," the old soldier cried, with a burst of enthusiasm, "you are a noble woman 1" He stopped, and looked from the maiden to her lover' and then back again, and a sign of doubt that had manifested itself upon his brow quickly disappeared. "1 must tell you," he resumed, with much feet- ing, "that of late I have feared for our dear Percy. Since I promised him that he should return to, England with me and accompany me to Devonshire, I have marked his eagerness. There have been. times when I knew that he had spent the silent; watchea of a long night, not in sleeping, but in thinking of what he should find down here in Devonshire; and in those times I would have given a great deal if I could have whispered to him a single word of hope. But I dared not speak; so L held my pe_ue.. Yet I worried on his account. Yçu were idauy Carinitc 43EY child of an earl-- itnd a Proud earl at that, ii 77.4: ifspld the woman: receive the hero of her girlheod ? it heti not loved the boy as deeply and truly as I could IN, loved a son of my own flesh and blood, I might not have cared so much. However, I brought him with me; and half an hour or mere ago, when I saw you alone, I determined to let my boy determine his own fate," _ _ _

"General," said the proud and happy youth, holding Caroline by the hand, "she is an aogel of truth and goodness; and she is mine-e-mine!" Maxwell gave him joy, and then turned to the other. "Sweet lady, I know not what you father will say, but I know what I shall tell him. I shall re- mind him that both himself and his child owe life and liberty to Captain Gordon. I shall tell him that I am an earl, wealthier than he, and of an older house, and that, if I had a daughter, I would deem myself both happy and fortunate could I consign her to the love and keeping of Percival Gordon.' "Dear General," cried Caroline, in the fullness, of her heart, "I must kiss you for that l" And sbe kissed him and blessed him, and the stern, battle-scarred soldier was as happy as a petted boy. After this Maxwell drew the maiden's arm with- in his own, and gave her an account of Percival's wondrous rise to promotion in the army. "From the time of his introduction to our great chief at Salvaterra," he commenced, "that true- hearted man did not lose sight of him. It was two years and a half after that, at Ceidad Rodrigo, that he made his first exploit under Wellesley's own eye. The chief desired much to know the exact position or a certain division of Marshal Massena's army. Percival chanced to overhear his remark to that effect, and he volunteered to go upon the mission. Suffice it to nay, in the face of such denger as not one man in ten thousand could have overcome, hO made his way through the enemy's lines; made a critical survey of the situation; drew an accurate plan of his entrenchments, with a bit of charcoale on a piece of white cloth which he managed to ob- tain, and returned with his report before morning. That report enabled the chief to lay his plans intel- ligently, and a victory was the result. For this Percival was made a sergeant by Wellesley's own order, and he assumed a sergeant's position, the old soldieis under him well-nigh worshipping him. Remember how they had loved his father and his grandfather. "At Waterloo he won the distinction that brought him prominently to the notice of the government." "Oh ! I read all that," cried Caroline, with en- thusiasm; "and I saw, afterwards, the good duke's speciel mention." "Well," pursued Maxwell, "for that he was breveted a lieutenant, and later ho received a full commission. I, for my share in that affair, was , promoted to my present rank, and I avaiued the appointment of Percival upon my staff. A year bii.;o we accompanied Wellington to Verona—Per- . c'esal and myself—and went with him thence to Paris, where his miesion was to the Frenoh king, to induce him to desist from his designs against Spain. During this time our hero was able to render such valuable assistance to the duke that. he procured for him a full captain's commission-- the first and only case, I believe, in our arroY where one so young has been so elevated upon his own unaided merits. Of course, his grandfather'e —Arehy Gordoes—recerd helped him, and the known fact that he was of gentle blood removed compunctions from the bosoms of our lords and gentlemen who might have been ecandalised by the elevation of a Phelim Nobody's child to officisl rank in the English army. "Truly, my dear lady, he is a noble man, and one of nature's noblemen; and I assure you mar chef regret at leaving the service is in the thought that I must lose his companionship. Ire has be' come no far a part of my life, and I have learned to love him so deeply and so well that the separation will he hard." "Cannot he leave the army also?" asked Caro- line. "No, no. . It is his profession, and his on'''. source of income," The lady was on the point of saying more, but- she retrained herself, and simply remarked.: " Well, well, we shall see." The truth was, she was thinking to herself that as her husband, to love her and make her hap Pit and to make the long days cheerful and pleasant' and the dark days bright, he would have prof' sion enough. She had a considerable fortune is her own right. An inheritance of her mother's was hers, and, moreover, all that part of the °fie nal family estate which she had not relinquished° her Uncle Roland—altogether far more than marl a peer was forced to maintain his dignity u 1043; But all this she could not tell the general, 130 cool.: she mention it at that time. Shortly after this Percival came up, giving the maiden a beautiful bouquet whicii he gathered and secured with a few whiles of gills's' for which she thanked him, the Together they ascended the steps leading tsaao verandah, and together entered the great n"'" Where they met. as chance would have it, CI: line's father. The earl was very glad to niee ed general again, and having greeted him, he tu. with a warm smile, for an introduction to tbe wine young stranger. ('Jo be continued),

div.head: AN ELOPEMENT TO WARRINGTON.
div.p: AN ELOPEMENT TO WARRINGTON.
EXCITING EPISODES.

Dallam-lane was, on Monday evening, the scene of unusual commotion, consequent on one of those exciting scandals which recurring ever and anon, throw such an unpleasant light on the conditions of matrimonial life. It seems that on Good Friday a middle-aged journeyman baker, named Moran, a married man, eloped from Bootle:Liverpool, with a woman for whose bakery establishment he had been acting as manager, and took up their resi- dence at No. 73, Dallam-lane, Warrington. They remained there till about three weeks since, when the man went to Runcorn to enter upon

a Situation he bad obtained there, leaving -the woman behind. He telegraphed to her the day after for her to join him there, and she did so. They lived at Runcorn several days, and then returned to Warrington, not to their former lodgings, but took others in Laira-st., off Battersby- lane. Ile had left his boxes at 73; Dallam-lane, and on receiving an intimation that he must call for them or they would be disposed of, on Monday night he drove up there in a cab, accompsnied by the woman. He left her in it. and entered the house, when to his great consternation and sur- prise his wife confronted him in the house. She said to him "Well, Jim, what are you going to do with me r His reply was to the effect that he was going to have nothing more to do with her." She, however, stuck to him, and a crowd collected about her, including of course a considerable contingent, of females, who threatened to" chuck " nirn out of the house, and altogether conducted themselves so demonstratively that the position of the man became somewhat alarming. The police were informed of the state of the matters, and Inspector Spinks and Detective- Sergeant Monaghan arrived, and escorted Moran to whom his wife still closely clung to the Central Station, having considerable difficulty in protect- ing the man from molestation,as they were followed by hundreds of persons, old and yqung, shouting at the top of their voices; and ready, if the chance offered, to give more forcible expression to their feelings. On reaching the ticket office,the wife, still clinging firmly to her husband, and assuring him, . that if be wonld only go home with her, she would forgive his inconstancy and never reproach him • by even mentioning the name of the other lady. The finale of the whole affair was that the couple left for Liverpool by the 10.5 p.m. express, ap- parently re-united by the bands of imperious cir- emmstances,at any late, if not by those of affection; - while the other woman was left disconsolate.

div.head: CATHOLICS AND FREE EDUCATION.
div.p: CATHOLICS AND FREE EDUCATION.

The Right Rev. Dr. Knight, the Catholic Bishop of Shrewebury,paid a visitation to Runcorn on Sun- day, and attended 11 o'clock mass at St. Edwards Church. Mass was said by the Rev. Father Martin, and the assistants were Fathers Odenbach and Riese (Ditton.) The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, the pastor, was present. The Bishop afterwards delivered a sermon, in which he referred at length to Free Education. Under the Education Act of 1870 Board Schools were intended to be supplemental, that was to complete what was defective in the existing voluntary schools. A gnat work was done thereby, and the Act if fairly carried out might have been a very, excellent one. As it was the system which was intended to supplement or pefect their voluntary schools bad, in its growth and development, tended very much not to supplement, but supplant, to take their places and supersede them. Thera was the alarming fact that a few years ago, a return was made of the voluntary schools which had given way before the School Board system and it was stated— be believed on good evidence—that eleven hundred schools in the country had been handed over by the managers to School Boards. • Amongt these eleven hundred there was not a single Catholic School. No Catholic School was ever surrendered. That was upon the principle that education should not be inculcated irrespective of religion. They could not retire from that principle. By it they must stand or fall. At the present time there was contemplated by Government a measure of Free Education. It was an equivocal term which might mean a great many different things. He only hoped that it might be carried out with a yegard to fair play towards Catholics, who as a body were poor and the revenues of whose church had been taken away. Des- pite these disadvantages the Catholic body had met the need and would meet it in future if necessary. Hitherto as Catholic, or denominational schools they received, in common with the rest of their countrymen, certain grants in aid of their schools according to the results which were found in them by the Government Inspec- tor. Over and above that the entire rate which was gathered went not to their support in any way what- ever, but the denominationalists representing two-thirds of the schools must pay the rate whatever it was and whenever demanded, into the hands of those who repre- sented one-third of the country's education to employ as they thought well. 'That was an injustice against which they protested, that. two-thirds were compelled to pay the rates of the ether _third—rates over the expenditure of _ .

which they could have no power. When therefore the new measure came forward, they should look well to the interests of their schools. Let them bear in mind that any education built without the foundation of religion was a house built on sand. Somebody had well des- eribed secular education as sharpening the intellect to do evil. They need only read the newspapers to see what somebody had well called the enormous amount of educated crime existent in this country—crime that ' could not be without a sharpening of the intellect such as forgery and dishonesty. He urged his hearers to sup- Port their schools, as one of the great duties of their lives, end in c.,nclusion referred to the evils of drunken- ness, remarking that if a man put himself in circum- stances that he knew would lead him to excess, he was bound to avoid the occasion—bound under the penalty of sin. It was pleasing to see, and a subject of thanks- glving to know, that, notwithstanding the small means of the Runcorn Catholic population, they should have been able to get up such a church as this. This result vas largely owing to the efforts of their pastor' and he hoped they would respond to that work, that energy and that zeal which he hadshown amongst them. After _the Benediction, Mr. N. J. Goodall, on behalf of St. -Edward's League of the Cross, presented Bishop Knight with an address of welcome, which was signed by Mr. Alchard Clinch. president; Thomas Houghton' vice- President ; and Thomas Rape, secretary. His Lordship replying, said he was happy to find the League of the \ Cross established on a solid basis in Runcorn Mission, most willingly did he bestow upon their society his °leasing, wishing them at the same time a happy and rosPerons future. The members of the League then aelt and solemnly renewed their pledges. "The pro- ?l'edingß then terminated. In the afternoon a confirms- "On service wa, held, over 200 persons being confirmed.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

- _ HOUSE OF LORDS.—Moimay. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four. THE MANIPUR REGENT.—The Marquis of RIPON asked as to the truth of a paragraph in a London newspaper. in which it was stated that blood money had been offered for the capture of the Regent of Manipur.—Vis- count CROSS had no knowledge of such an offer, and ex- pressed his belief that the Viceroy of India would not issue suck a proclamation. ARABI Pasze.—Replying to the Earl of Kithberley, Lord SALISAURY said the nealth of Arabi Pasha, had not suffered during his residence in Ceylon, and as the Egyptian Government opposed his return to Egypt, no hope at present could be held out of his liberation. SECOND READING &c.—The Copyright Bill was road a second time, on the understanding that it would not be further proceeded with this Session. The Newfound- land Fisheries Bill Was read a third time and passed. The Trusts Amendment (Scotland) Bill passed through Com- mittee. The House adjourned at seven o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. PRIVATE BUSINESS.—The Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Bill and the Wirral and Seacombe, Hoylake,and Deeside Railway Company's Bill were ordered for third reading. Bills were introduced to confirm certain provi- sional orders of the Local Government Board relating to the urban sanitary districts of Ashton-under-Lyne, Black- pool, and Southport. A Bill was also introduced to con- firm certain provisional orders of the Local Government Board for constituting joint Committees to enforce the provisions of the Rivers Pollution Prevention Act. 1876, in relation to parts of the rivers Irwell, Mersey and the Ribble. These Bills were read a first time. NEW MEMBER.—Mr. BRYMER, the new member for South Dorset took the oath and his seat amid Unionist cheers. FREE EDUCATION.—Sir W. HART DYNE told MT. Sum- mers that all schools would benefit by the Free Educa- tion Bill except those which violated the conscience clause. ' SLAVES IN MOROCCO.—Sir J. FERGUSSON informed Mr. S. Smith that the sale of slaves by public auction con- tinued in Morocco, but efforts would be made to induce the authorities to observe the promises given to Sir John Hay in 1884. laisH LAND BILL.—The House again went into Com- mittee on the Irish Land Purchase Bill, the eliscussion on clause 6 being resumed.—Mr. S. KEAY moved to omit sub-section 3,which empowers the Treasury to authorise additional advances in the county not exceeding the capital value of the sinking fund .—After some discussion, Mr. BALFOUR moved the closure, which was carried, and Mr. Keay's amendment was rejected by a majority of 94 votes.—Otber amendments proposed by Mr. SEXTON and Mr, KEAY were negatived, and during the course of the discussion Mr. BALFOUR said it was a mistake to sup- pose that under the new Act the landlords gained any advantage as compared with the old ones. On the con trary, the tenants would be the gainers. The House adjourned at 12.30. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TIIESDAY. The Lord Chancel or took his seat on the woolsack at, twelve minutes past four o'clock. THE MANIPUR REBELS —Lord Coon referring to an answer be had given on the previous day with regard, to the Manipur rebels, said be had just received from the Viceroy of India the following telegram :—" There is no foundation for the report that a reward has been offered by us for rebels dead sr alive." (Cheers.) TEE MARRIAGE LAWS.—The Marriage Acts amendment Bill was, on the motion of the Bishop of London, road a third time. On the question that the Bill be passed, the Bishop of Carlisle moved the addition of a new cause, providing that it should be the duty of the Registrar- General to prepare and cause to be printed a form of banns book suPed to the provisions of the Act, and to transmit upon application from time to time a copy of it to the minister of the church in which banns might be lawfully published. The clause was inserted, and the Bill passed. • Their lordships ros3 at a quarter to five o'clock tin Tuesday, the 26th inst. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at five minutes past three. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.—Mr. CALDWELL moved the second teading of this bill.—The motion was agreed to.—Mr. Philip Stanhope rose to move the following instruction, of which he had given notice :—" That it be an iastruction to the committee to consider the advis- ability, in the public interest, of requiring the fulfilment of the provisions of clause 199 of the Manchester Ship Canal Act of 1885, which provides for the vesting of the undertaking in a public trust, as a condition precedent to the sanction of any municipal guarantee for the raising of additial capital." The SPEAKER said the motion could not be taken at this stage, and it was accordingly postponed till next day.—Mr. STANHOPE asked if it would be in order to vary the form of the instruction.—The SPEAKER : If the hon. gentleman puts a notice on the paper varying the terms of the instruction, that will be in order. EXPULSION OF CAPTAIN VERNET.—Mr. W. H. SMITH then rose to make a motion respecting Captain Verney, who was convicted of misdemeanour at the Central Criminal Court. In the course of his remarks, the right hon. gentleman said he was sure he had the unanimous sense of the House when he said that the circumstances were such as to render it impossible for the hon. mem- ber to remain a member of that House in the discharge of the duties which belonged to it. He also expressed a hope that there would be no debate on the question, as it would be most painful tothose connected with the hon. member. Mr. Smith then moved that the letter addressed to the Speaker respecting Captain Verney's conviction and the record of the proceedings upon his trial to be taken into consideration. The motion was seconded by Mr. CAMPBELL BANNERMAN, and carried in silence. Mr. SMITH then moved that Captain Verney be expelled the House, and this having been formally sisconded by Mr. CAMPBELL BANNERMAN, the SPEAKER put the question but as no member uttered a word he was compelled to declare that the ayes had it. The LAND BILL.—The House then went into Com- mittee on the Irish Land Bill, the consideration of clause 8 being resumed. After some amendments had been submitted and rejected, the Chairman put the question that the clause as amended stand part of the Bill, which was agreed to without debate, in the ,absence at the time of Mr. Sexton and his colleagues. Clause 7 was then proceeded with, and progress was reported at 11.59. BRINE PUMPING IN Caasnins.—The House took into Consideration in Committee the Brine• Pumping (Com- pensation for Subsidence) Bill, as amended by the Select Committee. On clause 22 Mr. HASTINGS moved an amendment to limit the ammint of compensation to one half of the amount of damage sustained.—Mr. GATHORNE HARDY, opposed the amendment.—Mr. Bauman bore willing testimony to the care and zeal of the Committee who had considered the Bill. Where a person lost from sub- sidence it was only equitable that those who caused the loss thould pay the whole of it. He said that as one web would have to pay the largest sums if this Bill passed, and as such he thought he had a right to appeal to the hon. member to withdraw his amendment. He knew of cases where time after time working-man had lost the whole ef their savings through these subsidences. Mr. HASTINGS, who remarked that he spoke mere of Worcestershire than of Cheshire, withdrew his amend- ment. The remaining clauses were then dealt with, and the Bill was reported as amended. The House adjourned at 12.40. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Wetwestiay. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter-past twelve o'clock. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. Nearly an hour after the Speaker took the chair was occupied with an earnest discussion upon Mr. P. Stan- hope's oft-deferred proposal to instruct the Committee upon the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, to consider the ad- visability in the public Interest of requiring the fulfil- ment within a stated period of the provisions of clause 199 of the Manchester Ship Canal Act of 1885, which provides for the vesting of the undertaking in a public trust as a condition of the sanction of any municipal guarantee for the raising of addi- tional capital. Mr. Stanhope disclaimed any hostile feeling against the general object of the bill, but argued that the Corporation of Manchester had no right to make a" huge loan" of three millions unless with a view to the undertaking coming under the con- trol of a generally representative public body. He dis- played a complete familiarity with the local conditions affecting the question,and as usual,put his point sturdily. SirJ. Pease seconded his preposal, which was opposed by Sir William Houldsworth and Mr. Jacob Bright. Mr. Ritchie was obliged to confess that as president of the Local Government Board he could not regard the matter with much satisfactidn ; but appreciating the unanimity of feeling in favour of the canal, he favoured an excep- tional course on the part of the Corporation, and peinted out that the adoption of the proposed instruction would cause delay that might he fatal to the bill. After Mr.' Schwann and the present as well as a past Chairman of Committees had taken part in the debate, Mr. Stanhope withdrew his proposal, and the bill went forward in the usual way. THE LAND BlLL.—Committee on the Land Bill being resumed at half-past one, cause 8 was soon carried\ by a large majority, and clause 9 was easily agreed' to. Ani- mated controversy arose upon clause 10, which makes the Land Commission perpetual, and provides for the pay- ment of their salaries cut of the consolidated Fund. A proposal by Sir GEORGE TREVELTAN to enable the Lord
