Chancellor to remove an inefficient Commissioner was sternly and rashly resisted by Mr. Balfour, who conse- quently caused a sad waste of time, for in the end he was obliged practically to accept the amendment under cover of formal amendments at the behest of Sir Henry James. Several divisions were taken, and the clause was still un- disposed of when progress was reported at twenty minutes to six—ten minutes after the usual time. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUVREMAT.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QUESTIONS Sm.—The Landashire and Yorkshire Rail- way Bill was read third time. Mr. Rrromt, replying to Mr. H. J. Wilson, admitted that irregularities had occur- red in connection with the last election of the Birkdale Local Board, and suggested the means by which the validity of the electionl should be tested. Sir W. Hart-Dyke, in reply to Mr. T. Ellis, promised to do what was possible to make a change ,in the inspectorial divisions of Wales as regards elemen- tary education, so as to make the areas more convenient. Mr. MArrzews, replying to Colonel Sandys regarding the playing of roulette at a Catholic bazaar in Manchester, said the police had instructions to prevent such practices in future. Mr. RITCHIE informed Mr. Picton that the Government did not intend to propose legislation in regard to matket rights and tolls during the present session. TILE Ennui:mow BILL.—Sir W. HART-DYKE, in reply to Mr. Thomas Ellis, said the state of business would not allow the introduction of the proposalsof the Government in relation to free schools before the Whitsuntide recess. Mr. BALFOUR informed Mr. Carew that the Government felt there was no choice.but to levy the recognisances for the appearance of Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien at Tipperary. The Attorney-General informed Mr. Summers that he had not given any instruction for proceedings to be taken regarding the case of Evelyn v. Hurlbert. Sir James Fergusson in- formed Mr. Bryce that the modus vivendi with Portugal in regard to East Africa had been extended for a month. THE LAND BILL.—The twelve o'clock rule was sus- pended by a majority of 128 to 77, in order that the pro- ceedings in Committee on the Land Purchase Bill might proceed without interruption. Several clauses were dealt with, and rapid progress was made with the second part of the bill.

same time, he could not help thinking that these gentle- men were trying to attack something which did not need reform. There were some people who were notoriously bad, but he looked upon railway men almost -as mis- sionaries. (Laughter and applause.) Where would they find anyone who conducted himself better than did Mr. Ashurst—(hear, hear)—or their excellent friend Mr. Braide, who was one of the finest specimens of humanity he had ever seen? (Applause.) He (Alderman Fran- comb) had been a magistrate four or five years, but he had never seen a railway man brought up for any offence before the Court. He had known some of the audience for 14 or 15 years, but to his knowledge no charge had ever been preferred against them. With reference to railway strikes, he was pleased to know that they had not arisen in Warrington. The wonderful mission at Liverpool did away, with a great deal of unpleasantness between employer 4 and employed. Railway strikes were brutalizing, like wars, and if disputes could be settled by arbitration, they would be much better off. A great deal of hardship would be saved by a fair hearing being given to both sides—masters and men—whenever a dispute arose. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He be- lieved that one of the objects of the mission was to take such disputes into consideration. A better state of feel- ing would exist if working-men would begin to help them- selves ; and the masters would have to inquire into little grievances which at the present time were passed over thoughtlessly as not being worth consideration. The movement in question• had his sympathy and support. (Applause.) Mr. ASFIIIRST, having apologiled for the absence of Alderman Sutton and Mr. Thomas Morris, observed that the mission was started over two years ago, when a ser- vice was held in one of the railway, waiting-rooms on Sunday evening. In course of time it was found that it would not accommodate all who were anxious to attend, and the large room over Arpley Station was engaged: and a service had been held there every Sunday evening since with one exception. They did not wish to create anew sect; they were purely undenominational, and their service commenced at 8.15, to as not to interfere with other services in the town. Great good had been done by the mission, and he wished it every success. They had been incorporated with the Liverpool Evange- lical Mission for Railway men and others, and the Coun- cil meetings were held in Liverpool. They had the Lord Bishop of Liverpool and the Lord Bishop of Sodor and Man at their head, as well as Mr. Edward Whitley, Sir W. E. Forwood, Sir David Ratcliffe, and Mr. E. R. Russell. Addresses were also given by Mr. Tharme and Mr. J. S. Tomson, of Liverpool, and Mr. Harrison moved resolution to the effect that Mr. Ishurst be elected to re- present the mission at the Liverpool Council. The Rev J. H. Vikewes seconded the resolution,which was carried. The Rev. J. W. Varley proposed a vote of thanks to the Mayor for presiding,which was seconded by Mr. Tharme and carried. During the evening songs were admirably rendered by Mrs. Varley and Miss Fanshawe. THE CENSUS OF LIVERPOOL

Taking the whole of the three divisions together a total increase is shown of about 41.000. The figures of the latest census are as far as can be gathered— Liverpool 155.550 Tosteth 127,388 West Derby

RUNCORN MUSICAL iiOCIETY.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the members of the Run- corn Musical Society was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall on Tuesday evening, and there was a good attendance. In the absence of the president (Mr. J. Brundrit. J.P.,) through illness, Mr. T. Handley took the chair.
THE REPORTS..

Mr. Pierpoint, the secretary of the Society then read the annual report of which the following is an abstract: —" The report I have the honour to present for the past season so far as vice-presidents and practical members go, shews a decided increase on the previous season. We have had the advantage of having Mr. Brundrit as president, and it is to be regretted that through illness he is unable to preside to-night. When you did me the honour to elect me secretary I took the opportunity of calling the Committee together during] the summar to arrange well before hand for the season. At the first Committee meeting it was suggested to male an effort to obtain 100 vice-presidents. The idea was considered a little far fetched by the Commit- tee, but by the great aid rendered to me by Mr. Frith, our honorary treasurer' I am enabled to report that we succeeded in getting 92 or an increase over last year of 60. (Applause.) This enabled the committee to ar- range a rather ambitious and costly series of concerts, which have been carried through with the amount of success to be expected considering the artistes and band engaged. The first concert was given in the Public Hall, on November 4th, 1890, with a miscellaneous pro- gramme, and Madame Clara Samuel] and Mr. Grime. as chief artistes. The second concert was the "Messiah," on the 16th December, with Madame Fenna, Miss Hall- wood (in place of Miss Dews, indisposed), Mr.Houghton, and Mr. Lucas Williams, as principals. Prior to this concert. I received a letter from Mr. Humphreys con- taining his resignation, his reason being the inability of the committee to secure the Drill Hall for the perform- ance. The committee, after fully considering this letter, felt it. then their duty to accept it subject to the appro- val.of the society, a special meeting being called for the purpose, at which their decision was reversed by a small majority. We now come to the last concert "Elijah," which we were enabled to give in the Drill Hall,on March 17th, the principal artistes being the Misses Conway. Taylor, Lloyd, and Pierpoint, and Messrs. Guy, Morri- son, Banock, Pierpoint, and Whitworth. This concert appears to have been the most popular of the series, and we were favoured bY the largest audience &min., the season. There is nothing more that I need report on, and I can only express the hope and wish that a much better season is in store for the society, both musically and financially than the one just concluded. With a chorus numbering 41 sopranos,lB centraltos, 30 tenors and 32 basses, total in all 121 members, with a subscrip- tion list such as the Society has enjoyed during the past season, naturally much will be expected by the public, and if the Society will only keep as its one great aim the advancement of the divine art we love so well and work on sound business lines I feel sure neither the pub- lic or the Society will be disappointed. (Applause.) Mr. Frith, hon. treasurer, read the statements of accounts. The part showing the profit and loss on each of the three concerts is the principal feature of interest in it :—Mis- cellaneous concert.—Expenses, £59 13s. 5d.; receipts, £2B-us. 2d. •, one third vice-presidects,£3l 3s. ; balance profit, 9d. Messiah concert.—Expenses, £62 13s. 5d.; receipts, £3l 7s. 2d.; one third vice-presidents, £3l 3s. •, balance loss, 3s. 3d. " Elijah" concert.—Expenses, £7B Os. sd. ; receipts,£43 17s. Bd. ; one third vice-presidents, £3l 3s. ; balance loss, £3 ss. 9d. Loss of general work- ing of the Society, £8 19s. id. The subscriptions were —the president. £1 is. ; 88 vice-presidents, £92 8s ; 2 honorary members, 15s. 61. ; 58 lady members, £8 14. a.; 50 gentlemen members. £l2 10, and 1 junior member, 3s. The cash now available in Parr's Banking Company is £1 Is.—The Chairman moved the adoption of the re- ports, which he said were on the whole satisfactory and had it not been for the exertions of the Secretary and Treasurer they would have been far on the wrongside. I—Mr. P. Speakman seconded the motion which was car- ried unanimously.

THANKS. Mr. Speakman proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Kay the accompanist. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys the conduc- tor, Mr. W. B. Frith the hon. treasurer, Mr. R. W. Pier- point the hon. secretary, Mr. W. B. Kay the orchestral secretary. and Mr. R. Moores the librarian.—Mr. Jones seconded the motion which was carried by acclamation, and the several gentlemen acknowledged the compliment. A vote of thanks was also accorded tc the Committee and the chairman replied.

PRESENTATION TO MRS. NAY. The Chairman said he had a very pleasing duty to per- form. Ever since the society was formed Mrs. Kay had been the accompanist and she had spared neither labour nor effort to make herself perfect in the difficult pieces of music the society had taken in hand. (Applause.) He had often wondered at the patience she had displayed when the conductor had been drilling them night after night and the readiness with which she responded to his call. (Hear, hear.) It was with extreme pleasure that he on behalf of the members presented to Mrs. Kay a case of silver, consisting of a solid silver afternoon tea service and spoons complete. (Applause.) If ever anyone deserved a testimonial Mrs. Kay did, and that present came from the hearts of the members. (Loud and pro- longed spplause.) Mr. Kavin acknowledging the gift on\ behalf of his wife said Mrs. Kay knew nothing of what was to be done when ske entered the room. He was sure she felt like himself quite overcome, and he could only say how much she appreciated their kindness. (Applause.)

APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS. Mr. P. Speakman proposed the re-election of Mr. Brundrit, as president of the Society. They could not have a gentleman who took a deeper interest in music.— Mr. Taylor seconded the motion which was carried by acclamation. On the proposition of Mr. W. 11. Frith, seconded by Mr. Littler, the vice-presidents were re- elected, the Committee having power to add to their aumber.
THE CONDICTOR9HIP.-LIVELT . DISCUSSION,

Mr. Taylor proposed the re-appointment of Mr. E. Wyline-Humphreys as conductor. All would admit that he had taken a deep interest in the Society since it com- menced, and he, had i bestowed a very great amount of i labour n bringing t up to its present successful condi- tion.—Mr. Speakman seconded the motion.—Mr. Kay suggested that the time had arrived when they should employ a professiFnal canductor. (Applause.) He did not wish in the slightest degree to detract from anything Mr. Humphreys had done, and he threw out the sUgges- don as one who had only the interest' of the Society at heart. H. e should like to enlist Mr. Humphrey's services as organist i . and sub-conductor and if he could work har- moniously n way he thought the Society would pros- per more. He pointed out that if they had a professional conductor they would be able to secure a better band at a less cost, and concluded by moving that they employ a professional conductor.—Mr. T. Clegg seconded the motion; remarking that the expenses would be curtailed by employing a professional conductor. He hoped all would be loyal to the Society whatever the vote might be.—Mr. Scott said he bad had 20 years' experience of musical societies and his knowledge of a professional con- ductor was that he was not to be compared to their pre- sent one. (Applause.) All the societies he had been connected with, having a professional conductor, had ended in debt and a kind of "shamble." The SUCCORS of that Society was largely due to the energy and en- thusiasm of Mr. Humphreys,and it was base ingratitude to ask him to retire from the position he now held. (Ap- plhaise.)—Mr. Harrison said he should vote for Mr. Humphreys,but he should like less expense incurred in the way of band. (Hear, hear. and laughter.)—Mr' Speakman urged that the success of the Society depended upon unanimity 'and he asked Mr. Kay to withdraw his motion.—Mr. Rogerson said he should like to know the grievance against Mr. Humphreys, and a merrßier replied that it was personal feeling—Mr. Clegg said there was no personal feeling whate.ver.—Mr. W. Crosby said there was a grievance last year and he hoped such a thing would never occur to the Society again as did on the occasion to which he referred. Would Mr. Humphreys pledge himself to take them through the season if he were appointed. (Hear, hear and applause.)—Mr. Tay- lor said one grievance appeared to be the band, but surely the Committee had the ruling of the decision in that matter. He asked them to sink their little differ- ences and act with one desire for the success of the society.—Mr. Pierpoint supported the amendment, 'and dealing with the matter from the business standpoint, showed from an estimate that he had prepared that were they to engage Mr. Argent, of Liverpool, the concerts could be worked much cheaper, and they would he able to give several high-class and modern works. There had been some talk about lo)alty whichever way the voting went. He should like to know if that applied to Mr. Humphreys. He would be the last one to say a word against Mr. Humphrey's musical ability or energy, but in the past they had not been able to depend upon They work" floored" before the last "Messiah," and " floored " the season before. As far ashe was concerned he could not consent to join the Committee without some binding agreement.—Mr. F. Norman hoped Mr. Kay would withdraw his motion and thus avoid anything that would lead to friction.—Mr.Kay was sorry that per- sonal motives had been introduced. It was best that these grievances should be ventilated and he had spoken mostly on behalf of Mr. Humphreys, whom he hoped would have said a word or two on the subject. He had only the success of the Society at heart, and after the discussion he would withdraw his amendment.—Mr. Humphreys was then elected non con.—Mr. Humphreys said he recognised to the fullest extent Mr. Kay's motives in bringing the matter forward. (Applause.) He wanted to say this that it was only by letting the dead bury the dead that they could go on—(hear, hear)—and as to that unfortunate breeze he was perfectly prepared to admit, although he did not think it, that he was wrong and they were all right. (Applause.) Since that time he had acted as if the disagreement had never been, and in that spirit he was prepared to act in the future. One word as to the band. If they were to maintain the efficiency of their concerts they milstot all hazards and all expense main- tain the efficiency of the band. They had created a desire for good music, and unless they kept up to the high water mark already attained, they would be sure to , find public support falling efl. His work had been a labour of love, and unless lie got notice from the mem- bers he was not likely to go. Personal motives had been

imputed and he believed there was personal feeling existing between Mr. Pierpoint and Mr. Frith and him- self. He was prepared to put out the right hand of M.. lowship and work as hard as ever he had done in the past. (Applause.)—Mr. Frith denied that he had any personal feeling. and Mr. herpoint objected to this per- sonal attack,and said he wculd not give Mr. Humphries or anybody else the gratification of krnwing his inmost thoughts.—Mr. Pierpoint was then re-appointed secre- tary; Mr. Frith treasurer; and Mr. Kay orchestra secre- tary ' • Mr. R. Moore librarian,and Mrs. Kay accompanist. The following were constituted a committee—Miss Janet!, Miss Wright, Miss Simister, Miss Stubbs, Miss Norman. Messrs. Thos. Handley, Scott, H. Hughes, J. Littler, and R. Moms.

div.head: ELECTION NEWS.
div.p: ELECTION NEWS.
HARBOROUGH ELECTION. GREAT LIBERAL VICTORY. The result was declared on Saturday as follows : J. W. Logan (L) G Hardy (C) 5,493

Majority 489 A crowd of some 5,000 people had collected, and when Mr. Logan's large majority was announced the greatest enthusiasm prevailed. Even the most sanguine of the local Liberal leaders had not expected such a victory.

Majority STRAND DIVISION.

Mr. W. H. Smith was on Tuesday morning nominated as a candidate for the Parliamentary representation of the Strand Division, to fill the vacancy caused by his acceptance of Lord Wardenship of the Cinque Ports. No other nomination being handed in before one o'clock Mr. Smith was declared duly elected.

div.head: HR. SMITH AND FREE EDUCATION
div.p: HR. SMITH AND FREE EDUCATION

After the nomination of Mr. Keevil asked Mr. Smith what proposal the Government intended to make with regard to free education with respect to the present School Board rate. Mr. Smith said he did not think they would expect him to disclose provisions of a bill not yet introduced to the House of Commons. He could, how- ever, say at once that no portion of the cost of free edu- cation should fall upon the rates.

div.head: MR. DE COBAIN'S SEAT.
div.p: MR. DE COBAIN'S SEAT.
Mr. Gustavius Wolff, partner of Sir Edward Harland, M.P.. has been adopted as the Conservative candidate for East Belfast in the case of a possible vacancy owing to the charges against Mr. de Cobain.

div.head: INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.
div.p: THE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC.

The registrar's return z for the past week show that twenty deaths occurred in Liverpool from epidemic in- fluenza, as compared with eight during the previous week. The epidemic is still very prevalent, but it is asserted that its spread is not so rapid as in many other towns. In Bolton its ravages have been very severe.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE'S ILLNESS
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE'S ILLNESS

Mr. Gladstone, who attended oluirch in London on Sunday morning, was seized in the afternoon with shivering and illness. Sir Andrew Clark, who was sent for, said Mr. Gladstone must not leave his room for several days. Mr. Gladstone was found to be suffering from influenza cold; but his condition is not serious. Sir Andrew Clark, who visited Mr. Gladstone on Thurs- day morning, remained with his patient for half an hour, and issued the following bulletin :—" Mr. Gladstone is progressing favourably, and the temperature is rather lower."

THE PRINCE 'OF WALES,. ATTACKED. - The Prince of Wales was viiited at half-past nine on Thursday morning by Dr. Laking. The rest which the the Prime is taking has already had a beneficial effect. His Royal Highness has been ordered to keep himself quiet. Mr. Tyssen Amherst, M.P., is suffering from influenza, but is progressing favourably. DEATH OF THE HIGH SHERIFF. Mr. George Preston. the High Sheriff of Lancashire. died on Wednesday from pneumonia, following influenza.

div.head: 'DEATH OF AN M.P. AND A CANON,
div.p: 'DEATH OF AN M.P. AND A CANON,

Mr. W. B. Barber, M.P. for Paisley, died at Brighton, on Wednesday from influenza. The deceased gentleman was well-known in Liverpool, where he was at one time in business as a South American merchant. The death of Canon Cadman, chaplain to the Archbishop of Canter- bury, from influenza,was also announced on Wednesday. DEATH OF A NOTABLE ODDFELLOW. - -
Mr. George Vaughan, ex-director of Manchester Unity of Oddfellows, and candidate for the Deputy-Grand Mastership of the Order, died on Thursday of in- fluenza.

div.head: LABOUR COMMISSION.
div.p: THE LABOUR COMMISSION.

The concluding meeting of the Procedure Committee lf the Royal Commission on Labour was hell on Tues- day, when the members agreed upon their report. It is understood that the Committee recommended that for the purpose of taking evidence the commission should divide itself into three sections devoted to leading indus- tries or groups of allied trades: viz :., one with refer- ence to mining, ironmeking, engineering, and shipbuild- ing ; the second with reference to the textile industries, building, gas, ckemica,ls, and miscellaneous trades; and the third with regard to transport trades and agriculture The full commission will be summoned to meet on the 26th inst., previous to which date the report of the Pro. cedure Committee will be printed and supplied to all the members.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. S. IL HARTLEY,
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. S. IL HARTLEY,
OF PRESCOT.

• Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Prescot Board of Guardians, and clerk to the Rural Sanitary Autho- rity of the Union, died suddenly at his residence, Eccleston Park, Prescot, on Monday night. Mr. Hartley attended the meeting of the Board on Thursday last, and was then apparently in robust health. His wife and children left for Blackpool on Fri- day, and it was on Saturday and Sunday that he com- plained of feeling unwell. He attributed his illness to a slight attack of influenza, and contented himself with walking about the house and garden. He remained in- doors on Monday,and in the afternoon went to bed. He was afterwards heard snoring heavily by a servant, who, towards night, grew alarmed as to his condition. She accordingly ran to the house of Mr. Wm. Newsome, on the opposite side of the road, and on Mr. Newsome and his son, Mr. J. G. Newsome, entering Mr. Hartley's bed- room, they found that he had expired. Mr.Hartloy was only in his 39th year, but had officiated with excep- tional ability as clerk to the Guardians for about a dozen years. He was also clerk to tho Rural Sanitary Autho- rity, clerk to the Prescot Union Assessment Committee, clerk to the Education Board, and superintendent regis- trar of the district. In addition to holding these public offices, he was a director of the Lancashire Watch Com- mittee, a trustee and steward of the Prescot Wesleyan Chapel, and about two years ago was • candidate for the County Council. In politics he was a Conservative, and took an active part in nearly all local affairs. He was born at Bolton, and before his removal to Prescot he was assistant clerk in the West Derby Union, under the late Mr. Cleaver.

div.head: TEIE INQUEST.
div.p: TEIE INQUEST.

On Wednesday morning Mr. Brighousa,county coroner, held an inquest at the Wellington Inn, Eccleston. The coroner and jury proceeded to the residence of the de- ceased gentleman in Eccleston Park, and viewed the body. On their return, the first witness was Mr. John Robert Smith, cotton manufacturer, of Ful- wood, near Preston, who Ltated that deceased was his brother-in-law. Witness had not seen him for about two months. He saw the body yesterday afternoon, and identified it as that of Mr. Hartley, who was thirty-eight ' years of age. Witness did not know that he had suffered from any particular complaint and had considered him a man of good health. Witness said Mrs. Hartley was too unwell to appear, and the coroner and jury agreed that her presence was unnecessary. Annie Houghton, domestic servant, said that on Fri- day last Mrs. Hartley and the family left for Blackpool. Mr. Hartley was then very well, and continued so until Saturday night, when he said he thought he was going to have influenza, but took no remedy. On Sunday he got up as usual, and in the afternoon walked out with Mr.Newsome. On Monday morning about seven o'clock he called her to his bedside and asked her for a drink, saying he thought he would lie still a little and get up shortly. Witness gave him part of a small bottle of champagne. He said he had been down- stairs earlier, and had had one, small bot- tle of champagne. He afterwards drank the remainder of the small bottle and also had another before noon. Before dinner she asked him if he would have any dinner, and he said " No," but would have a sleep, and then get up. He (lid not seem wars'. He thought then it was the influenza, and if he could keep quiet he should get rid of it. He did not suggest that a doctor should be called in. Between one and two o'clock she went up and found he was sound asleep, and an hour later he was the same. Between four and five o'clock she went in again, and he was apparently in a nice calm sleep, but a little after fivewhen she looked again there was no sound. Witness fetched the other servant,'and a doctor and Mr. Newsome were sent for,but it was found that he was dead. By the Coroner: In her opinion Mr. Hartley was tak- ing the champagne medicinally, thinking it would cure the influenza. He was not addicted to drink. Mr. Newsome, coal merchant, Eccleston Park, deposed that he was with Mr Hartley about three hours on Sunday afternoon, and they walked out. When he left him Mr. Hartley said he would have a sleep. Wit- ness did not again see him until sent for. They tried his breath with a mirror, and foand he was dead. He.had been troubled with heart disease. The Coroner expressed the deep sympathy both he and the jury felt with Mrs. Hartley and the family in their deep sorrow, and paid a feeling compliment to the able and efficient public servant Mr. Hartley, with his extraordinary administrative abilities, had been. The jury returned a verdict that death was due to natural causes, probably heart disease.
The funeral took place at Breiahtmet, Bolton, on Fri- day. The deceased gentleman leaves a widow and four children.

div.head: WARRINGTON 11A1LWAY MISSION.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON 11A1LWAY MISSION.
TEE MAYOR ON STRIKES.

The week of special services in connection with the Warrington Railway Mission, which bad been conducted by Mr. William Tharme,superintendent of the Liverpool Evangelistic and Temperance Mission, was concluded on Monday evening, by a public tea meeting held in Bold-st. Wesleyan Sunday School. About 200 persons, including railway men and their wives, families, and friends, were present. Tea over, and the room re-arranged, an entertainmer.t was given, under the presidency of the Mayor, who was supported on the platform by the Revs. J. W. Varley (Latchford) and J. IT. Skewes (Liverpool), Councillor Dixon. Mr. C. Ashurst (station master, Latchford), Mr. Tharme, Mr. William Hickman, Mr. J. S. Thompson (Liverpo)l), and Mr. W. H. Atkin- son (a detective in the service of the London and North-Western Railway Company.) The MAYOR, in the course of an addreQs said he had had a great deal to do with railway men for many years, and he naturally felt that if he could further their inter- ests it was his duty to do so. He was pleased to find that in this great association, which was known as the Liverpool Evangelistic and Temperance Railway Mission, neither politics nor any particular form of religion was introduced. The simple object of the association was to do good to railway men and their families. No doubt Mr. Tharme and Mr. Skewes would give them a report with reference to the work of the associa- tion, but he (the Mayor) could give no details. At the

div.head: OLDHLM MURDERER.
div.p: THE OLDHLM MURDERER.

Tuesday. the 19tk inst., has been fixed by the High Sheriff of Lancashire as the date of the execution of Alfred William Turner, who murdered his sweetheart, Mary Xllen Moran, at Oldham, on the 29th of March. Should the condemned man not be respited in the mean- time, the execution will take place at 8 a.m. in Strange- ways Gaol. He is in good health, and eats hea•tily. He has not expressed any regret at having committed the crime for which he was sentenced to death.

div.head: MANIPITR DISASTER.
div.p: THE MANIPITR DISASTER.
CAPTURE OF THE REGENT.

The following telegram from the Viceroy of India, dated Simla, May 10, has been received at the India Office: "Maxwell telegraphs 7th : Tongal General surren- dered himself to-day, and is now in custody.' "Collett telegraphs Bth 'The Regent was arrested this morning by some Manipuria sent out by Major Maxwell, and is now a prisoner under a military guard.' "Efforts are being made to capture other Princes."

div.head: WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON VOLUNTEERS.
PRESENTATION TO SERGEANT-MAJOR FEN N ELIA .

On Saturday afternoon there was a march-out of the Volunteers, who assembled at their headquarters at the Drill Hall at four o'clock. About 280 men, including a number from Newton,put in an appear- ance, ana several movements having been gone through, a brief address to the men was given by Colonel Greenall, commanding. The other officers present were—Lieutenant-Colonel Bolton, Captains J. D. Duckton, R. W. Baynes; Lieutenants J. T. Smith, J. A. Edelston, F. M. Appleton, R. J. Chorley, .J. D. Fairclough, Captain F. A. Adam, Adjutant, and Quartermaster. T. Hutchinson. Colonel Greenall said he had a pleasing duty to perform, namely, to pre- sent a silver medal to Sergeant-Major Patrick Fennelly (late 2nd Battalion Bth Foot,) " as a reward for his long and highly meritorious service." The officer command- ing the Bth and 40th Regimental District had received a communication from the Commander-in-Chief intimating that her Majesty the Queen had been pleased to approve, on the recommendation of his Royal Highness, of the grant of an annuity of £lO to Sergeant-Major Fennelly, together with the silver medal. The annuity would date from the sth December 1890. He had previously spoken to the Sergeant-Major on the subject, and had informed him that he thought the honour was well deserved. The Sergeant-Major had been with them eight years, and he had admirably performed his duties, and .had given general attention to all the orders. He had also endeavoured to obtain the good wishes of all, and 'in that respect he had been eminently successful. Colonel GRENNALL having fastened the medal to Ser- geant-Major Fennelly's breast, the men then left the Drill Hall for a march through town and suburbs. They were headed by the band; following which were Colonel Greenall and Lieutenant-Colonel Bolton on horseback. The route taken was as follows —Legh-st., Sankey-st., Bridge-st., Wilson Patten-st., Parker-st., over Bank Quay Bridge, to Lovely-lane, Policy-lane, Win wick-st., Horse- market-st., and Sankey-st. back to headquarters, which was reached about half-past. Colonel G lIRENALL again addressed the men, and referred in complimentary terms to the late Major Litton, who, he said, had been one of the greatest friends and supporters of the Volunteer movement. The Colonel referred to the good feeling existing among the men, and expressed a hope that it would continue. He was pleased to see that an addi- tional room had been provided for the rank and file, nam.ly, a reading and recreation room, and he koped it would be made good use of. The men were then sup- plied with refreshments, after which they were dis- p emed.

div.head: THE. LATCHFORD VACANCY.
div.p: THE. LATCHFORD VACANCY.

MR. JAMES FAIRCLOUGH RETURNED. A meeting of the Liberal Committee of the Latchford Ward was held on Saturday evening, for the purpose of considering whether or not a Liberal candidate should be nominated for the vacancy in the representation of the ward in the Town Coun- cil, caused by the resignation of Mr. Joseph Taylor. There was a full attendance, and Mr. Stringer pre- sided. It was decidea, after borne consideration, not to nominate a candidate in opposition to Mr. James Fairclough, who was the Conservative nominee.

The period allowed for nominations closed on Monday, and as Mr. James Fairclough, corn miller, 5, Wilsoh- Patten-st., was the only person nominated, he was, of course, duly elected. Mr. Fairclough was proposed by Mr. Wm. Tinsley, and seconded by Mr. John Hartley, and the assenting burgesses were Messrs. William Wallace, John Hughes. Joseph Grounds, William Albert Banning, JOhn Starkey, James William Marsh, William James, William Dakin. In a second nomination Mr. Fairclongh was proposed by Mr. Joseph Ashton, seconded by Mr. Robert C. Cooper. and the assenting burgesses were Messrs. Peter Knight, John Boscow, James Hallwoodo J. P. Welsby, Henry Lloyd, Wm. Co3k, John Hewitt, and John Clark.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
TIIIIIMIDAY.—Before his Honour Judge Pfoulkes. CAUSE LIST.—The cause list contained-1 adjourned plaint, 2 default summonses, 197 original plaints, and 41 judgment summonses.

_ . A NON-SIIIT.-James Froggatt, slotter, Vulcan, New- ton, was sued by Richard and Edward Bailey, of Earl. town, executors of the late George Bailey, for the pay- ment of £4 ss. 6d., arrears of rent. The plaintiffs were represented by Mr. H. .1. Longton, and the defendant by Mr. P. Davies. It was stated on behalf of the plaintiffs, that when the defendant left a house, belonging to them, there was a certain sum of rent in arrears. At the suggestion of an agent of the plaintiffs, they handed over a sewing machine as security for the repayment of the debt. It was, however, contended that this machine was not handed over in full discharge of the debt. For, the defence, evidence was given to show that the mac- hine was worth £4 10s. or £4 15s. at the time of the transfer. His Honour said that until the security was given up the plaintiffs had no right of action, and he therefore, nonsuited the plaintiffs.

A NOTHRA WATCH TRANSACTION— Two Earlestown colliers, named James Stanley and Charle3 Lowe were sued by Henry Wolfe, of Manchester, for £5 83., the bal- ance of the price of a watch, purchased by Stanley. It appeared from the evidence that Stanley purchased the watch. He was a lodger at the time with Lowe, and the latter, as a friendly action, signed the contract for the purchase along with Stanley and thus became equal- ly responsible for the payment. Stanley had paid £1 of the purchase money but, it appeared, bad declined to pay any more, and it was said that the watch was in pawn at Wigan. Stamley did not appear, but it was said that he still worked in the same pit as Lowe, al- though not now lodging with the latter. His Honour said he was sorry for Lowe who had acted foolishly in signing the paper, but he was afraid he must make an order against him. He found, however, that only £2 ss. had fallen due on the agreement to pay ss. a fortnight for the watch, and he would make am order to that effect, 10s. a month to be raid. Lowe must see Stanley and try to make him pay.

div.head: NEW BATHS FOR WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE NEW BATHS FOR WARRINGTON.

It would be seen from our report of the Town Council last week, that the long-talked of scheme fcr improving the iocal baths has at last tel.-en a tdngible shape. Pans have been prepared by Mr. Longdin, the borough surveyor, and accepted by the Town Council, subject to future consideration, when detailed estimeteg as to costs are submitted. The proposals of the Baths Committee, as they stand, provide for a very considerable reconstroc- tion and enlargement of the existing baths. Those who are at all familiar with the interior arrange- ments of the somewhat dingy and certainly " un- pretentious" building in Legli-st., will know that along the frontage to Legh-et. there are at present a number of private baths, while behind these there are " first- class " and "second-class" swimming bath;. Beyond making the much-needed minor improvements and embellishments, it is not proposed to inter- fere very much with this structural arrangement. The present first-class bath will, howevei, he trans- formed into a second-class bath, 39 feet by 25 feet, white what is now spoken of as the " secend-class" bath—and which is 39 feet by 25 feet—will be set apart entirely for the use of ladies. The proposed first-class bath will be an entirely new structure, 112 feet in length by 62 feet in breadth, and it will be erected at the rear and separate from the existing buildings. me new swimming bath will be 80 feet in length and 39 feet in width. Around the sides there will be dressing boxes, soap, and shower baths, and above these there will be a gallery. The new building extends to the full limits of the land at the dis- posal of the Corporation, and the reason for keeping it apart from the old structure is that, in ease of future enlargements, there may be room between the two for more private baths, sr Turkish haths, era new entrance from Bath-st., as the occasion may require. The scheme, in fact, is not intended as a final one, and in preparing his planq the borough surveyor has kept in mind tiler probability of still further extensions later on. So far as the bath-keeper's house, the engine shed, &c., is con- corned there will not at present be any material altera- tion.

div.head: CRUEL FRAUDS ON JEWESSES
div.p: CRUEL FRAUDS ON JEWESSES

At the Thames Police Court on Thursday, a young Jewess applied for a warrant against a man whom she alleged had gone through a mock inarrage with her and robbed her. The police were informed that the same man had obtained money from eight other Jewesses in a similar manner. The magistrate instructed the police to obtain further evidence.

Catholics THE Right Rev. ).J/GET, the and Catholic Bishop of Shrewsbury, Education, paid a visit to Runcorn, on Sun- day, and delivered an important address, which was directed, in the main, to the question of educa- tion. Like other Roman Catholics, he has no sym- pathy with the spread of Board Schools; and I spoke of it as an alarming fact that 1,100 voluntary schools had been handed over to School Boards. But why alarming ? Surely the managers wile thus surrendered their duties and responsibi- lities knew what they were about,and foresaw that children under the new conditions would receive better tuition, in better schools,than under the old conditions. The State pays for secular education and secular education alone; and it is not W be gainsaid that this education is given in Board Schools under conditions as to health, comfort, and decency which are, as a rule, far superior to those obtaining in Voluntary Schools. There is need therefore for rejoicing rather than alarm at the change which is taking place. It is an evolution- ary process in which not only the fittest but the best survives. The Bishop's chief concern, of course, is that denominational education is losing ground. He said : Lit them bear in mind that any education built Iwithout the foundation of religion was as a how" built on sand. Somebody had well described secular education as sharpening the intellect to do evil. There was no education of the heart and will to do what was right, but there was an education of the intellect, to quicken it in carrying out its desigs, which often meant sharpening the intellect to do evil. They need only read the newspapers to see. what somebody had well called the enormous amount of educated crime existent in this countrl —crime tnat could not be without a sharpening of the intellect, such as forgery and dishonesty. The Bishop's theory is stated clearly enough; but it is unfortunate for his theory that the facts are against it. If he will look up the annual returns,ho will find that,with the growth of secular education under the direction of the State, there has been a considerable falling off in crimes which as• associated with intelligence, namely, forgery and offences against the currency laws, while as to crime as a whole the diminution is remarkable..lia 1869—the year before the Education Act we° passed—the number of persons in England and Wales sentenced to transportation and penal Ben" tude was 2,013 out of a population of 22,223,000' In 1889, after twenty years' experience of the AC' the number of criminals of this class was reduced to 921,while the population had risen to 29,000,000' Perhaps it will be said that there is less inclination than of yore on the part of judges to sentence roe° to penal servitude. Let us turn then to " ofleeee6 tried on indictment." In 1869 the number of Per* sons committed to prison under this head Was 12,002; in 1889, the number had fallen to 7,857 P notwithstanding a growth of over 25 per cent. iu the population. Facts like these tell a pleasing tale; a tale of progress; a tale of the blessings °f National Education. We are on the right track, and must continue on the track. Free Education we must have; but so far as the State is concern it must be as it has been—there must be no State payment for sectarian teaching. Why shoud schoolmaster be called upon to do the wo h priest or clergyman ? At the cobbler stick tois tr last. THE Tories are bewildered by the The By-Election staggering blows they have s.re- ceived in the recent by-elections. Usually they are disposed to say these contests are of no importance; but, in the belief that Free Education would serve them a good turn, they had actually begun to think of an appeal to the country. That is " off " novr, when, as the "Morning Post" admits, the Liberals have at Harborough " accomplished the rare feat of beat- ing their own record of 1885." Even the "Times " 14aYs the beating is "undeniably bad," and that, too, "upon an unusually heavy poll." The" Stan- dard" speaks of "a falling off in the Unionist strength such as no possible explanation can allow na to regard without anxiety." It is only fair to the Tory organ to say that it is consistent in still oPposing Free Education, and that it is at least Justified in urging that the bribe has not succeeded in bribing anyone. The agricultural voter knows that Free Education must come soon whichever Party is in power; and it would seem that he is sufficiently observant to perceive that the Tories have nothing else to offer. As Sir WILLIAM HAR- QOURT put the matter at Newton Abbot, on Monday:— The Unionists have damped off the farmers and the clergy, and the great cry of free education, so far from doing them any good, had done them harm with their friends. But that was no reason why the Liberals should not pin them to it. The real truth was that the Tories were not the fathers of free education; they were the step-fathers (laughter). and the Liberals must look after the bringing up of that child. They must have no baby farming of free education. (Laughter.) If the State was to pay for education, then the public must have the control of it. Summing up the results of the by-elections, Sir WILLIAM said : The gain made by the Liberals since 1886 was at least 20 per cent., and if at the general election there was anything like the result which they had had upon the eighty or ninety seats which had been vacated, the Liberal party would have a niajority in the next Parliament as great as that 'which the Unionists had in 1886. But it was Rot only the seats. At Harbor°, the Liberal gain was 1,400 Totes, and the Tory loss was 200; and then in Seutk Dorset, the Liberal gain was 758 'votes, and the Conservative loss was 193. In Stow- market, there was a Liberal gain of 983, while the Unionist gain was 226. (Cheers.) It comesito this, that the country has had a long spell of Tory rule, and the usual thing has hap- Penedo—it is tired of it. There has been plenty in the way of promise, but very little performance. Ireland was to have local self-government "straight off the reel," but, after over four years of wait- ing, the subject is coolly ignored. Even Sir GILBERT GREENALL talked of autonomy for the lister isle, but now he never mentions it; he never names the word. The only thing the Government can be depended upon to do, is to back up brewers and cling to the Treasury benches They have been twice beaten on the question of compensation, and yet they still harp upon it. Oil, that they would make it a plank in their elec- tion platform! Their beating would he a big one, 4nd they would thoroughly deserve it.
A week ago we could all say with Holiday GOLDSMITH—" But winter linger-

Thoughts. ing chills the lap of May." Since then it has been much different and much better. There have been freshening showers followed by days of sunshine; and the hedgerows, waiting for the word,have burst into leaf, effecting a transformation scene of the most brilliant kind. Already the peo- ple who complained about the cold have exclaimed How warm it is I" and there are some who have begun to think the time is approaching when, as LAMB once said, it would be nice to take off one's skin and flesh and sit in one's bones. "The bee, the bird, and butterfly are on their lightest wing"; and if man were as wise as he pretends to be, he, too, would be "on the wing." We have always had a sneaking regard for the lazy, loafing fellow who Worked in winter only, and went on the tramp a-bogging as soon as he could cover two daisies with °tie foot. Perhaps it is unjust to speak of him as lazy, for it may simply be that he had more of the Poet's feeling and tender susceptibility than ordin- ary mortals. As EMERSON has it— Alive to every influence Of landscape, or of sky, And tender to the spirit-touch Of man's or maiden's eye.

It Certainly seems wrong to be moiling in offices tad stewing in factories and at forges on a bright -"AY day, when "the lark is aloft on the fetterless wing," and when sun, and air, and sky and every green and blossoming thing unite in making a Para- dise of this world of ours. Broad, too, are the ways to the Paradise; for every highway that leads from tile town loads to it, and yet how few there be that tied it I Oh, to think of the millions of ferns and ficlvers, and the acres of fruit blossom, that are at this moment baring their beauty to the wanton Wind, and to know that to ninety-nine out of "ery hundred of the denizens of cities their sweet- lees will be wasted on the desert air! Yes, there is something wrong somewhere when such things can he. It is a poor sort of civilisation Which results in masses of mankind herding to- gether in stifling courts and close-packed dens, While birds are singing and flowers are blooming, and they hear and see them not. Will the time sver come when the labourer shall of his own free will be able to say—" The day is too fine-to Work; it shall be as a holy day ;it shall be sacred to enjoyment." It is to be hoped so, and that" St. Monday" will be devoted to recreation, not disipa- tion—to something which will strengthen and purify heart and body. and brain. It is Whitsun- tide, and that means a holiday, however brief. Civilisation must at least be credited with the means of rapid transit; so that within an hour or two of leaving the smoky town it is possible to get Where fresh breezes blow by mountain, or lake, or There is plenty of choice ; " the readiness is

div.head: "TOTTCII AND GO."
div.p: "TOTTCII AND GO."
"Across the Atlantic" is the title of an interest- ing descriptive article. It has been specially written for the Evatniner by a Warrington " Townsman," and will be found on our second page.

There is a musical critic at Namur who doesn't know everything, lie recently wrote of "a sym- phony in C minor by Von Beethoven, of a bizarre and rambling character, but dominated by a reminiscent theme." It is not unlikely that the critic will have become a" rambling character" ere this, having got marching orders.

A story is told of an Irishman, who, on receiving a windfall, set up a library, amongst other things, and took to reading. He had not been at it long before helwrote to his bookseller to say he liked some of the " poethry books" very well, especially those wri ttcn by "Mr. Shakespeare" and " Mr. Miltoii." If those " gintleman " wrote any mole works, would he p! ease to send them. Pat, it must be owned, stands better than the continental critic; for, if his know- ladge was 'at fault, his judgment was right.

The member for Warrington completed his gbh year on Monday; and a contemporary, thinking of Sir Gilbert Greenall as a brewer, regards his longe- vity as a testimony to Warrington ale. But, if report speaks truly, it is no testimony at all. On the contrary, ho is an abstemious man. He has al- lowed other people to do the hard drinking; and in this way hs has filled his pockets, while the drinkers have emptied theirs.

By a printer's error in the report, last week, of the proceedings of the Warrington Town Council, the total of the rates collected was. referred to as £7,613, when it should have been £17,613. The fact that the total of the uncollected rates was £3 25., only, speaks volumes for Mr. Fairhurst and Mr. Woodcock, as collectors. It shows how thoroughly the work has been don 3 ; and it is an indication,too, of the financially healthy condition of the town.

Mr. Brunner is to he complimented on the skill and perseverance he is showing in pilotin,, the Brine Pumping (Compens4tion for Subsid- ence) Bill through the Rouse of Commons. He was successful, on Tuesday, in getting the measure re- ported as amend2d. so that it is in a fair way for becoming law. His action is all the more credit- able to him because he is amongst those who will be largely called upon to pay compensation.

Mr. Cuningham Graham, -M.P., seems to be like the celebrated Irishman—" agin the Govern- ment" wherever he may be. He has been in gaol in England—for resisting the police, and he has been expelled from Portugal, and from France for attacking the authorities. Why not try Russia next? But no; perhaps the Bear would pat his paw on him; he might be marched to Siberia, in- stead of being sent back to his mother.

The influenza epidemic is, directly and in- directly, the cause of a large increase of the death rate. It has risen in Warrington to a rate of over 30 per 1,000; but at Chesterfield, and some other places, it is us high as 60 per 1,000. As the weather continues to be very changeable, people cannot be too careful as to their clothing. It ,is not safe to "cast off" until the season is further advanced.

The Servians got rid of. deir King by giving him "cash down," and promises for the future; but the Queen is not so easily disp.)sed of. She has been told that her room is preferred to her company, and that, if she declines to leave the country, recourse will be had to forcible measnres. She had better retire. "Chucking out" comports better with Cuningham Graham than Queen Nathan°.

What a revelation of Muscovite villainy is that which comes from Warsaw! The police visiting student's quarters and taking with them seditious proclamations in order to bring back something which they have "found." Russia is indeed a most unhappy land—unhappy alike for Czar and citizen. It is certain, alas, that many an old and ninny a young head has been laid low through lying evi- dence. Reflecting on these things, who is there that does not say—" England with all thy faults, I love thee still."

The Tories and Mr. Parnell are hoh-nobbing together over the Irish Land Bill. Both parties distrust each other; but they laavo this in common —they desire to damage the Liberals as much as they can. What they do in the way of playing into each others' hands doesn't much matter. Mr. Parnell is on the inclined plane which leads to political perdition; and he is slipping down steadily but surely. It may not be pleasant to him ; but the way of the transgressor was alwnys hard.

Mr. Chamberlain seems disposed to persevere with his scheme of National Insurance against old age. His idea is that there should be State assist- ance, and that the benefits should come in force at the age of 65. This is in a line with the German pinn ; and there is reason to believe that it will be found workable. Details can, however, be moth- fled; the chief thing is to determine on the princi- Pe. It is to be hoped Mr. Chamberlain will keep his hand to the new plough; he will be better em- ployed than in beating time.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, a baker named John Roberts, was fined 20s. and costs for having his bakehouse in an unsanitary condition. Curiously enough, it transpired that, in the firat instance, the case had been considered by the Sanitary Committee "who decided to fine the defendant £2 25." But whence comes the authority for this new court? And what is done with the money, when offenders meet this extra- ordinary levy? The system is, on the face of it. a had one. If people break the law, let them he dealt with publicly, and by a legitimate authority.

At the meeting of the Dareshury Highway Board, on Thursday, Mr. Hall called attention to what looks like an impudent attempt to deprive the public of a right of road near the Waterworks. When a "No Road" sign is put up, and the path ploughed up, it is something more than what Mr. Burgess described as an intimation that the road is " not repairable by the public." It can- not be too well known that an ancient footpath, or bridle way, cannot be closed except by order at Quarter Sessions, after due notice has been given, and after objections, if any, have been considered. Meantime it is the duty of the Highway Board' to see that the path is properly kept, and a path can- not be said to be properly kept which is ploughed up.

WIITIIINTIDB EXCURSIONS. It will be seen from our advertising columns that plenty of facilities are offered for getting to the Isle of Man during Whitsuntide. There is the short sea route from Barrow, and there are extra boats from Liverpool. The Isle of Man Steam Packet Company have made their usual special arrange- ments for Whit week in view of the expected increase in the ordinary traffic. At present the steamers sail daily from Liverpool at 11.30 a.m., and from Douglas at 9 a.m., a boat also leaving Liver- pool at 5 p.m. on Saturdays, and returning from the island at 1 a.m. on Mondays. From May 15th to 132 r d an additional steamer will leave the Mersey at 2 p.m..and from May 16th to the 25th.another extra boat will leave Douglas at 4 p.m. SIIMM=Ft FASHIONS now Showing at J. A. W. A receiv- ing order was made on the debtor's own petition. The liabilities amounted to £lO9 16s. 7d., and the assets, after deducting preferential claims .E 9 8s 6d,leaving a deficiency of .£lOO Bs. hi. In answer to the assis- tant official receiver (Mr. Potter) the bankrupt said that the causes of his insolvency were bad traile,bad debts, competition and household expenses. Ile had been aware of his insolvency for at least ten years, and the whole of the debts scheduled had been con- tracted with a knowledge of his insolvency. his - were 30s. a week. lie had had no idea of profit or losses of his shop had been. LOCAL NEWS.
TRIY_ITY WESLEYAN CHAPEL, FULTON.
The annual sermons in aid of the choir funds were preached on Sunday by the Rev. J. Pulford Williams, of Runcorn. There were good congregations. HOLY TRINITY CHURCH BAND OF HOPR, RUNCORN.

The annual tea party and concert were held on Mon- day evening, when the young pe•ple went through an attractive programme with much credit. The Rev. Dr. Preston presided, and distributed the prizes to those who had been regular in their attendance at the weekly meetings. INFLUENZA AT RUNCORN AND WIDNES. '

This disease is very prevalent in both these towns, and in a number of cases the attack is of a verysevere type. Although it is not named as one of those infec- tious diseases which have to b 3 notified to the Local Sanitary Authority, medical men are generally agreed that it is infectious. SUDDEN DEATHS.

Mrs. Richardson, of Devonshire:square, was found dead on the hearthrug, at her house, on Thursday morning. The deceased, who had carried on the busi- ness of a butcher since the death of her husband, three months ago, had been ailing for soino time, and the doc- tor having granted a certificate, the coronet considers an inquest unnecessary.

div.head: SACRRD CONCERT AT It UNCOUN
div.p: SACRRD CONCERT AT It UNCOUN

I a connection with the Conway Brass Band and the Band of Earl of Chesters Mlles (Runcorn), a sacred con- cert will be given in Runcorn Public Hall, to-morrow (Sunday) evening. An interesting and suitable pro- gramme has been arranged, able artistes have been engaged and those who take advantage of this opportu- nity, will no doubt spend a pleasant evening.

div.head: PRIBLITIVH METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL. RUNCORN. –
div.p: PRIBLITIVH METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL. RUNCORN. -

The anniversary of this school was celebnced on t'ua- day last when special services were held in Green- way-road chapel. The Rev. F. N. Shimmin was the preacher, and he delivered eloquent discourses to large congregations. The musical portion of the celebration, was a pleasing feature. Tilt Rev. J. Pulford Presbyterian minister, occupied the pulpit in the after- noon. The collections raalised a good suns.

div.head: CLERK TO TRH WIDNES LOC tL BOARD.
div.p: A CLERK TO TRH WIDNES LOC tL BOARD.

For the pos tion of clerk in the accountant's office at Widnes Town Hall, the Finance Coinmittee received 21 applications, and the following were selected to appear before the Committee—Mr. Alban Dennett (Appleton), Mr. A. T. Kyle (Ditton), and Robert W. Ruslitoa (ltun- corn). After interviewing the candidates the Commit- tee unanimously recommended Mr. Dennett for the post which is worth 30s. a week. The Local Board ratified the appciatmont on Tuesday. MURDEROUS ASSAULT By POURS AT WIDNES. _ •

At Widnes Police Court on Monday, two Poles named Martin Miller and Frank Miller, were brought up on re- mand charged with having unlawfully wounded Domi- nic Dovilch, on the the 25th April. It was alleged that on that night prosecutor was walking down Barn-st., when the prisoner Frank struck him on the head with a stone and Martin struck him with a glass bottle.—Dr. Hutchinson said there were three serious wounds and for some days the man's: life was in danger. Mr. Knowles called witnesses to prove an alibi. Thil prisoners were committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. RUNCORN_ BURIAL BatRD. The monthly meeting of this Board was fixed for Wednesday last, but there was not a quorum of mem- bers present, and no business could be transacted. The secretary's report stated that the interinents for twelve months, ending March 25th, 1891, numbered;49l, correa- pondina period last year, 408 ; increase 83. The fees re- ceived for twelve months, to March 25th, £449 Os. 4d. ; last year, £377 17s. ; increase £7l 93. 4d. The number of interments since the Cemetery was openei, on the let March, 1830, is 9,083; namely, Church, 3,681 ; Dissen- ters, 4,656; Roman Catholics, 726. The interments for one month, ending April 25th, 34; corresponding period last year, 41 ; decrease,7 ; fees reed i ved the same period, 33 2s. ; last year, £36 7s. ; decrease £3 ss.

div.head: BRUTAL YOUTH AT WIDNES,
div.p: A BRUTAL YOUTH AT WIDNES,

A youth named John McCabe, of Alidwood-street, was brought before the Widnes Bench of magistrates, on Thursday, to answer a charge of assaulting his brother and sister Henry and Rose Ann McCabe on the eleventh inst. It was alleged that the prisoner without any pro- vocation struck his sister a number of heavy blows on the face with his fist, and threanned to kill her. When he received the summons for that offence the prisoner "pounced upon" his brother and knocked him senseless with wstone he held in his hand. He also kicked him, and gave him two black eyes.—lnspector Keighley said the woman's face was in a dreadful state when he saw hen—The prisoner, who had been 13 times previously convicted, was sent to gaol for one mouth on each charge. BREAKING A CONSTABLES LEG AT RUNCORN. div.head: BUNCOGN BOWLING CLUB.
div.p: BUNCOGN BOWLING CLUB.

There is every prospect of this club, which has its headquarters at the Bridge Hotel, having a successful season. Mr. T. C. Cooper is the president. Mr. S. Yar- wood the vice-president, and Mr. James Woods the secre- tary. and the ordinary members number over 100. The green is in splendid condition, the proprietor had spared neither money nor labour in repairing the turf, and the improvement effected since last autumn is very great. The opening game was played on Wednesday, when a handicap main confined to members tookiplace. Mr. Woods added £2 to the entrance foes and the prizes were well worth competing for. Mr. W. White succeeded in carrying off the first prize. Mr. S. Johnson the second, and Mr. J. Woods the third. The other prize winners were Messrs. W. Anderton. John Stevenson, Thomas Dean, T. Woods, -James Pricli, H. Millar, John Forster, and George Harrison. FUNERAL OF MRS. JOHN HAZLIHURST.

The remains of Mrs. John llazlaliurst-, of lloche House, High-st., were interred at Runcorn Cornetery,on Wednes- day at noon. The Committee of the House of Commons on the Bill of the London and North-Western Railway for running powers over he Wrexham, Mold, and Con- nail's Quay line, on Tuesday, decided that the pre- amble, so far as the running powers were concerned was not proved. The Committee hoped that the proposed junction at Hope would be made by the Sheffield Company. LAWN MowEns.—Garland, 51. Bridge-st., Warrin;ton. and at Barlestown.—Advt.

"•OOrkBIONAL COURT. At this Court, on Thursday, before Mr. John Itylands, John Dolan, carter, from Widnes, was charged with being drunk while in charge of a horse and cart at Sankey on the 13th inst., and was fined 2s. fid and cogs.
SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-et.. Warrington.—Advt.
DR. MACKENNAL AND HIS CONGREGATION.

Dr. Mackennal, whose name has been associated with the secretaryship otthe Congregational Union, has intimated that it is not bis intention to break his pastoral relations with the Bowdon Downs Congregational Church. END OF TIIE PAINTERS' STRIKE AT LF/GII.

The painters' strike at Leigh has now been settled after lasting for upwards of a week. The men originally demanded an advance of wages from sevenpence to eightpence per hour, but perceiving that the masters were unanimously against this they agreed to accept sevenrence halfpenny. The masters at first refused to Rive more than seven- pence farthing, but have nft decided to give seven- pence halfpenny, and the strike is therefore ended.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.

On the 27th ult., John Heath, whilst engaged in shunting operations in the yard of Messrs. Hall Brothers, and Shaw, was knocked down by a wagon, and the wheels passed over his left leg. He was at once convey9d to the Accident Hospital where it was found necessary to amputate the injured limb. He died on Wednesday last. An inquest was held at the Accident Hospital, on Fri- day afternoon,before Mr. Brighouse, eountly coroner, when a verdict of " Accidental death was re- turned.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF A YOUTiI AT WIDNES.,
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF A YOUTiI AT WIDNES.,

Walter William Boast, 15 years of age, son of a widow named Margaret Boast, who lodges at 8, St Mary-st., died suddenly at half-past five yestarday morning. The youth had been in delicate health for several years and had ben attended by Dr. Cooper', for lumps in his neck. On Wednesday he complained of pains in his side, which he said had been caused by falling into a shed near his home. He lay on. the sofa the whole of Thursday, and dur- ing the night was very restless. He died at half- past five.

div.head: SINDOW /T S. HILIMS.
div.p: SINDOW /T S. HILIMS.

Sandow, the noted srong man,visited St. Helens on Thursday night and attended an assault-at-arms in the Young Men's Christian Association Gymnasium as a complimentary benefit to Mr. .J. H. Harrison, instructor, who is leaving the town. There was a large attendance and Col. W. W. Pilkington pre- sided. Various gymnastic exercises were given by the leaders and members, and Mr. W. H. Pollitt won a silver meaal in a single stick contest. Sandow's feats consisted of lifting Weights varying from 56 lbs. to 280 lbs. and his p.:rformance was loudly cheered. Mr. Harrison was presented with a gold medal by the members in recognition of his services.

div.head: WIOIN MYSTERY.
div.p: A WIOIN MYSTERY.

On Wednesday a man was fishing in a pond in a field off Poolstock-lane, Pemberton, Wigan, when he saw something in the water about a yard from the side. Ile got it out and found it to be:a box containing the remains of a male Child, which had the appearance of having been in the water a con- siderable time. The box was tied round with a strap, and it wee weighed down with a stone. The county police are making inquiries into the ratter. Yesterday Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at Pemberton, Wigan, on the body of the unknown child. A verdict that the child was still born, and that there was no evidence to show how it got into the pond was returned. 'SUMMBH FASHIONS now showing at J. & W. Zurroar's Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: " GASSED " TO DEATH.
div.p: " GASSED " TO DEATH.

John Doolin, of 10, Helsby-st., Sutton, S. 'Helens, died on Wednesday night from the effects of .bring "gassed" whilst following his employment as a chemical labourer at Bold Manure Works. On Tues- day forenoon, the deceased and two men named John Joseph Moran and William Myers wore work- ing at the vitriol chambers when the deceased sud- denly commenced to cough violently, and he told his companions that he was "gassed" by the fumes from the vitriol. He was taken home, where he made a similar statement to his wile, and Dr. Casey was called in. Notwithstanding every attention, the man rapidly grew worse, and expired as stated. SINGULAR CLAIM FOR A WIFE'S M.AINTENANCB.

At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Judge Shand, Thomas Bond, of Aston-inMakerfeld, sought to recover the sum of .E 5 ss. from John Saxon, glass polisher, Parr, for 13 weeks' maintenance of the defendant's wife. The parties had not long been married when the defendant's wife left him in consequence of his cruel treatment. She stayed at the plaintiff's house and said her hus- band would pay for her maintenance. The defence was that there was no justification for the . defend- ant's wifo,to go.away, but the judge held that the husband behaved with such cruelty as to render it unsafe for his wife to live with him. Ile therefore gave judgment for the plaintiff._ .

SUDDEN DIIATH AT THE VULCAN.

On Sunday night, a man named Henry Mee, of 474, Vulcan Brow, Wargrave, who was employed as a boiler maker, by the Vulcan Foundry Company, died very suddenly at his residence. The deceased was seen at the Wargrave Inn at half-past nine, at which time he left there to go home. His wife who had been on a visit to Warrington since Saturday at noun, returned home at half-past ten on. Sunday night, anti on going into the kitchen found her husband on his knees with his head on the sofa,quite dead. The body was still warm and he could not have been dead many minutes. The matter was reported to the police, but as the deceased had been under the care of Dr. Mouncey for a couple of months, the coroner did not consider it necessary to hold an inquest, death being due to heart disease.

PRESCOT AGRICULTURAL SCCIRTY. The seventh annual show in connection iwith the Prescot and District Agricultural Society was held, by the permission of Lord Derby, in Knowsley Park, Prescot, on Thursday afternoon. The arrangements were carried out by an energetic conim ittee,of which Lord Lionel Cecil was president, and Mr. E. Range secretary, the stewards for the various classes being Messrs. T. Dennett and 11. Williami (cattle), O. Silcock and A. T. Johnson (horses), W. Goldsworth and J. Cop* (dogs), J. Sumner (poul- try), J. Whittaker (pigeons), A. E. Bennett (rab- bits), and W. 1106(111 (pigs). For the first time in the history of the society, it was decided to make , the exhibition of an open chiracter, and the new depart are proved a great success. The total num- ber of entries was 457, a number exceeding last year's entries by no less than 350. The prize money was also increased from £lOO to £t4lo, and in many of the classes there was a keen competi- tion. The judges were as follows :—Cattle. Messrs. It. B. Smith (Bangor), and J. Hanson (Gisburne) ; light horses and turnouts, Messrs. A. R. Gladstone (Roby) and L. Pilkington (Roby) ; heavy horses , Mr. W. Balharry. Ilaydock ; dogs, Mr. G. Sheffield : pigs. Mr. C. E. Duckering, Kirkton Lind- say. Lincolnshire ; poultry, Mr. W. Birch. Sefton; pigeons. Mr. A. Edwardson, Birkenhead; and rab- bits, Mr. T. B. Mason. Bradford. During the after- noon, the park was visited by some thousands of persons, and the band of the Ist L.R.V. (Liverpool) rendered selections of music. SIIIOOIII FASHIONS now Showing at J. & W. Durrox'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. TEE LANCASIIIRR HUZZARS.

This fine body of yeomanry assembled at Ormsl kirk on Saturday, and rode to Soutt.port for their annual week's training, their arrival, about • three o'clock in the afternoon, drawing large crowds into the streets. Headquarters are as usual. at the Victoria Hotel. Lieutenant-Colonel Lord Gerard is in command,in the absence of Colonel Lord Lathom. who is detained in London on account of his duties as Lord Chamberlain: and the other officers are Major Walmesley. Major Hopwood, Captain and Adjutant Willoughby, Captain Legh, M.P., Lieuten- ant T. C. Edwards-Moss, M.P., Lieutenant Sir Humphrey de Trafford, Lieutenant W. Lee Pilking- ton, Lieutenant Earle,' Lieutenant M'Corquodale, Lieutenant Viscount Molyneux, LiEutenant Ernest Sinclair Pilkington, Surgeon Damar Harrison. Vet. Surgeon W. G. Dixon. Regimental Sergeant-Major Easthain, and 220 troopers, including the. band, which is un •er the leadership of Bandmaster Batlek. On Sunday morning, in splendid weather, a church parade vra.s held, all the officers and men being present. Headed by the band, the Huzzars marched by way of the promenade and Seabank- road (where . Lieut-Colonel Lord Gerard, Major Walmsley, Sir Humphrey de Trafford. about 20 troopers fell out and attended Mass at St. Marie's Roman Catholic Church) to Holy Trinity. After service the Huzzars marched back to the Victoria ' Ho` ,el where they were dismissed in presence of a 'large crowd. The programme for the week included a sword competition on Wednesday, a horse compe- tition on Thursday, tile review on Friday morning by General Drury Lowe, late of the 17th Lancers , and one of the Balaclava heroes, and the military 'tournament in the aftn-noon, and the training to be brought to a close on Saturday.
