div.head: WIDNES LOCAL -BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL -BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town hail on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage seconded, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Mc6srs. Wrigt.t, Brown, Midwood, Cook, Tilley, Reyes, Saddler, Oppen.heim (clerk), Hoyle (a6Bistaut), Sinclair. (surveyor) and Carr (engineer.)

div.head: DEATH OF MR. HARTLEY.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. HARTLEY.

The Chairman referred to the sad and sudden death of Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Prescot Mon, of which information had been received that morning. The Board had ssauy dealings with Mr. Hartley, and had always found him to be an able, energetic, and efficient servant; and a man who did his duty according' to his ideas. They must all regret the sudden loss which the commu- nity had sustained.
TUE RAINEILL SEWAGE F'Aint

Mr. Wright reported that the deputation .appointed by the Board had attended the Local Government Inquiry .on this matter,- and the Chairman of the Committee:hay- iag the managetnent of the farm - had promised that the new works should he thoroughly carried out ; and the irrigating channels were repaired and more land utilized. The Inspector informed them that it he sew- age were not properly treated the Local Board had power to apply for an injunction.
PROPOSED ROADWAY ACROSS TME MERSEY.

The following letter was read from Mr. B. Marshall, secretary to the Runcorn Board of Improvement Com- missioners I am desired by my Board to say that for sometime they have thought it desirable that communica- tions should be opened with the County Councils of Lancashire and Cheshire with a view to inducing them to construct a bridge across the Mersey suitable for vehicles. Will you kindly say if your Board is disposed to receive a deputation from my Board for the purpose of conferring on the desirability of approaching our res- pective County Councils with respect to this matter :" The Chairman said the Runcorn Commissioners had acted very courteously, and he suggested that the Board should hold a special meeting to receive the deputation. —On the motion of Mr. Brown, seconded by Mr. Cook, it wad resolved to hold a special meeting at 12 noon on Tuesday next.

div.head: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION
div.p: TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION

Mr. Lloyd Evans wrote as follows from the County Offices, Preston: Having been instructed by the Technical Instruction Committee appointed by the Lan- cashire County Council to carry out " The Local Taxation (Customs and Excise) Act, 1890, to visit and report on your application for a grant, I beg to notify you that I intend being at Widnes Town Hall on Thursday, the 14th of May from 12 to 1, when I hope I can meet you or someone able to give me all the local information I may require "—The Clerk was instructed to request the attendance of the sub-committee, which consists of Messrs. T. Snape, E. K. Muspratt, Carey, Mornsnn, Mid- wood, and Dr. O'Keeffe.

div.head: CODIPLAINT
div.p: A CODIPLAINT
Mr. J. 0. Rhodes, of 5 Mersey-road, Viridnes, com- plained that the nightsoil men had removed a quantity of bricks from his yard, and asked the Board for redress.
THE MOSS AN SEWER DISPUTE.

The Clerk read a letter from Messrs. S. Cowburn and Sons, contractors, who signified their acceptance of the Board's offer of £550 in settlement of their Moss Bank sewer account. They could not for one moment bring their minds to think that the Board had sustained any damages beyond perhaps a few slight road repairs over lines of sewers which might naturally be expected to arise where sewers were laid at such depths and in similar strata as those laid by them.—Mr. Sadler said they had arrived at the end of a very disagreeable business. He thought that the public ought to know that Messrs. Cowburn having settled the matter on these terms was a complete vindication of the action of the Highway Com- mittee eighteen months ago. With regard to the latter part of the letter, the sewer on the marsh had collapsed, and in repairing it they found that the specification had never been adhered to at all. He moved that a cheque be drawn for the account.—Dr. O'Keeffe seconded the motion, which was carried.

div.head: GAS AND WATHR.
div.p: GAS AND WATHR.

The Gas and Water Committee recammendel that the amended tender of Mr. Chapman, contractor, to mac e two bore holes at Netherley, for £1,336 Ids., be accepted.—The Engineer reported that the contractors' workmen arrived at Netherley on the 27th ult., and the first bore hole had now been sunk to a depth of ten feet. The estimated quantity of coal required for the coming year was 14,000 tons. The mean rainfall for the month had been 1.73 inches. The water in stock on April 29th was 8,04,726 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 18.17 candles. The Com- mittee recommended that, subject to satisfactory in- quiries being made, the members of the Fire Brigade be insured in the Imperial Union Accident Assurance Co., Ldt., against accidents sustained in the execution of their duties—the officers at a premium of .6s. Bd. per annum and the men at a premium of 4s. per annum.— The Engineer reported that the Liverpool Corporation were laying down mains and services to profit in Gerrard's Jane and Lydiate-lane, Halewood, within the Board's limits of supply ; and the clerk was instructed to investi- gate the matter.—Mr. Brown moved the confirmation of the minutes, which were carried without discussion.
HIGHWAY MATTERS.-THE SURVEYOR.

'lhe minutes of the Highway Committee contained a report on the Moss Bank Sewer, the Clerk stating that the matter had remained unsettled in consequence of the solicitors of the late Mr. Bibby having refused to accept the conditions laid down by the Board with respect to the proposed sewer in Tanhouse Lane.—The Surveyor reported that the wall near to Peelhouse•Lane, erected contrary to the byelaws had been removed. It was re- commended that Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co. be allowed to erect a temporary boarded fence on the foot- path in Victoria road, during the building of a new lavatory for the United Alkali Company. An application from Mr. J. S. Sinclair, surveyor to the Board, for an in- crease of salary, was read and considered. It was re- solved that this Committee, being satisfied with the manner in which Mr. Sinclair had discharged the duties of his office since his appointment in May last, recom- mend that his salary be increased as from this date by the sum of £5O per annum. The following plans were approved :—Laboratory, Victoria road, for United Alkali Co., Limited; additions to St. Mary's Schools, Newtown; 3 dwelling-hoses, Frederick-st., for Messrs. Jones, Jones, and Bowden. The Committee disapproved the following plans :—four dwelling-houses, Birchfield-road, for Mr. R. T. Hurst; one shop and three dwelling-houses, Birchfield-road, for G. Pownall ; and two houses and shop, Wid nes-road, for H. O'Donnell. —Mr. Sadler moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. Midwood drew atten- tion to a nuisance at Moorside Terrace, and said the Leigh Estate ought to be made to remedy it.—Mr.Sadler replied that the Committee had the matter in hand.
HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

The Medical Officer reported to the Health Committee that during Anril there were 103 births and 62 deaths being at the respective rates of 39.87 and 24 per 1,000. Thirteen deaths occurred amongst children under one year and 14 between one and five years. Zymotic diseases caused 7 deaths and there Were three inquests Notifica- tions of infectious disease, as follows, had been received: —Enteric fever 2, scarlet fever 3, puerperal fever 3, continued fever 1, erysipelas 2, croup 2, total 12. Dur- ing the month 6 patients had been dismissed from the Accident Hospital and there were still five patients. At the Fever Hospital, one patient had died, three were dis- charged, and there were four still in. Recommended that the tender of Lea and Son, of £75 9s. for painting the Fever Hospital be accepted.—That gowns be obtained for visitors to the Fever Hospital. That the Board advertise for tenders for the supply of provisions to the Accident and Fever Hospitals for a period of 12 months. —Mr. Wright moved and Mr. Tilley seconded the adop- tion of the minutes.—Mr. Haves said he understood there was an epidemic of influenza in the place. Why was it not notified ?—The Clerk : It is not one of the diseases Inentioned in the Act stif Parliament.—Mr. Midwood said £75 was a large amount to spend on beautifying a new building. What were those gowns Wanted for P—Mr. Sadler said the gowns ought to be made in different sizes, or how would he and his friend Mr. Heyes do? (Laugh- ter.)—Mr. Wright said Dr. O'Keeffe could answer better than he as to whether influenza was an infectious disease. —Dr. O'Keeffe : Ask your medical officer of health. Mr. Wright said as to painting the hospital it had not beeii done for four years, and at Warrington the hospital was painted every year. The gowns were reqvired according to the rules of the hospital, and their use was to prevent the spread of infection. There were 96 patients in the hospital last year, and the Committee managed the hospital as economically as they could, but they must either have it efficient or non-efficient.

TIIE FINANCE BUDGET.—irgavy RATE. The minutes of the Finance Committee contained the following under the head of "General District Rate." Estimated expenditure. 1890-91 £13,700 4. id. ; expen- diture 1890-91, £14,213 ss. 4d. ; estimated expenditure, 1891-92 £14,782 19s. 7d. Add balance te ebit of rates account---£14,88 us. 51. Recommended that a General

District Rate of 2s. Bd. per 2, with the usual deductions for land, railways,&c., be laid for the year 1891,92, pay- able by two instalments—the first on date of demand and the other on 30th September next, estimated to pro- duce £14,944, estimated surplus, £62 18s. 7d. Mr. Mid- wood in moving the adoption of the minutes, said last year the expenditure was £423 ever the estimate, made up as follows :—Highway Committee, £4B ; Health, £88; Finance, £307. The excess in the Finance Com- mittee was due to legal expenses entirely. They had estimated that item at £3OO, and it reached £698. They had the Brine Scheme and the Ship Canal to contend with, and the expenses were heavier than as a rule. They would see that in the estimate of the Highway Com- mittee there was an increase of £559, a little over ld. in the and in the estimate of the Health Committee there was an increase of £321. nearly id. in the £, and in the Finance Committee of £ll3, one farthing in the £ ; total increase £993, or a little over 2d. in the £ on the rateable value. He was sorry to have to propoae a rate of 2s. Bd. in the £, being an increase- of 2d., but the ideas of the Highway Committee were some- thing tremendous. It was only right that the ratepayers should know where the bulk of the money went. In tbe Highway department last year there was spent for manual labeur £1,841; this year £2,067; and team 1 labour was also at a much higher figure. There were public improvements that must be done, but the expen- diture of this Committee had increased year after year, and still kept moving on. With respect to the Health Committee the fever hospital was the crown of all. It seemed to him to be the white elephant of the Board. It .cost £1,353 12s. a year to keep that place going. The , Committee asked for £5OO for the maintenance of a place like that, and £lO3 for labourers. He did not know what the labourers had got to do except walk about thega.rden and took at each other. Then there were gardeners, £llO I.os. a year, and the repayments Of principal and interest , amounted to £255 a year. It was high, titne the Health Committee thought of what, they were doing.—Mr.Cook seconded the motion.—Mr. Sadler said if it were consi- dered necessary he would go through the .items of his Committee in detail, and then the Chairman of the Finance Committee would be Male to point out what should be struck out.—Mr. Wright said he should , also be glad if. Mr. Midvrood would show what ; should be curtailed. As the population increased the population would become a more expensive institu- tion and before long an additional building would have to ne erected to make the place efficient.—Mr. Brown said the rate was very excessive and was higher than many of the works could afford, and it was quite time more economy was shown in both departments.—Mr. Midwood said it was no business of his to show the Health and Highway Committees how to spend their money. The assessment had now reached £149,000, and still they required a 25.8 d. rate. There would have to be more economy displayed or there would be more heard about it.—After further discussion, the Chairman said he did not see that they got any nearer, and called for a vote. The minutes were adopted and the vota ' approved.

div.head: INCORPORATION.
div.p: INCORPORATION.

The General Purposes Committee reported that the Clerk to the Board produced and read a letter, dated April 29th, 1891, from the Clerk to the Right Honourable the Lords of Her Majesty's Privy Council, and it was re- commended that the Clerk be instructed to prepare and submit to this . Committee for their approval a draft Charter and scheme in accordance with the terms of such letter, and that provision be made in the latter for the representation of the Corporation on the Governing Body of the Farnworth Grammar School, and also that this Committee be empowered to authorise and take all such proceedings as may be expedient for obtaining a grant of a Charter of Incorporation for the district of Widnes and H. M's. approval of the proposed scheme. The minutes were passed on the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe.

div.head: PRESBYTERIAN CONFERENCE AT RUNCORN
div.p: PRESBYTERIAN CONFERENCE AT RUNCORN

The teachers' association in connection with the Sunday schools of the Liverpool District of the Presbytery held their quarterly conference in St. John's Presbyterian School, Runcorn, on Saturday, About 70 teachers and friends were present and after tea bad been partaken of, the conference was held.—Mr. Daniel Lloyd, of Liverpool, occupied the chair.—Mr. R. H. Thomas (Liverpool) read a paper on the subject selected for discussion, entitled How best to promote temperance principles among the young." The sin of intemperance, he said, was doing more than any other to impede and undo the work of the Sunday school, therefore every means available should be used to combat the foe and to insure the stabi- lity of the work among the young. He believed that total abstinence was the only antidote to drunkenness and he argued that pastors, superintendents, and teachers should set the example to their scholars by being abstainers themselves. A total abstinence society should be appointed and suitable total abstinence books included in the library. The pastor ought to give an address once a quarter, and one Sunday in the year should beset apart for total abstinence. The most effec- tual means to reach the young was through the Band of Hope, and so far as he had been able to observe, the relation between Sunday school and Band of Hope was by no means satisfactory. The school (and the church) should make the Band of Hope an intregal part of itself, and should nourish and cherish it.—A discussion ensued, Messrs. Williams (Garston), William Thomas (Liverpool), 'J. Ellis Jones (Liverpool), Roberts (Liverpool). Bird (Hovlake), R. Baxter (Runcorn), and Rev. J. Pulford Williams speaking on the subject. In the course of the evening Miss S. P. Hayes, Mrs. Temperly, and Miss Outhwlite contributed vocal selections. The customary votes of thanks concluded the proceedings.

div.head: WIDN ES COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WIDN ES COUNTY COURT.
Yesterday, before His Honor Judge Shand. THE LIST comprised 234 original plaints, 5 adkburned summonses, 2 default smmonses, 73 judgment sum- monses, and 11 adjourned cases. _

ADMINISTRATIVE ORDER.—Mr. J. W. Knowles solici- tor, applied for an administrative order on behalf of Peter Fitzsimons, a chemical labcourer, of Ditton. The total amount of his debts was £4B. Mr. F. Poole and Mr. T. J. Peters opposed the application in the interests of several creditors, but after a short hearing. His Honor made the order asked for, the full amount of the liabili- ties to be paid at the rate of 15s. per month. COMPANY PROMOTING AT WIDNES.—J. F. Whittle, commission agent, Vic`oria-road, sued Edward Lloyd Clarke for £36, wages due under an engagement made on the 7th October, 1890.—The plaintiff said the defen- dant was the manager of the Widnes Iron and Chemical Company, and on the 7th October he engaged him as a clerk at 30s. per week. At that time the Company was net formed, and the duties of the plaintiff were to look after the office, and send on time letters to the defen- dant at London. He fulfilled these duties up to three weeks ago, when he was taken ill of influenza. He had received no wages whatever.—The defence set up was that the defendant was not personally liable, but had simply acted on behalf of the directors of the Company which was being formed. The Company had not been formed.—The plaintiff said defendant had made cheques in his own name.—The Judge held that defendant was liable, and gave judgment for £l2. ,No doubt, had the Company been formed, the defendant would have kept to his engagement. The work had only been light, and the plaintiff would be amply compensated at 10s. per week.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. Tnnamsr.—Before Mr. H. Wade-Deacon and Mr. J. fireball. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence a fine of si. and emits was imposed upon each of the following John McLoughlin,fridget Carthy;fleDry Pitt,Henry Andrews, George Hunt, and Mary Crosby. CHIMNIES ON FlRE.—William Houghton, Caroline-st., and Thomas Breen were each fined is. and costs for this offence. BREACHES OR THE PEACE.—Edward Lightfoot, Water- at., John Clarke, Halton View, and Thomas Brown, George-st., were bound over to be of good behaviour for three months fol. creating breaches of the peace.—John ' Saat West-st.,was dealt with in alike manner for assault- ing a youth named William Walton; and Mary Cullen, of Browne-st., was also bound over for assaulting Mary ,Mullarkey. &Hoot. BOARD CASES.—k number of parents were charged with not sending their children regularly to school and the usual fine of ss. was inflicted in each case. r ASSAULT ON THE POLICE.—David Hatton was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assauiting P.C. Worsfold. When taken into custody on the former charge, he violently kicked the officer on the lees. He was fined in a total of 15s. and costs or in default 21 days' hard labour.

div.p: FRODSRAM.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT FIELSBY.-01:1 Tuesday an inquest was held at the Chester Infirmary before Mr. J. Tatlock (city coroner) on the body of Matthew Clark, aged 55, farm labourer, Helsby, who died' at the Infirmary on Sunday, from the effects of an accident. It appeared from the evidence that on 6th 461, Clark was engaged on the farm ot Mrs. Wright, Helsby, cutting hay with s steam cutting machine. While feeding the machine he got his left hand between the rollers, and it was rapidly &awn towards the knives, where his hand and lingers were cut off inch by inch almost to the wrist. Thomas Lewis, hearing him shout, ran to the machine and re- versed the motion. Clark was eventually taken to the Chester Infirmary, where the remaining portiou of his hand was amputated. After the operation the patient went on fairly well for a week, when the stump of the arm became affected with erysipelas, which graduallY , got into his head, and he died on Sunday. The jury re- turned a verdict of " Accidental death." TER CONSERVATIVE Cr.un.—The annual general meet- ing of the members of the Frodsham Conservative aub was held in the club rooms, Church-ot., Frodsham, on Wednesday evening. Mr. Alfred Thomas, J.P., presi.da, and there was a good attendance. A letter was read trom

the Misses Wright, Castle Park, thanking the int mbere for the resolution of condolence passed with regard to the death of their lite father, for their attendance at his funeral, and for the beautiful wreath contributed. An audited statement of accounts for the past year, compris- ing the furnishing fund and the general fund, was sub- mitted and adopted. A cordial vote of thanks having been unanimously passed to the retiring officers for their services during the past year, the following appointments were male for the ensuing year. viz. :- ['resident, Mr. Alfred Thomas, J:P. '; vice-presidents, Colonel Ashton, Messrs. W. C. Collinson, George Pryde, James Reynolds, J.P., M. Steele, M.D., J.P., and F. P. Weaver, M.D.; honorary treasurer. Mr. Samuel Davies; honorary secre- tary, Mr. Henry Tiley • auditor, Mr. John Austin; and Committee, Messrs. Ralph Bate, George Bennisen, F. W. Dunsford, George Gleave, Joseph Gorst, F. W. Jolley,ll. A. Rigby, T. D. Timmins. and Richard Watson.

div.head: THINGS IIEA.RD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
div.p: THINGS IIEA.RD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
- . Br A.N OCCASIONAL COILMISPONDANT.

-• Notwithstanding the Serious defection from their ranks, the sub-committee appointed to draw up a Cottage Hospital scheme, have proceeded with their task, and the results of their deliberations were published on Saturday. No doubt the ratepayers will shortly be called together to discuss and to ap- prove or reject the scheme. That the subscribers should manage the institution is well and good, but why introduce the system of plural voting into a charitable institution like this? Why should the viorking-man, who from his hard-earned wages contributes a crown, the irmost he can afford, be I swamped by the 20 votes of a gentleman who gives £5 from his well-filled coffers? Probably taken in proportion to his income, the working-mania' sub- scription will be relatively far the more generous of the two, and his interest in the welfare of the hospital be not one whit less keen than that of the more highly favoured individual. Surely in a mat-. ter of this sort, all men should be equal, and" one I man one vote" would bo a good rule to adopt in I managing the hospital. Of coarse a difficult matter to decide will be the site of the proposed Hospital. The Committee sug- gest Highfield House, at preseht occupied, by NEL E. Imison, at Halton Brook. as a suitable building for the purpose. Perhaps so far as the structure itself is concerned no fault can be found, but is it not too far away from the centre of the town, and, approached by a road set with boulder stones, the poor unfortunate sufferers would have a terrible jolting, before they arrived at thoir haven of rest. One thing in favour of this house is the quiet neighbourhood in which it is situated. However, these are details for discussion, and there is unanimity on one point—the need for the hospital. The first thing to be done to ensure the success of this or any scheme is to show that secta- rian prejudice and feeling will not enter into its constitution and management. There is more than a suspicion that the meeting which appointed the sub-committee was packed with a purpose, and that was to jealously guard the interests of an exist- ,ing institution, which should not have the Cottage Hospital as a rival but as a co-worker in the same Samaritan-like cause. Alas, that sectarian jealousy so often usurps the place of Christie.) co-operation! The annual meeting of Runcorn Musical Society, on Tuesday evening was a strange mixture of har- mony and discord. The whole of the members sympathised with the president Mr. Brundrit in his illness; and with one accord they acknowledged by a handsome present the valuable services rendered to the Society by Mrs. W. B. Kay. The discord arose on the election of conductor, and it was plain to he seen the assembly was divided into two camps one for the amateur and the other for professional talent. Considerable feeling was displayed, but eventually the wellbeing of the Society outweighed all. other considerations and a rupture was prevented by the re-election of Mr. Humphreys, who strongly proclaimed his loyalty to the Society and his love of the work. Perhaps the breeze will have cleared the atmosphcre,and affairs will move more smoothly in the future than they appear to have done in the past. - . . -

- Increased population, increased value of property, and increased rates—such is the state of Widnes at the present time as described by Mr. Midwood, chairman of the Finance Committee of the Local Board.. To meet the financial burdens of the com- ing year he had to ask for a rate of 2s. Bd. in the an advance of no less than 2d. Mr. Midwood attri- butes the increase to the Highway department and the Fever Hospital, and certainly it would appear that there is much room for the practice of economy in the management of that institution. The neces- sity of a place in which infectious diseases can be isolated is palpable, if the town is to kept in a healthy state, but a charge of nearly £1,400 a year seems much too high a figure to pay for what is accomplished. Evidently Mr. Midwood does not. mean to allow the matter to vest where it is, and Mr. Wright, as chairman of the liospital Committee, would do well to explain in detail how the money is spent. Had this increase in the rate become necessary after the town had attained the dignity of a boroagh,incorporation would have been credited as the cause.

The need of better communication between Lan- cashire and Che .hire, an especially between the twin towns of Runcorn and Widnes, is not of recent origin, but up to the present time all efforts to effect an improvement vave failed. The Runcorn Com- missioners are now soliciting the assistance of Widnes Local Board in an attempt to get the County Councils of the respective counties to take action in the matter. A roadway for vehicular traffic would be an incalculable boon to both towns, and the sur- rounding districts which are rising in importance every year, and it is to be hoped that the conference of the two authorities will have a practical result. A few years ago the county of Cheshire paid a good many thousands to free the Dee Bridge for the peo- ple of Chester, and it is only carrying the same prin- ciple a little further to build a bridge connecting Lancashire and Cheshire.

The Runcorn Burial Board may not be the most important of our local administrative bodies, but the property under its control is of .11 valuable and important character, and care and good judgment are required to enable affairs to move on smoothly. The majority of the members do not appear to attach a very high responsibility to their office, for their faces we never see, their voices we never hear. A remarkable unanimity seems to have prevailed for the past two months, as a quorum has been wanted at the two last meetings, and the patriar- chal Secretary has had the whole weight of the re- sponsibility on his own shoulders. Offenders please note.

It was an uncommon tribute to the ability and worth of Mr. Sinclair, the Surveyor to Widnes Local Board, on Tuesday last, that his salary was increased from £250 to £3OO without a single obser- vation of any descriptson. 'The Highway Com- mittee who make the proposal were of opinion that his claims needed -no advocacy, and the rest of the members apparently thought the advance well- deserved. Mr. Sinclair is credited with carrying' out his duties in a strict and methodical fashtou, and with a single eye to the good of the community he sorves.

div.head: LORD CROSS AT FAILSWORTIL
div.p: LORD CROSS AT FAILSWORTIL

Viscount Cross, Secretary of State for India, addressed a meeting of Mr. H. G. C. Mowbray's con- stituents on Thursday night in the Co-operative Hall, Failswerth. Alluding to free education, he said that the Government had come to the conclu- sion that, compulsion having been put upon parents to send their children to school, the best thing to do was to put into the bands of parents the means to pay that which they were compelled to pay. At the same time the Government might be relied on not to do anything which would injury the Volun- tary schools. Rumours, he said, had been circulated that the Government intended to dissolve Parlia- ment immediately. He thought it would be sheer madness on their part to do any such thing, but as a general election must come within the next twelve or eighteen months he urged his political friends to prepare for the fight. A resolution expressing oppreval of the home and foreign policy of the Government was adopted.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

CHARGE OF STEALING LEAD. At the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday, Patrick *Han- lon, rag and bone dealer, 8, Halifax-st.„ was charged with stealing, some time between 7 and 10 o'clock the previous Friday mornine, 191bs of old lead, the property of Thomas Williams, broker and general dealer. The prose- cutor said he saw the lead safe in his stables about 7 on the morning in question, and afterwards missed it. George Howard, marine store dealer, Hall-st., said the ,prisoner brought to him the lead produced about 5 p.m. •the same day, and sold it to him for 3s. 3d. Detective- Sergeant Monaghan deposed to apprehending the pri- soner on the charge of stealing the lead, and to his say- ing that he had found it amongst some small bags and sold it to Mr. Howard the same day. The prisoner was committed for trial to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions. A CRICKET SHIRT IN STRANGE HANDS. James Collins, Ship 'Canal labourer, was brought up on remand at the Borough Police Court, on Monday, .e.harged with being in possession of a flannel cricket ..shirt, value Bs. 6d., supposed to have been stolen. The prisoner apered to his former statement that his sister had given him the shirt the night before he left Ipswich; and the police had been unable to discover that the article had been stolen.—The Mayor said the Bench thought there was a considerable amount of truth in what he said, and they were going to imprison the shirt instead of him. He would now be discharged, and if he called for the shirt any time after two weeks he could have it unless the police discovered that it was not his. —Chief-Constable Punt told him to keep the police in- formed of his whereabouts, and he then left the court.

MALTREATMENT OF • DONKEY. At the Borough Police Court on Monday, John Whit- taker, hawker, 4 Mill-st.,was charged with cruelly treat- ing and torturing an ass, by beating it with a stick on Tuesday evening. The constable who proved the case said the defendant was driving the ass in a cart at full gallop and beating it with a stick. Witness called out to him to him to stop doing so,and he replied " You cannot summon me for furious driving, it's only a donkey." Alderman Harrison (to the defendant) : A pity ibut somebody had given you the stick about your back.— Walter Humphries, a boy, said he was in the cart with the defendant, and he only hit the donkey once, and the " bobby " put his hand up to him, but said nothing. The animal was only trotting. The defendant shouted at it. In reply to the Bench as to whether the blow would have been sufficient to dust his jacket the witness said, amidst, laughter" It would make me shout if he hit me that way." Th.? defendant was fined 53., including costs; in default 7 days. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF • CAL—THE RESULT OF PLYING

A BOY WIT/I W ISICY Edward Tully, of 6, Cloth-hall yard, who said he was 20 years of age, but looked much more boyish, was charged with being drunk in charge of a horse and cab on the 30th ult.—A Constable having given evidence, In- spector Bowen made a statement. He said the defen- dant was not a licensed cab driver, and on account of his youth would net be allowed a license. He stated that the lad had had some whisky given him, and he fell under the wheel of the cab as the result. He was not plying for hire, and required no license in that case.—The de- fendant said he had taken a lot of gentlemen to Appleton, and they gave him two or three glasses of whisky.—Ald. Harrison: Shame.—The Mayor (to Aid. Harrison) : It is a common thing to do. (To the defendant) I should not 'like to see you go to prison, because I fancy that is often 'the commencement of a very bad life afterwards.—The ‘defendant said he was not going to have any more drink. —The Mayor: People ought to be thoroughly ashamed of themselves for giving a youth like you whisky.—The defendant was fined 55., including costs ;in default seven days. OVE RCROWD IN el EXTRAORDINARY .--TI II RTEEN PERSONS

COOPED IN SPACE FOR TWO. Edward Coulter, 12 Ship Yard, off Bridge-st., was charged at the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, with keeping a lodging-house without having his pre- mises re,,istered as such.—lnspector Cox deposed that on the night of the 4th inst. he visited the house, which was very small, and found John Ward and Patrick Coulter sleeping in a room downstairs; and upstairs in one bed the defendant and his wife and five children; and in another bed in the same room the four children of the man Ward, 13 persons in all in the three beds.—Mr. Norman said the house was in a most deplorable state, and as for morality there was none, men and women sleeping in heaps together; all the crockery on the floor, and the children were never washed. He never saw a filthier place in his life. The house was only adapted for two persons ; and there was no ventilation —The defend- ant's wife: These children were thrown out of Bakehouse Yard.—Mr. Norman: You had na right to let them in, because you were overcrowded alroad.,-. The defendant was fined 10s. including costs.
OBSTRUCTION or THOROUG/ITARES.—A QuusTroN OF RI GET.

Messrs. McGinn Brothers, cab proprietors, were aura- moned on charges of obstructing on the s'h inst., Sankey-et.,with three conveyances, and Arpley--st., with two cabs, four dogcarts, and one trap. The defendant as to the first admitted that he had offended unintention- ally, and as to the second pleaded that he had a cab stand there which had been given to him by Mr. Whitley, and the vehicles were standing on his own pmperty. Chief Constable Hunt pointed out that there were no horses in the cab shafts.--Inspector Spinks having given evi- dence as to the two charges; the magistrates fined the defendant Ss. including coats on the rirst char,e, and dismissed the second, stating that the Bench were no guise clear alit° his right to keep cabs there. So far as be coud see, if he made that place a cab stand there would have to be horses in the cabs.—The defendant said in that case they might as well begin to summon kim again next week. (Laughter.) The cabs were his own property.—The Mayor slid that had to be con- sidered and invited the defendant to meet the Watch • ammittee on Thursday next, to discuss the subject with them ; and he expressed his readiness to do so.

A FURNITURE DF.ALER AND MIS Doo. At the Borough Police Curt, on Monday, Samuel Gough, furniture dealer, Winwick-St.. was charged with allowint his dog to be at large unmuzzled in the street, on the 4th inst.—The constable who had reported the case, having given evidence, the defendant; subjected him to a long and harrying cross-examination ; one of his questions being whether the witness had been instructed by the Chief Constable to watch his house, to which the officer replied in the negative.—The defendant then con- tended that the summons was informal.as it charged him with not having the dog muzzled, whereal the constable said it was improperly muzzled.—Alderman Harrison: If the dog is not properly muzzled, it is not muzzled accord- ing to law.—The constable in answer to the Mayor, said the muzzle was a strap muzzle, a strap round the jaw. not round the nose. It was not a muzzle that woisld prevent the dog biting.—The defendant then catechised the constable, as to the position of the "hinge" of a dog's jaw, and as to whether he did not pull the muzzle off himself. The constable denied having done so, and the defendant exclaimed," Why,l saw you do it myself." —Mr. Gough then maintained that the constable had failed altogether to prove his case, and re-asserted that the officer forced the muzzle off himself.—Henry Hall, a youth, called for the defence, said the muzzle was a proper one, and the constable forced the muzzle off. The dog could not have eaten a niece of meat with the muzzle on.—The Chief Constable: I think the muzzle should be irodaced.—The defendant said he objected to the Chief Constable making remarks upon the case. They were

entitled to be heard without Mr. Hunt interferiering. ide had been reminded not long since about the very same thing.—Mr. Hunt asked the witness Hall a question, when the defendant intervened with the remark: I do not think you have a right to ask the witness a question, except through the magistrates.—Alderman Harrison: Oh yes, he has.—The Mayor pointed out that Mr. Hunt having in this case signed the information he had, as advised by the magistrates' clerk, a perfect right to cross- examine.—Mr. Hunt then questioned the witness and was answered, after which George Hunt corroborated that witness's evidence, upon which the Bench dis- missed the case. the Mayor remarking that tlilere was a doubt in it.
LIIAVING His WORY_WITHOUT GIVING NOTICE,

At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, a respectable looking Man, named Walter Hall, was summoned at the intance of Messrs. T. and J. Jolley, for leaving their em- ploy, on the 4th inst..witheut giving notice,putting them to the loss of £3.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the pro- secutors and said that case was brought up as an example to the other workmen in the prosecutors' em- ploy. He left his work at 12-20 in the afternoon of the 4th inst. without giving any notice. He left the engine, of which he was in charge,running, and this was not dis- covered until some tune later.—The defendant said he could leave his employment at a moment's notice, ae there were no rules to the contrary. He did not leave the engine running when he left; in fact, he did not get up any steam at all.—The Bench decidel to fine the defendant two guineas, this amount to cover all costs. _ ILL-TREATING HORSES. _

At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, Peter Kelly was summoned for ill-treating a horse, on the 2nd inst., by working it whilst it was in an unfit state, and Joseph Caldwell, the owner of the horse, was summoned for causing the same to be worked. Inspector Dowty, R.S.P.C.A., said he saw the defendant, Kelly, working the horse on the day in ques- tion. On examining the animal, he found a large wound on its back, from which blood and matter was issuing, and which caused it great pain. He afterwards saw the defendant, Caldwell, who said that he was aware that the horse had a wound on its back. Cald- well was fined 103., and Kelly was ordered to pay the costs. 3s. 6d.—Wm. Goodenough, 'bus driver, was sum- moned for ill-treating a horse on the Bth of May. In- spector Dowty stated that he saw the defendant driving a grey horse attached to a wagonette cn the ay in question, in Bridge-st. Witness noticed that the horse I looked uneasy. He followed the conveyance into Ship- yard, and examined the animal. Ho found an old wound about the size of a five shilling piece on its back. Blood and matter was issuing from the wound, and was adher- ing to the pad which covered it. Ihe defendant said the wound had only been there since the previous Satur- day. P.S. Bell gave corroborative evidence, and the de- fendant was fined 103. and Costs. SENT TO GAOL FOE AN ASSAULT.

At the Borough Police Court, yesterday,'..Tolin Murphy labourer, was charged on a warrant with assaulting Mary Ann Davies, on the 11th of May. Mr.A. Browne appeared for the defence.—The complainant deposed that on Mon- day the prisoner accused her of neglecting his child, whom she nursed. Some words ensued between them, and about 12 o'clock the same night prisoner broke into the house in which complai-nant lodged, and a row took place. The next morning about 5.30, the prisoner again forcibly entered the house and struck her violently in the face and on other parts of the body. This statement was corroborated by Mrs. Brown, landlady of the house, and a man named Harry Reynolds. The latter, cross-exam- ined by Mr. Browne, denied exchanging blows with the prisoner as he (the prisoner) was said to be the champion boxer of Warrington, and could eat him up. (Laughter.) —Mr. Browne for the defence said he had no charge to answer.—The complainant had stated that the assa ult took place on Tuesday morning, but he was charge d with assaulting her on Monday.—Alderman Harrison said it was only a technical mistake, and it would be unfair to put the complainant under a disadvantage through it. Mr. Browne said complainant had sworn to the magis- trates' clerk on getting the warrant thatthe assault took place on Monday. She could, therefore, be liable for perjury.—Alderman Harrison said she could not be liable for perjury unless a ntotive was proved.—Mr. Browne then called several witnesses one of whom stated that he saw the man, Harry Reynolds,strike the complainant on Monday, inflicting the black eye which the complainant had alleged,, had been done by the piisoner.—Alderman Harrison said the assault had been proved,and the pri- soner was bound over in the sum of £lO and a surety of £lO to keep the peace for six months, and would have to pay the costs, or in default he would be sentenced to im- prisonment for 14 days.

div.head: FiLTHY BAIEIIOIISE.
div.p: A FiLTHY BAIEIIOIISE.

John Roberts, baker, 3 and 5 Dial-st., was charged at the Borough Polico Court, on Tuesday with being the occupant of a bakehouse the walls, ceiling, and floor of which were in such an unsanitary condition that it was unfit for occupation as a bakehouse.—Mr. Norman Inspector of Nuisances, said the proceedings were taken under the 16th section of the Factories and Workshops Act, 1883, and this was the first case of the kind that had been brought into that court. He went to the defendant's bakehouse on the day mentioned and found the walls, ceilings, and floor in a very dirty condition - they could not have been dirtier, and the flopr was at least half an inch thick in filth. He reported the matter to the Sanitary Committee, and at their request invited Mr. Roberts to attend before them, but he did not do so. rhe'committee decided to fine him £2.25. ; and witness informed Mr. Roberts that he must pay this or he would be summoned. He did not pay, and the committee gave him until the Bth inst to pay, but he did not do so.—The defendant said the place was white- washed twice last year: and Mr. Norman com- plained in January that it was dirty, though it had been whitewashed in December. Mr. Norman said it would do with whitewashing once a month as it was so crowded, and badly ventilated, and an unfit building for a bakehouse.—The defendant said he had had it built as such by a practical man ; and said that , the letter inviting him to meet the Committee had been , mislaid on delivery and did not reach his hands till al week after. He admitted that the floor was very dirty, but there had been a lot of rain, and thro:,gh the neglect of the Corporation or the landlord, the gulley had been without a grid for months, and the result was that men brcught in thejlirt with their floury shoes.—Thos. Tilley,employed by thedefendant, said Mr. Norman had varnished the case a good deal.—Mr. Norman (produc- ing what appeared to be a very dirty looking piece of mortar, from the defendant's place) : Is this the varnish you mean? That is a specimen of the varnish.—Wit- ness : That was near the door.—Mr. Norman: That is Hot my varnish; that is yours.—The witness further said that his employer had done his utmost to keep the place clean.—Thedefendant was fined 205., including costs.

WARRINGTON _BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MONDAY. —Before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- comb), and Alderman Harris•n.

PITELL AND Toss AND ASSAULTINO A CONSTABLE.—John William Stockton was charged with playing at pitch and toss for money at the Black Bear Bridge, and also with assaulting P.C. Amson, on Saturday night, and Frank Simmonds, was charged with attempting to rescue him from custody. P.C. Amson deposed to seeing Stockton playing at pitch and toss on the bridge, with another man, and said when the defendant saw Wm he took a running kick at hint. He apprehended the man, and when he had got him to St. James's-st., Siminonds care up and asked Stockton what he was to be locked up for; and he replied "for tossing." Simmonds said "Well give me your money," and than he can't prove you were tossing. Witness said to Simmonds, "You keep away, or else you will be locked up very likely." Simmonds got Steckton's money, 55., from him; and then said he had got his money, and witness wculd have to take both of them, and attempted to rescue Stockport. Witness had to have the assistance of P.C. Cooper,36,and three work- ing-men, but the latter did not care to give evidence. P.C. Cooper, 36, having given evidence, the prisoner was fined 203. and costs and Siminonds 2s. ed., includ- ing costs. AN UNPROVOKED ASSAULT.—JamesJordan,lBth appear- ance, was charged with assaulting Albert Allcock, in Rose and Crown-st., on Saturday night.—P.S. Jones said he saw Jordan strike Allcock two violent blows in the mouth, and knock Jordan to the ground, whore he lay bleeding from the mouth. Jordan told witness that Allcock wanted to "have ado" with him in the public- house, so he thought he would give it him outside.—All- cock said the defendant tried to pick a quarrel with him in the Rose and Crown, but witness would not speak to him, and afterwarda the man struck hint outside vio- lently several times in the mouth. The defend- ant implied, by his questions to Alleock, that the latter had said in the public-house that he could fight any- body in it,especially Jordan, but Jordan denied this. The landlady of the house said Jordan was saying in the bar, as he always did when he had a pint, that he would fight any man, and she pushed him out. There was no quarrel in the house. Willcock went out three or four minutes after; then some one ran in and said Jor- dan had given Allcock a knack in the mouth. The de- fendant, in reply to the Bench, admitted he had a bad character, but said he was trying to reform. The Chief Constable said the man was one of a gang that went about and asked for coppers or for a match from persons, and if they could get neither, assaulted them. The Mayor told the defendant he was a perfect nuisance to anybody's house; and it was such men as he that brought public-houses into disgrace. His talking about reform was nonsense, and he would have to go to prison for two months with hard labour. DRUNK AND DISORDERLT.—P.C. COOPER MAKES AN- ()THE R MISTAKE AS TO IDENTITY.—Patrick Tewney, drunk and disorderly on Saturday night, in Bridge-st., was discharged on payment of ss. and catsts.—Mary Wilson, tramp, of Chester, drunk and disorderly in Mersey-st., on Saturday night, was discharged.—John Ba.g,uley, in the Market-place, on the 30th ult., lined 10s. and costs; in default seven days.—Wm. Butler was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st., at nine o'clock on Saturday night. P.C. 20, Cooper, gave evi- dence as to the circumstances. A female witness de- posed that the defendant was in her company at the Empire Theatre at the time in question,and up to twenty five minutes past ten, only leaving her at a quarter to ten to gei; a gill of beer. P.C. Cooper, re-called, denied that he was mistaken as to the man. The defendant

said the/ Men whoought tohnve been brought up 'as in court ; and was his brother. (Laughter.)—The Maler Cooper, you base made iv mistake once before.—The fe- fendant's brother was then plated close beside him, anti there, was certainly a remarkable likeness between the two; and P.C. Cooper, after carefully scrutinising the second man, said, "That in the one, now I come to look at him." William Butler Wah therefore discharged, and his brother, Mark Builerewas then charged in his place, informing the Bench that he would prefer being dealt with there and then to being summoned —the Mayor commended nim for his conduct in exculpatinc, his brother, and he was discharged on payment of 23.65. —Mary Mannion, drunk and dice.rderly in a yard off Winwrck-road, on Saturday night, was discharged a caution, the Mayor remarking as to her case, thanie did not know how some of these women would do if they had to be dealt with by women magistrates:, he was afraid they would catch it.—Frank Ma4oney was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Dial-court, on the sth inst. The prisoner said he had never done anything wrong in hislife, but the Court record showed quite the ,contrary. He was fined 53. and costs, in default seven days,

irsorrAmcv.—.Tohn Collins, was charged with sleeping in the straw shed of Mrs. Elizabeth Monks, Arpley, at half-past two on Sunday morning, and having no visibler means of subsistence. -A constable who proved the case said there was a respectable navvy sleeping with the" prisoner • he load money in his pocket, therefore was. allowed to go. The prisoner had no money on him.-- The Meryor :—I wish somebody would build a registered lodging-house amongst these stables. (Laughter.). It must be a favouritesleeping place.—The Chief Constable remarked that a good stick would rouse some of these men up, and prevent them sleeping there again.—The Mayor: Perhaps Strangeways would do him good—go, ing up those steps.—The Chief Constable He is in strange ways now. (Laughter.)—The prisoner was sent for].* days' hard labour.

INanniar.--' -Frederick Rbgers was charged with begging in the Market Place on Sunday afternoon.—The Mayor (looking at the prisouer).: We meet with some strange company in the police court don't we? (Laughter.) This prisoner was also sentenced to 14 days' imprison- ment witk hard labour.

The defendant's wife, who ad- vanced up to Mr. Riley and threatened what she would do if he came near her again, was called before the Bench and informed that it was only through him him that her husbancrhad not been fined at least 103. ; and was ad- monished for her exhibition oflteroper. FIGHTTNG.—James Couslini. and Alfred Monks, were summoned on a charge of fighting in Bridge-st. on the 2nd inst. Couslin was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs, 53., and a warrant was issued against Monks. Pima AND TOS9. —Tho mas -Brown, Joseph Bradshaw, John Da.kin, Richard Houghton, George Pendleton, Wm. Potts, Edwin Spencer, Wm. Baxter john Lally and John Nicholson, all youths, were charged with playing at pitch and toss for money in Halifax-st., on the 3rd inst. P.C. Turner who gave evidence against them had got into a railway carriage. on the line and from thence watched their proceedings. Some °Palen, he said played cards after pitch and toss. Several of the defendants pleaded guilty, others said' they merely played at cards and others that they were only' looking on. Brown, Bradshaw Potts, Spencer, and Nicholson, were fined 6d. each; in default three 'days confinement in tho cells ; and the other defendants were dismissed. TUBSDA.Y.—Before Messrs. R. RUNCORN V. SALTNRY.—PIayeh at Runcorn, on Satur- day. The home eleven went first to the wickets. ar.4l their innings were remarkable ?or the very high score of ; the Rev. G. H. Kingston, who carried out his bat for-an admirably played 105. In the endeavour to dislodge him, the Saltney Captain tried: six changes of bowling, but he treated all with the same impartiality. His dzience ' could not be broken down, And anything loos in the bowling he punished most unmercifully, and sorts* of his cuts and drives were very fine. His score included one 6, four 4's. fourteen 3'B,ten Zs, and 21 singles. Mr.Ringston has joined the club and will play in the matches as often as possible, a circumstance which has given great satis- faction to all concerned. Wright partnered Kingston while he made a large share of his total, and playing with good judgment and patience, was credited with 19 runs. After his departure "dry rot" appeared to have set ia,anti the three next wickets were unproductive, but there was a grave doubt as to the accuracy 1 of the umpire's decision in Frith's case. D. Limb, however, made a good stand, and eventually Run- corn declared their innings closed when there remained four wickets to fall. FIOKTING.—Thomas Farrell was charged with fighting the previous night in Bridge-street. and Alfred Monks with not appearing to a summons charging him with fighting in that street on the 2nd inst. Fhrrell was fined ss. and costs and Monks bound over in.his own sureties to keep the peace for three months, and ordered to pay costs.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Thornas- Glavin, 18th ap- pearance, drunk and disorderly in Bank-street, on the previous night, and John Reid, in Bridge-street, the same night, were each fined 10s: and costs.;. in default 14 days.

NON-ATTENDANCE AT SCSOOL. —The following persons were dealt with at the instance of Mr: G;. Riley, school attendance officer, for not sending their children to school :—Edward Coulter, 12, Ship-yard,. had his case adjourned.—William Crighton, 5,, King-street, /B.—John McDonald, Back Ship-yard, employed at White Cross works, 2s. 6d.—Thomas Moody, forgemat4 afF,Flerpoint- street, ss.—John Graham, tanner, Back Ship-yard, was charged with TIM complying with an attendance order. Mr. Riley applied that the boy might be sent to the training ship Clio, as recommended by the-School Attend- ance Committee. The Bench made an order accordingly. At this discision the boy, as is almost invariably the case under such circumstances, burst into-a bud fit of sobbing, and the mother, who appeared,.p/eaded that he might have another chance, but her plea being unavailing she also gave way to her grief r and they botb sobbed so loudly that they were removed from court.—Michael Cain, forgeman, 87, Watkin-street, Is.—Tiam, Browne, joiner. Albert Terrace, 2s. 6d.—Michael Cryan. agent, 49 Laura-street, 2s. 6d.—John Kermode, painter, 53, Marsh House-lane, 2s. 6d.—Peter Hinds, forgeman, Cockliedge- lane, ss.—Joseph Egginton, wiredrawer, I/lEN Liverpool road, 2s. 6d. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. J. Fairclough. DESERTION FROM THE ARMY —TIIOOMLS Birch was charged with deserting on the 9th instr..from the Durham Light Infantry stationed at Aldershot. P.C. Turner deposed to meeting the prisoner in Horsemarket-st., and asking him whether he had not been in the army on which he replied that he . had been -bought out by his mother for £lO ten months ago. He•haci4military boots, trousers, and braces on. He finally, admitted being a deserter. He was sent to Strangewayajail to await an escort.
FRIDAY .—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gornall.

HUGGING THE LAMP POST.—Jarnes McMahon—, ; dis- charged soldier, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in liettermarket-st., the previous night.—D.S. Monaghan said the prisoner was kneeling on the footpath with his arms round a lamp post. (Laughter.) He was drunk and witness brought him, to the police station.— Prisoner was discharged on promising to leave the town. MAINTENANCE ORDERS.—Tho following were ordered to pay different sums of money weekly towards the main- tenance of their mothers who were chargeable to the Warrington Union ;—John Collins,. IS. 6d. ; Wm Gore, ; Wm. Hallowes, 25.; and Samuel Taylor, is. 6d. AN APPRENTICE LEAVZS ,11 Eft Vo roc.—Erarri et War- burton, apprentice, was summoned for a claim of 3s. damages, by her employer James Welsby,eaused through her leaving her work, on the 28th April.—Defendant was ordered to pay the money at 13. a week, and to go back to her .work.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAT.—Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Major Hazle- _

Scott and Thomas Hodge were Ened 2s. 6d. and costs. PITCH AND Toss.—William Henry Millar, Peter Haukey, and Thomas Robinson were each fined /Cs. and costs for playing pitch and toss at Halton on, Sunday. DISORDERLY.—Sarah Burton was sentenced to 14 days hard labour for having behaved indecently in a public street on Saturday night. A TRAMP named John Ridgate waschargel with being in an outhouse in Parker-st. on Sunday night, without visible means of subsistence. ile was sent to gaol for 14 days. . .

TIIiFT OF A COAT.—CharleS Smith was charged with stealing a coat worth Bs. 6d. the property of Mr. Wm. Marsh, pawnbroker, Church-st. The prisoner was seen by Edward Lamb, a, carter, to take the coat from the shop, and P.C. Woodrow afterwards found him in an entry, exchanging his old one for the new one. He was sent to gaol for 14 days. ASSAULT.—Wm. Inglefield„was charged with assault- ing his sister Mary Brooks on the sth inst. The parties bad" some words" and then defendant seized her by the throat. Fined ss. and costs.

Gaskell.

DRUNKENNES.4.—Patrick Ward, Michael Mulligan,Jane Jones, and Reuben Hewitt, were each fined ss. and costs for this offence. George Powell (Ditton), was charged being with drunk and disorderly in Ditton-road on Sun- day and with wilfully smashing a window of the house of George McKay. SLEEPINQ OUT.—For sleeping in the Chemical Works, of Messrs. Hutchinson on Sunday night, Joseph Killalia was sentenced to seven days hard labour.

ASSAULT ON Tug Pouez.--John Conroy, wds charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C.'s McGuiness and Reid. On Saturday afternoon in Anne- St., the constables took prisoners into custody on. the former charge when he kicked them savagely on the legs and throwing himself to the ground he could not be removed without further help.—Superintendent Noblett said the prisoner was a very violent charactor and' had been several times convicted. He was only released on Saturday morning after serving twelve months for felony. The prisoner pleaded guilty and was fined ss. in each case or 21 days' _hard labour.

ALLEGEM ASSAULT.—Wm. Stewart, Water-st., was brought up an remand charged with assaulting Ellen I Mulligan, aged 34- years, daughter of Michael Mulligan, of 3, Water-st. The Bench thought there was a prima I facie case and committed the prisoner to the Quarter Sessions for trial.

That- Catford CC held an interestinx and successful meating at the -Paddington Recreation Ground on Satur- day, most of the events being confined to bicyclists. The, greatest interest was evinced in the race for the Werioam 50-guinett Challenge Shield and N.C.U. cham- pionship,, for which eight of the most noted Southern clubs competed. The preliminary heatn only were run through,.and the second round and final will be held at futner meetings, as arranged by the ion. The ulti- mate-victors will hold the shield, and by its possession become entitled to call themselves "the champion cyzling ln the third heat oti: the club race Scheltem-Bednin, who was riding for the Catford C.C., rode the last quarter of a mile in 311 sec.,,thus establish- ingta,new record, the previously existing one being 311, made-by W. C. Jones; of course, this is,with a" flying start "

The-brothers DIA Cros were again "'out" at Belfast, ancl;.as.usual, they cleared the board. Macredy failed to mhibit anything litre the magnificent fornl he showed when in London last year, and Arthur Ittt Cros defeated himNfor the half mile Irish cycling championship very clevorly by about a length. The two fought their battle o'er.'again in the five miles handicap, as both occupied the post of honour; a most exciting ra e. throughout re- sled in.alltt limit brigade being defeated, Du Cros managing to pass the judge a yard or co in front of the erstwhile champion, Macredy. Another of the Du Cros family won the half-mile bicycle handicap, but he was disqpalifled for fotling, and the first prina.was presented taXennedy, of Ballymena.

div.head: NE CELLANEOUS.
div.p: NE CELLANEOUS.

Among those who have arrived at Stockholm to take port in, the international gymnasium fete which is to be aeldthere are some officers and non-counaissionod officers of the British army, as well as ten pupils from the gym- nasium, of the People's Palace, London, and three members of the Nationa I Recreation Society of Liverpool. 'Fhe mtlitary squad, which is under the charge of Colonel Pur...,.consists of a captain and 16 subalterns and non- Commissioned officers. The People's. Palace contingent is,under the leadership of Mr. Harry H. Burdett. The object of these fisitors is to illustz.ate practically the system of gymnastic training followed in England. The party had already given an exhibition at Gothenburg, d were enthusiastically received. Mr. James Dickson, merchant at Gothenburg, entertained the officers at , dinner. The Pzitish civil contingent was also entertained at supper before leaving Gothenburg for Stockholm.

At Exeter Hall, London, on Saturday evening', the final comnetition for the National Challenge Shield, pre- sented by the N. P.R.S.. was decided between the teams of the Liverpool Y.M.C.A. Gymnasium and the Newport (non.) Junior Conservative Gyinnasiura,before- a large concourse of spectators, the former winning after' a close struggle. The chair wasoccupied by the Marquis. of Lorne, who was accompanied by H.R.H. Princess. Louise, and amongst others on the platform were M. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., president of the society; Lord Kinnaird, and Sir George Elliot, M.P. The judges wave Messrs. R. Winter and W. Whittaker, and Colonel G. 14. Onslow officiated as referee.

The competitions were contested in the following, order, vie. 1-1, horizontal bar; 2, high jump; 3, rope climbing; marks being awarded for the best exhibition of strength, skill, and grace. The performances ors the horizontal bar were of a very high order on both skies, and the Liverpool team showed to particular advantage, their average being better, and their total 120, against 102. The high jump contest was extremely keert, and here the Newport team held their own with a total of 104 against 101, though the best jump was made- by Mr. Cookson, of Liverpool, who cleared 51t. 6in. Newport also secureda higher number of marks for rope.ctimbing, their total reaching 106 b, 101, but the difference V7a9 not sufficient to avert defeat, as the aggregate of the Liver- pool team amounted 322; whilst their opponents scored 10 points less. The highest individual total of sol marks out of a possible 60 was secured by Mr. J. C. Huxtable, of Newport.

THE truly generous man is he who denies 'simself some luxury, or, better still, some necessasy, in order that he may have, wherewith to give ta those who are in need. The;millionaire gets greali praise for his gifts and large donations; but iu all;proba- bility the signing of his big cheque does not entail the sacrifice of the smallest pleasure or the slightest gratification. PEOPLE whose dispositions are naturally irritable or unhappy think it is no use trying to be other- wise; but that is a mistake. If they will patiently and perseveringly try to keep always pleasant, after a while they will get in the habit of smiling instead of frowning, of looking bright instead of surly, and of giving a kind word instead of a cress one. And. the beauty of it is that pleasantness is catching„ and before long they will find themselves in the, midst of a world full of bright and happy people, whore every one,is as good-nature a and contented as they are. No good impulse, no generousymotion, no heLrk- fclt desire to do right is ever( lest. We are, we roust be, better than if we had not had it. But in proportion as it is deep it will not be transiant. /be memory of such momenta will be with not to atrengthen and renew our courage. They. are opportunities for good whicht we should Gaunt among our richest treasures. No one can tell how much he owes to them; nor Need he be disc,euraged if they do not seem to be s-sRh powerful fa,-ktrs in his hie as hufwould desire.

TheCerwegational Union of England and Wa holding its. 59th annual gathering during the•- preseel week, in London. The week's. proceedings began Monday with a prayer meeting in the Memorial Hon, vr?sided over by the Rev. Thomas Green, MAI, Vet ballot for the Chairman and the .Committee followed, and in theevening an important meeting was held, a 5 which representatives alone vverndmitted. This meet" ing was presided over by Dr. John Brown, the chairmen of the Union,. and the ordinary annual business sva° transacted,including the adopt:3n of the repor3 and tho appointment of officers. The reoort made special refer once to the death of Dr. Alexander Hacnay, for: noir": years thetrhion's secretary, and stated that a memorial fund had. been initiated, and had received contributions to the extent of £2,400. The repert further stated that Dr. R. W. Dale had been nominated as president of tbe IfitornationalCouncil, which is.to meet in 1-cadan. in July. The report having been agreed to, it was an- nounced that Dr. Herbert Evans, of Carnareon,. had received 33' votes out of 711 at the ballot, and has accordingly been elected chalrman for neat year. Dr. Parker moved an amendment, of which he had given notice, to the effect that tho consideration of the se 3?etaria t should be post- poned to a special or annual business meeting-,,and that in the meantime the Committee should make temporal/ arrangements for secretarial service. Dr. Parker claimed any regponsibility for the attacks which !Au been made on the Cenirbittee:by aronymous-writers ii the religious prose. He felt, however, that there was a great question of sequence at stake, and it was. necesssari for the Union, as a matter of constitutional principle, tn consider qoestions bearing on the service which the secretary was expected to render before 3proceecii2g the election. LIVERPOOL UNIVERSITY COLLEGE.
MR. BRUNNER'6 GIFT OF £lO,OOO.

A meeting of the Court of Governors of University College, Liverpool, was held on Saturday, Mr. W. J. Stewart presiding. Among those present were Principal Rends.ll, the Revs. 11. H. Higgins, J. H. Thom, and A. Slotnan, Drs. Campbell Brown and Caton, Professor Mackay, Messrs. R. Bushell, J. W. Alsop, W. Crosfield, H. W. (lair, G. Holt, A. Booth, M'Diarmid, A. Hughes, and E. M. Hance. From the minutes of the Council (read by Mr. Londini, the registrar) it appeared ' that during the past six months the following gifts had been received on behalf of the college :—£6oo raised by Professor Campbell Brown towards the expenses of the chemical depart- ment ; two silver goblets from Mr. H. S. Thompson, of Thingvrall Ball, to be annually awarded for success in ....zngtish orations; a donation of £5OO from Mr. Charles W. • Jones, of Field House, Wavertree, to be placeci at the dielictsal'nf the professor of engineering; a donation of ,% .ti•,000 from Mr. Ludwig Mond to the chemistry depart- ment ; £5OO from Miss M. L. Hornby for the foundation of a Greek scholarship associated with the name of the late Rev. Thos. Hornby, vicar of St. Mary's, Walton-on- the ; £1,300, which had been raised by various con- tributions towards the £1,500 required for the endow- ment of the Italian lectureship ; a legacy of £l,ooo,left by the late Dr. Gee for the foundation of a medical scholarship ; and lastly a donation of £lO,OOO from Mn 3. T. Brunner, M.P., for the endowment of a chair of economic science. In regard to the latter gift the esetincil had passed the following resolution :—The Coun- cill Cordially accepts the generous offer of Mr. J. T. Brun- ner, to provide permanent endowment for a chair of econoraic science to be associated with the memory of his father, the late Rev. John Brunner, schoolmaster, Liverpcol, and his son, Sydney Herbert Brunner, who at the time of his death was a student of the college ; and the Council request the chairman to convey to Mr. Brunner their warm and grateful appreciation of the object of the ft, and of the terms under which it is conveyed to the c•ollfge." The Council had also decided to appoint to the chair of economic science the present lecturer on the sub- ject, Mr. E. C. K. Gonner,at a salary of £375 per annum, !ogether with two-thirds of the fees of all students attend- ing his day and evening classes. The Chairman said the list of gifts and the foundation by Mr. Brunner of a chair of economic science showed, What they all hoped in the year 1877, that when the People of Liverpool and the neighbourhood began fully to understand the objects of the college they would not hesitate to come forward in a generous and liberal way to support the college. Buildings were growing around them, and he hoped before long to see the whole space covered with a handsome quadrangle of buildings in 'which the work of the college could be carried on un- impeded by the present conditions of cramped space and bad air. (Hear, hear.) Principal Rendall remarked that in no previous six Itionthshad the gifts received been so important. either in number or in magnitude. Almost every department of the college had experienced some benefit. Mr. Brun- ner, whose name and services to the country and his own Brun- per, were familiar to them all, desired that the chair a_ 11!)uld be associated with the memories of his father, .w.he was a most successful schoolmaster in that city,and • nig 8011 Sydney Herbert, a youth of particularly bright Promise, whose untimely death in Lake Como was a treat sorrow to his family. On the motion of Mr. W. Crosfield, seconded by Mr. 144.0nt1i, Mr. G. Holt we. 4 appointed to represent the court ent court cPf ViCtoria University for the 'lllllhg_fout Vag, M7Dia.rnald, ih proposing a vote of thanks to the ;f4.lairmasl for presiding, took occasion to congratulate rn, on behalf of the governors, upon his appointment etipendiery magistrate, which he said had met with _Unanimous approval of his fellow citizens of all sliajes of politics. (Hear, hear.) The motion was heartily accorded. and Mr. Steward'e a cm,oowledgetnent concluded the proceedings.
GOOD TEMPLAR CONVENTION. AT EARLESTOWN.

-- The quarterly session of the No. 1 Convention (South West Lancashire district) of the Indepen- dent Order of Good Templars, was held in the Co- (Verative Hall, Earlestown, on Saturday, under the "Vices of the " Hope of Earlestown" lodge, repre- sentatives and visitors being present from Warring- St. Helens, Hindley, and Golborne. The Wigan, widnes and Ashton lodges were not represented. Bro. p.. Clarice (Earlestown), C.C.T., although present, was .„.?* ill to preside, and the proceedings were opened by O. Colour-Sergeant Devlin (Warrington). C.C. After „.'"e oPeningceremony,Bro.W. Porter(Liverpool),P.D.C.T. et East York District, was welcomed, and after a short address presided for the remainder of the Session. Bro. 4; H. Musk (Manchester) D. Electoral Superintendent el South F.a.st Lancashire District, was present on the Platform during part of the Session. A resolution of sYmpathy with Brother and Sister Clarke (Earlestown), ti their recent severe illness was carried unanimously. The officers' reports were of an encouraging nature, that af the C.C.T. calling attention to the National Van Mis- sion Bazaar to be held in London from 6th to 11th of July, also to the reception to be held in Liverpool on Thursday, 21st May, to welcome R.W. Grand Ledge visitors from America. The Secretary reported that on the Ist May there were in the Convention 470 members in the 13 lodpes,being, an increase of 60 during the quarter; new lodges had been established at Prescot, Sankey Bridges, and Peasley Cross ; that at Hindley had been re- vived; two Executive meetings had been held ; the Tem- perance Mission and Young 40th Lodge of Warrington had collected about £lO in money and goods towards the Van Mission Bazaar. The C. ElectoralAuperintendent men- tioned the passing of the second reading of the Irish Sun- day Closing Bill on 15th Apiil, also the motion of Mr. J. Ellis on 28th April, and amendment, regarding" Equit- able compensation." He urged all voters to remember Who were their friends at the next election and recom- Mended formation of a Direct Veto League for this Divi- -140, b. All the reports were adopted. The report of the •mtecutive read by the Secretary, recommended (1) Acceptance of Examiner Office tender for printing Bro. Mantle's papers, entitled "Has our Convention been a ,nceess 2" (2) " Adeption of system of personal mem- bership. (3) "Fees for personal members to be six- Ponce half yearly, such members to be entitled to speak Said vote an all questions,except in elections,on financial goestions, or on a call for " yeas " and " nays " when Inly representatives shall be entitled to vote. (4) That ''"lledges give an entertainment once every half year in ef Convention funds. (5) That all lodges fix a night O r reception of Convention visitor. (6) That open air kission work be carried on by lodges during summer ntonths. (7)That programmes for public meetings contain More interesting items in future. (8) That public meet- Lnge preeeding institution of new lodges be concluded enough to allow full ceremony to be carried out. (,:) That a Committee of three be appointed to assist (10) That some members of the District Juven- ile Council be invited to early session to read paper or "therwise urge more attention to juvenile work. (11) a- a Committee be appointed to arrange system of `emperance education. (12)That an" Official Organ" be established for Convention. All these recommendations, ..sf,ter a slight discussion, were agreed to, except No. 12, fulen was ordered to be referred back to the Executive further consideration. Bro. Robertson (Warrington), ?Later J. Warburton (Earlestown), and Bro. Griffith lidindley), were elected on the Committee on juvenile Work. The appointment of the'Committee on Temper- ance Education was referred to the Executive. The tePorts of the Visitors to lodges and temples in the Con- vention were very satisfactory. It was stated that the Oolborne Ebenezer Lodge had lately madh a fresh start, and hoped to raise its number of members to the old standard, in a short time. The Prescet Safeguard Ledge W 8 niported as needing assistance,and Bros. Clarke and Porter promised to pay it a visit when the former was eufficiently recovered. Hindley was selected for the next Session, to be held on the 13th June. The Earlestown blvthren were thanked for their arrangements, and the distinguished visitors (Bros. Musk and Porter) for their Presence and assistance, after which an excellent tea Was provided and much enjoyed. The customary public aleeting was held in the 'evening, under the chairman- ' ship of Bro. Skaife, of St. Helens, at which addresses were deliveredby Mr. J.' H. Musk, superintendent of the Alliance, (Manchester), and others, interspersed with songs, readings, and recitations.
