div.head: RAVAGES OF INFLUENZA.-A REMEDY.
div.p: RAVAGES OF INFLUENZA.-A REMEDY.

• --- - - - Sir,—The extraordinary recurrence in every direction of the phenomenon termed Influenza may be referred to the long sustained easterly weather ; but there is no doubt the sickness is becoming more than epidemic among us demanding serious attention towards some easily procured preventive and possible cure. It cannot be too widely known that Quinine combined with Iron renders the system proof against and able to cope with tnalarious attacks caused by disease germs floating in the air—the unquestionable sources of Influenza. It is impossible too strongly to recommend every one in the least degree weak to at once commence taking Quinine, continuing until the summer has well set in, the period of recovery from the attack being the most critical. It is easily procurable from every chemist ; com- paratively cheap and abundant ; certainly each glass ef Quinine would cost less than a glass of beer. In cases of persons too poor to buy the medicine. if . the Clergy District Visitors, or others in your locality :likely to know,will stnd me the names and addresses of deserving cases, a bottle of the Quinine and Iron Tonic -prepared by my firm shall be forwarded by Parcels Post without any charge whatever.—l am, yours faithfully, T. E. MARSHALL (secty), Pepper's Quinine &Iron Tonic Co. Bedford Laboratory, London.
"INSANITARY CONDITION OF THE POLICE
COURT."

Sir,—l have noticed on more than one occasion that a question has been asked—Where are the magistrates? There is no doubt that if honorary positions are accepted it is necessary that the magistrates should discharge them with fidelity and consistent regularity. But mag- istrates are human, physically impressed by heat and cold, poisonous atmospheres, &c., and I protest against the manner in which the comfort of all who have to attend the Police Court of this Borough is catered for by the Watch Convnittee, which I am told is responsible for its sanitary condition. At the last Brewster Sessions, Mr. Robert Davies and others referred to the impure condition of the Court, and the great difficulty under such circumstances of doing justice to all concerned? As Medical Officer of Health, I also wrote to the Mayor on the subject, point- ing out the serious defects in ventilation, and the ill- effects induced by breathing an atmosphere nearly as much polluted as the Black Hole of Calcutta. To-day the Court has sat from 10 a.m. to 230 p.m. ; It certainly was not crowded but we were nearly perished with cold, as. like the Railway Compainies, whatever the condition of the weather is,when the Ist April is reached, it appears to be a custom to stop the supply of warmth by fires. As one via() is willing to make some sacrifice in the public interest, I must still protest against being exposed to both an impure as well as a cold atmosphere, especially when influenza and its attendant complica- tions are rife, and if need be shall absent myself on the day fixed for my attendance, if the court is not made fairly sanitary and less dangerous to healtn than it is at present.—l am, yours truly, JOHN H. GORNALL. Friday, 15th May, 1891.

R. JOHN GANDY'S QUOTATIONS CORRECTED. Sir,—On no account would I seek to re-open any further discussion with Mr. Gandy, but in justice to my- self and to several authors concerned I ask your permis- sion, Mr. Editor, tkat the latter be allowed to speak for themselves, and that the truth should be known as to what they actually did say, and not as they have been represented by Mr. Gandy. I give two quotations from Machtine's version of -Mosheiin—the one from which my quondam opponent professed to quote. Will your readers please notice I Rive the passages as they stand, on.pages 84 and 87 of Maclaine's version, and must also explain that the words in italics are those which Mr. Gandy omits altogether in his letter of the 7th _March. In the 'first century Moe- tern says :—" Seil,?rat Christians adopted that absurd and corrupt eustOm amongst the Jews of darkening the plain words of the Holy Scripture by insipid and forced allegories, ann of drawing them violently from their proper and natural significations in order to extort from them certain mysterious and hidden significations." p. 84. • The lives and manners of the Christians in ink century—the first—r.re highly celebrated by f most aut,lors and recomin, nded to succeeding generatidns as unspotted modets of piety and virtue ; and if these en- cona;untS be ronpted to the iir:•att.:t part of those who tm- loracq Christianity in the inea:.,-y of the church they are certainly dLtributcd mith, ju.tic,... But many run into ex-

tremes,and estimating the lives and manners of all by the illustrious examples of some eminent saints or the sub- lime precepts and exhortations of certain pious doctors, fondly imagine that every appearance of vice and dis- order was banished from the first Christian Societies." et. p 87. The next instance appears in his last letter (Examiner, 2nd May) in a quotation which he professes to give from Dr. Abbott, in the Enclycicepedia Britannie,a. The cor- rect passage is as follows "The earliest account of the origins of the Gospel is already legendary (Westcott introduction to the Gospels p. 255), as given in the fragment of Muratori A.D., 170, which Mr. Gandy distorts into—' The earliest account of the origins of the Gospels is legendary.' An utter falsi- flying of both Drs. Abbott and Westcott. Permit me to explain: Dr. Abbott had dealt with the subject of the three synoptic Gospels, and he is then dealing with the 4th Gospel only, and introduces, Dr. Westcott's words, touching the earliest legend extant as given in the Mora- rtorian fragment relative to the origin of John's writing his Gospel. The offence here is this, Me. Gandy changes the word Gospel into Gospels,' and makes Dr. Westcott apply wards to all the Gospels which have no a.pplication except to the 4th; in fact turning into a general state- ment regarding the whole four what only,affects a pri- vate incident touching the origins of one; and by stop- ping short at a comma in the above passage which lie quotes—omitting the words as given in the fragment of Muratori A.D., 170—he conceals the comparative unim- portance of this particular legend so far as it bears upon the great body of historical evidence to John's Gospel furnished elsewhere by Dr. Westcott."—Yours truly, JOHN DIGNUM.
Penketh, 12th May, 1891. We shall allow Mr. gandy to explain; and there the matter must end.—En. Ex.]

SCIENCE AND RELIGION. Sir,—l regret that the discussion raised in your columns a few weeks ago regarding science and anthropo morph. ism turned out so fruitless. In taking it up, I certainly thought that my opponent would present some reason or reasons for the faith or unfaith he maintained. In- stead of doing so, my arguments were entirely ignored, and the discussion ended in little better than word play. Nevertheless, the question so slightly treated is one of overwhelming importance, and at present is one of the burning questions of the day. The agnostic position is briefly comprised in the Corn- ptean assumption that all our knowledge is confined to the phenomenal, the conditienal,and the relative: and what- ever lies beyond this, such as God, mind, and matter, is relegated to the limbo of nonentity or to the unknowable. Such a position I regard as essentially false,and in order to test the truth of it one inust'inquire what is know- ledge? What do we mean by " knowledge ? " Now, In order to" know," there must be on the one hand one who is capable of knowing, that is, a subject; and on the other, there must be something to be known, that is,an object. In order to know, therefore, there must be a sub- ject and an object. Take away either of these factors, and the act of knowledge is annihilated. Deny the slab- ject, and one falls into Pantheism, Materialism, &c. Take away the object, and one oscillates into idealism or its modifications. Here, however, then arises what many regard as an insuperable objection? How can the subject or mind know an object which is matter. How can mind, which is conscious and unextended, know matter, which is un- conscious and extended? This objection, however, is futile, for how can the mind know what is past? The mind exist, in the present; by what bridge can it pass to what happened months or years ago and to what does not exist? The answer to this question is just as inex- plicable and difficult as is the case with the former. But if we compare our knowledge of mind as con- trasted with matter, we shall find that our knowledge of the former is much more certain than that of the lat- ter. It is very difficult to tell what constitutes the nature of matter ; for what is the verdict of science? Ssience tells us that matter is composed of atoms, and that these atoms unite to form molecules-:-the molecules forming systems on an infinitely small scale, just as the sun and planets form a system on an infinitely large scale. The atoms, moreover, are not in contact,but kept apart and together by attractive and repulsive forces. But another difficulty meets one here. How are these atoms related to the forces or energies of nature? These energies are. .f various kinds, heat, electricity, &c. ; and those energies are capable of transformation the one into the other, according to the great law of the trans- formation of energy. How are these various energies located together in the almost infinitely small atom? But this is not all. We are now at the point far bevoad the evidences of the senses; and we have to fall -back upon other sources—such as reason and consciousness; and neither reason nor consciausnem are located in material atoms,accordingly I hold a position which is the very reverse of that of the materialist. Instead of main- taining that matter is better known than mind, I hold that mind is better known to us than matter; and that cur knowledge of matter is phenomenal. In knyowing ourselves as conscious, rational, and responsible beings our knowledge is as certain and secure as knowledge can, be; and in denying this position one is landed in in superable and irretrievable difficulties ; such a step is one not in advance, but retrograde—a step far behind the position occupied by a Plato or an Aristotle. Nor is it possible to overestimate its importance. If we do not know ourselves as rational and responsible beings, neither is it possible to know God as a rational and responsible being. So on the other hand those who deny a God in nature are logically bound to deny the existence of mind in man. The two positions stand or all together.—l am, &c., May 12. 1891.

div.head: HAILSTORM IN CHESHIRE
div.p: HAILSTORM IN CHESHIRE

At half-past two yesterday morning, a hurricane of wind and hail burst in the neighbourhood of Willaston, Cheshire, and extended round a large district. Great damage has been done to the fruit crop, which mainly consists of damsons. These and other fruit trees were in full bloom at the time, and , being extra full presented a most remarkable sight. The orchards yesterday morning had a most win- try aspect, with the cold winds blowing and the bloom lying scattered on the ground like new-fallen snow. The force of the gale was so severe in the neighbourhood of Shotwick that two large oak treea were blown down.

div.head: LORD SPENCER AT EVESHAM,
div.p: LORD SPENCER AT EVESHAM,

Speaking .at the annual meeting of the South Worcester Liberal Association at Eveshans on Wednesday night, Lord Spencer, referring to recent election results, said the Liberals were in very jubilant spirits. According to present indications they would not only be placed in power at the next general election—which he would like to see very soon—but would also have an ample majority for carrying all the measures they desired. These in- cluded the disestablishment of the Church in Wales , and Scotland, electoral reform, the development of local government, inclnding the establishment of , parish councils, and the extension of allotment and small holding systems. Foremost, however, was the question of Home Rule, which,so far from being dead, was as full of life now as ever.

div.head: PFNKETH.
div.p: PFNKETH.
ITOMH AGAIN. Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., returned last evening week from the Holy Land, where he has been on an extensive tour during the last ten weeks. He appears to be in remarkably good health.

THE GAS SUPPLY. The work of laying the pipes for the proposed gas supply for Penketh and Sankey is being rapidly pushed forward. The pipes have almost readied the top of Heath-road now, and if the present rate of progress be continued, we may look for a com- pletion of the undertaking at an early date.

div.head: CONFIRMATION CLASSES.
div.p: CONFIRMATION CLASSES.

Confirmation classes for the teaching of the can- didates for the coming confirmation services are being held in the Sunday School, Great Sankey. They are held each Saturday afternoon. The Rev. E. S. Jackson is the instructor, assisted by the Rev. T. R. Winder. There are a considerable number of candidates. The confirmation services are announced to be held in July, at Runcorn. DEATH OF CAPTAIN PITSILL.

We regret to announce the death of Captain Thos. Pusill, which took place on Monday morning,about 8..30. Mr. Pusill was taken ill about three weeks ago with congestion of the brain, and despite the constant attention of Dr. Murray he steadily declined, and after much suffering passed away on Monday. The funeral took place on Thursday afternoon at the cemetery at 4 o'clock, the service being con- ducted by the Rev. T. B Winder. There was a large attendance of friends and relatives of the deceased, inoluding several representatives of the Widnes con- tingent of the Salvation Army, in which Mr. Pusill took an active interest. At the conclusion of the service, Mr. Dodds (Salvation Army Captain) spoke a few words on the. uncertainty of human life and the neces,ity of being prepared whenever the sum- mons came. Dir. Pusill had been employed by Messrs. Evans and Co., all his life,a period extending over 40 years. A large number of beautiful wreaths were laid on the grave by sympathising friends and relatives. Much annoyance was caused by the con- duct of the grave digger and his assistant who whilst the address was being delivered by Mr. Dodds com- menced to fill up the grave.

div.head: EXANHNER, SATURDAY., IVIAr 16, lB9l
div.p: THE EXANHNER, SATURDAY., IVIAr 16, lB9l
THE DEATH OF MRS. SAMUEL RIGBY.
The news of the death of Mrs. Samuel Rigby, following so soon, as it does, upon that of her lamented husband, was received in W arrington _ .
with the deepest regret. Soon after Mrs. Rigby at- tended the fuuneral of her jhusband at Warrington,

_ in December last, she left Fern Bank, Chester, (where she and Mr. Rigby had resided since their departure from Warrington), with the intention of spending the rest of her days with her sister-in-law, , Mrs. J. H. Kershaw, at Dobcrosss, Saddleworth, near Oldham, Here, she gradually sank, and for the past four or five weeks had been unable to leave her bed owing to an attack of paralysis, from the effects of which she died,on Tuesday morning,about half-past nine. The deceased, who wee 69 years of age, was a daughter of the late Mr. James Kershaw, of Dobcross. She was highly respected by a num- erous circle of friends, atid her death will be deeply

regretted. It has been well said of Mrs. Rigby that, during the whole of her residence in Warrington, she drew to herself a wide respect and very general affection. Naturally timid and retiring in her disposition she was yet always will- ing to show herself friendly and helpful to all with whom she came in contact. Possessed of a tender and sym- pathic spirit, she knew how to comfort the sick and sorrowing, and her hands was always ready to do deeds of kindness, and bestow gifts of thoughtful generosity. She was, in her sphere, and to the full measure of her power and opportunity, a devoted and useful adherent of the Wycliffe Church. For many years she was the regular Sunday morning teacher of the first female class In the school, for which duty she made careful an conscientious preparation, and many of her old scholars will bear her memory in loving regard. She devoted considerable time to visitation among the members of the congregation, and was an active helper and contributor to the Dorcas Society. It was to have been her lot to lay the foundation stenQof the pre- sent Wycliffe Church on Good Friday of 1872-' but illness prevented. The duty was, therefore, done for her by her husband. Together with him, she contributed generously to the pullding fund, £lOO standing to her name in the list of subscriptions. Always she seconded Mr. Rigby in his long career of Christian usefulness in Warrington, and her memory, along with his, will be held in long arid grateful affection.
MR. T. SEXION, M.P.

In the undivided Irish party Mr. Sexton held a - - after Mr. Parnell, and now lie is one of Noril the most, if not the most, in- fluential men in the Irish Parliamentary Party. Mr. Sexton is a Waterford man, and first saw the light about forty-three years ago. He was educated privately, and ,fterwards he was for about ighteen years on the editorial ~ff of the "Nation." He was

:eturned to Parliament by Sligo, in 1880, and very quickly made a great repu- tation as a debater and an orator in the House of Commons, In the short Parliament elected in 1885, Mr. Sexton still further enhanced his reputation as a Parliamentarian. It is said of him that he lay in wait for Mr. Chamberlain's great speech on Hotne Rule for days and days and that at last when it did come he "pulverized both speech and speaker in a long address which was certainly one of the very cleverest and most scathing ever heard at West- minster." Mr. Sexton's speeches in London during the election.especially one at St. James's Hall,where lie spoke of the " waste paper Unionists" made some sensation. His victory at West Belfast at the same election was the great Parnellite success of the 1886 election. He was returned by a vote of 31832. against 3,729 given for his opponent. Mr. J H. Hu- lett. It is, perhaps, worthy a note that at the same election the Orangemen of the East Belfast division returned a past" Grand Master" of their Order, Mr. E. S. W. Cobain, who has just lately ac- quired an unenviable fame. It is interesting, too,. to note the following language which Mr. De Cobain about that time delivered himself of:—" Mr. Glad- stone may betake himself to the repose of an en- forced retirement in the Jesuits' College at Rome, and perhaps the ecclesiastical dignitary who pre- side& over the system of sensualism, superstition, and ain may bestow on him a worn-out scarlet hat, that his ecclesiastical dotage may sport some symbol of supposed authority." 'the reference to " sensu- alism " and " sin " was rather good for Mr. De Main. Mr. Sexton, it is hardly necessary to add, has lately taken his stand strongly against Mr. Parnell, but he cannot be reproached with having done anything to promote unnecessary dissensions in the Irish party. On Sunday, Mr. Parnell, in speaking of Mr. Sexton's action with regard to the government's proposals as to Irish land, said he'ha.d on many occasions shown,far beyond hia colleagues, a statesmanlike grasp of public matters. But Mr. Sexton wins praise from others besides Mr. Parnell. The "Daily News" says :—" Mr. Sexton may not always carry with him the sympathies of every English Radical. As an Irishman,he naturally tries to make the best bargain for his own country. But his mastery of every detail in this most complicated Bill, his quickness of apprehension, his lucidity of exposition, the adroitness of his - tactics and the polished vigour of his style have established him in the highest ranks of Parliamentary debaters."

THE CHEMICAL Alin COPPER WORKERS' UNION. The first animal report of the Chemical and Copper Workers' 'Union, whose headquarters are at St. Helens, was issued a few days ago by Mr. P. J. King, president. It stated that though the union since its formation had advanced much more rapidly than had been expected. and notwithstanding the fact that the men had received a considerable advance in their wages and their condition otherwise improved, they had not yet reached that prosperous position they had marked out for themselves. Regret is expressed that the chemical and copper workers were not represented on the Royal Com- mission in regard to the relations between em- ployer and employed, because they had hoped to achieve quietly by legislation what would take years ef agitation to accomplish. It was, however, advisable that the proceedings of the commission shook] be closely' watched, and care should be taken that the herring of promise was not drawn across the path of the, British workmen in general. and the chemical and copper worker in particular. Reports have reached them that the syndicate of chemical manufacturers intended stopping some of the yards, and their object doing so was easily seen. But if the members of that organisation did not loose their heads and kept cool, all would be well. They were' determined to work with redoubted energy, and in a few &Ts branches would be formed at Gates- head, Newcastle, Hebburn. &c., by which means they hoped to counteract any desire to increase the trade of one locality at theexpense of another. The balances in hand at the end of the year were—St. Helens A 1,154 9s. lid., Widnes 2.559 17s. 2d., and Garton £45 2.§-. 4d.; total £1,759,85. d.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

Yesterday morning the remains of the deceased lady were conveyed from Saddleworth, where she resided, to Warrington, and subsequently to the Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church where a service was held, which was con- ducted by the Rev. J.Yonge. There was not a large at- tendance. The Rev. F. Barnes, 8.A., of Chester, delivered an obituary discourse. He said it was but a few brief months since they had met there on a similar occasion— to pay their last tribute to one who had long lived in that town, and long laboured in that church, and was highly esteemed and respected, in the whole neighbourhood. And now to-day, after a lapse of only five months, they were called together again in order that they might pay their tribute of loving respect to his beloved partner. .Had Mr. and Mrs. Rigby been able to order events according to their own wish,they would,he felt persuaded. rather have lessened than increased the interval which had taken place betvieen their departures. In their life they were closely united by the loving bonds of sympathy, and now they were united in the home above where there would be no sickness, no disappointment, no bereave- ment in any way to interfere with their unclouded peace and joy. They were once again together—in the presence of the Lord. It would ill befit him to-day to say many words about their departed sister. There were many in that congregation who were far more qualified to speak of her past history than he was. His knowledge of Mrs. Rigby extended only over the latter part of her life when her state of health prevented her, to a very large extent, from entering actively into the duties of church work' but that short time enabled him, through personal inter- course with her in her own house, to form, he thought, a true judgment on her life and character. If ever a woman lived a truly earnest, Ch ristli ke life that woman was Mrs. Rigby. As a wife, she was devoted, as they knew, to her husband, watching, with an earnest solicitude, every movement, and anticipating every desire he expressed. Her domestic servants could never have had a more kindly or loving, a more considerate and thoughtful mis- tress. As a neighbour and as a friend she was respected far and wide. But in connection with her Christian work, she brought to it perhaps no high intellectual attain- ments no strong physical constitution; but an earnest, devoted true, tender, sympathetic, and loving spirit. In her Sunday school work and in her visitation among the poor and the sick these qualities were conspicious. In her case it might be truly said that • her works followed her. She had left behind a living memory, and they to- day de-ired not tO grieve fo'r her departure, as they felt that their loss was her gain, but to rejoice that she had now gone into the presence of him whom she loved on earth,and that they were both in the presence of the Master who had said" Be thsu faithful unto death, and I will thee a crown of life." Of Mrs. Rigby it could be said as was said concerning one who anointed our Lord with precious ointment, "She bath done what she could." God grant that each oneof them might have the same tribute ac- corded to them, and that their friends, when they were assembled together in order that they might pay them the same loving respect, might be able to bear the testi- mony that their lives were as sincere, as true, as Christ- like, as the life which had just been severed by death. To all :hose who had-lost a loving relative or friend in her, he would say that she had gone but a little while before. They must all in a very little while bid adieu to the things of time and sense. When that time came for all of them, might they all as unbroken families, be united together in the presence of Jews Christ their Lord, and might they be in His presence for evermore. Mr. W. H. Payton who presided at the organ, played the Dead March in " Saul " as the body was borne from the church. The remains were followed to, their final rest- ing-place in the family vault at the cemetery, by a num- ber of persons on foot, and eight carriageapontaining the following mourners :—Mrs. Kershaw and Mr. Walter Kershaw, Mrs. Jno. Rigby, and Mrs: Brinsley, Mr. Arthur and Mr. Herbert Kershaw Mr. Nichols and Miss Gertrude Kerskaw, Mr. and Mrs. Kershaw, Haworth, Mr. and Mrs. Ziba Armitage, Mr. and Mrs. William Armitage, jun., Mr. and Mrs. S. R. Armitage, Mr. J. F. Armitage, Mrs. Jones, Miss M. Rigny, the Revs. Jne. Yonge, F. Barnes, B.A.,and Percival, Mr. and Mrs. Pearce. and Mr. Samuel Staniforth. The service was read at the grave- side by the Rev. John Yonge. The coffin bore the plain inscription : Sarah Ann Rigby. Born 19th December, 1821. Died May 12th, 1891. Wreaths were contributed by the following persons :—Mrs. Howarth, Mrs. Kershaw, the Rev. J. Yonge, Mrs. Armitage, Mrs. Brinsley, Mr. and Mrs. Townsend, and Miss Rigby. The undertaking arrangements were carried out by Mr. J. Harrison.

ILLNESS OF Da. Fox.—This gentleman has now re- covered from his attack of pneumonia, but is still suffer- ing great pain from the inflammation of the arteries of tne left leg. A decided change for the better has, how- ever, taken place during the last few days. It will be some weeks before the doctor will be able to resume his duties. PRIMITIVE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY. —On Sunday, in connection with the above Sunday school, sermons were preached,.morning, and evening, by Mr. Grindley, of Manchester. In the-afte.moon a ser- vice of song, entitled "Lost in the: Woods." was well rendered by the choir. There were geod congregations throughout the day. A collection was made after each service in aid of the school funds. SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—The anniversary Ser- vices of the Primitive Methodist Sunday School,Lymm,, took place on Sunday, when the sermons were preached morning and evening by Mr. Grindley, of Manchester. In the afternoon a service of, song, entitled "Lost in the wood," was ably rendered by the choir. The con- gregations were good, and especially at night, when the edifice was very crowded, Collections were taken at each service. • A SiLven WEDDING.—On Wednesday night, Mr. John Lowndes entertained a number of friends in commemor- ation of his twenty-fifth wedding day, and, after justice was done to the good things provided, preparations were made for the evening's entertainment, which was rendered amusing by various friends with songs and recita- tions. The chair was taken by Dr. Joseph Holt„ and after the health of the happy couple was drunk, the chairman amused the company with anecdotes. Songs were rendered by Mr. J. Gilbert, Mr. J. Lovrndes, and Mr. J. Bolt; also by Mrs. J. Davies, Mrs. H. Thomason, Mrs. Gillents, and others.. Altogether a very enioyable evening was spent to the delight et the happy couple. THE FUNERAL or Ma. Scuwaes.—The funeral of the late Mr. Cecil Langshaw Schwabe, under graduate of Oriel College, Oxford, son of Mr. Henry A. Schwabe, of Dingle Bank, Lynam, took place on Saturday, in the churchyard at Lymsn. The Rector read the burial ser- vice. Many wreaths and crosses of white flawers cov- ered the coffin on, the way to the grave, amongst them one sent by the undergraduates of Oriel College. At the time of the funeral at Lymm the bell of Oriel College was tolled, by order of the Dean. The unfortunate death of young Mr. Schwabe took place between 11.30 p.m. 'on the 4th and 1 a.m. on the sth. The inquest was held on the 6th. There was very little evidence as to how the unhappy incident toek place, but much as to the fact that the deceased was a young man of quiet and industrious habits, and of excellent conduct ; also that he was in no difficult!: or trouble ot any kind, unless an approaching estaignnation, for which he was well pre- pared, may be 404nsidered. There was evidence that he had a great IWO for firearms, but was very careless in handling them. The jury brought in a verdict which only decided the fact that he died from a pistol wound, and that no other person was instrumental in firing the shot: His previous evening had been passed in the most ordinary manner with his most intimate friend, first in reading for his examination, and then turnin, to an amusing book of Mark Twain. He was found dead in his sitting-room on the sth. As no one was with him when he died, there cannot be any certainity as to what occurred, but there are several points which were given in evidence, and some which have come out since the inquest, to lead to the supposition that Mr. Schwabe was pointing the pistol towards his head as he stood in front of a looking glass, and that he accidentally pulled tie trigger.

div.head: ACCIDENT TO A BOWLING PARTY:
div.p: ACCIDENT TO A BOWLING PARTY:

On Saturday a party ot about 80 glass bottle- makers and sheet glass workers had a bowling match at the Holt Arms, near Billinge. The bottle- makers were conveyed in three wagonettes, while the glass workers journeyed in an omnibus. They arrived safely at the Holt Arms, and proceeded with the match, the score being as follows :—Councillor R. Hun- ter'S•team, 210; Mr. Thompson's team, 192; majority for Mr. Hunter's tears, 18. After the match the party sat dewn to tea, which was thoroughly enjoyed. After an hour's enjoyment on the green, they left the Holt Arms for home. All went well until the party reached the brow in Billinge, and then a mishap occurred to the wagleette which was in charge cf Cuncillor Hunter, and which had.eight persons in it. The breach- ings traps gave way, and this forced the wagonette on to the horse's buttocks, with the consequence that the shafts caught the horsein the neck. The horse became affrighted, and dashed• down the brow at a good speed. Councillor Hunter allowed the horse to go on for about 150, yards,. when it swerved, and the wheel of the wagonette catching the kerbstone, the vehicle was up- set, the occupants being thrown out. Councillor Hun- ter sprang to his feat and got hold of the horse, which he endeavoured to quieten, but before it got settled it kicked hinvon the leg below the knee. He, however, turned his' attention to the other occupants of the wagonette, „John Rigby and William Brogan, both work- ing Managers at Messrs, Ca,nnington, Shaw. and Co., bottle works, were found to be injured. The former had alighted upon his head. while' the latter had dislocated his shoulder. Dr. Andersen was at onze sent for, and he found that Rigby was sulerine from concussion of the brain. The other occupants of the vehicle escaped with a shaking, and it was fortunate that the party escaped without more injury. Cue wheel of the wagonette was shattered, but otherwise not much damage was done to it. The party made all haste homewards,and the injured men were taken to theirhomes. Dr. Hynes attended to Rigby, and Drs. Reid anti Scott attended to Brogan.

div.head: CONCERT AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: CONCERT AT EARLESTOWN.

On Thursday evening Mrsa. Latimer, who is well known in musical circles, gave her fourth annual concert in the Co-operative Hall, before a fairly large audience. The programme coneisted of the first part, of miscellaneous songs, itc., and the second part of the comic opera,tta "Trial by Jury." The programme opened with an " Commedietta," played by she string band under the charge of Mr. Peplow, which was well received by the audience.. Messrs. Lewis and Huddlestone next contributed a duet, " Comrades in Arms," another duet, "Rkturn of Spring," being gives by Messrs. H. Green and. A. Limond, to which they did full justice. Miss Partington was quite successful in the song," Lords and ladiesrand was heartily applauded. The song, "The roll of the, drum," was sung with much emphasis by Mr. C. H. Lea .and encored... Miss Frances , Higgins was very successful ia the song, "Not far away." Master Andy Limond gave a capital interpretation of the song,. "The Sailor's Story," and receiving an encore repeated the last verse. A plan) duet "JarantelLa" by Mrs. Latimer and Miss Minnie Thorp, received skilful handling, and was warmly applauded. Mr. Walter Limond very care- fully sang the song The light of 'tome," and Mr. C. H. Lea, who at short notice took the place of Mr. John Highant. who was indisposed,aequitted himself remark- ably well under the circumstances. A flute solo by Mr. Stirrup was well received and re-demanded, but Mr. Stirrup did not respond. The quartette "Good Even- ing " by Master Limond and Miss Higgins, Messrs. Reade and A. Limond,concluded the first part of the programme. For the second part, the platform of the hall had been cootpletely snetamorphised to represent a court of jus- tice, and a good effect was produced. The characters were all sustained by members of the Earlestown Chiral Society, as follows :—The learned Judge, Mr. W. Limond • the Plaintiff, Miss Lewis; the Defendant, Mr., James Lewis ; Counsel ftlis the Plaintiff, Mr. C. H. Lea; Usher, Mr. Jac.. Huddleston.;.Foreman of the Jury, Mr. A. Limond. It would be invidious to select any one of the characters for individual praise,as one and all worked hard to ensure success. The solos were well sung, and with becominr spirit. The ckoruses were given with the require!" go," thebrideonsaids and jurymen being also members .f the class. The string band conducted by Mr. replow performed their part in admirable style, and Mrs.' Latimer presided at the piano throughout the even- bag, doing so with her usual efficiency.

SAD DROWNING FATALITY AT EAALESTOWN. On Tuesday morning, Mr. S.. Brighouse, coroner, held am inquiry at,thn Wargrave Inn, into the cir- cumstances attending the death of Jas Smith, a printer, employed at Afesers.McCorquodale and Co.'s works, who was drowned on the previous Saturday night in the Sankey Canal, near Hay locks, Vulcan The first witness-called was Mary Smilth, widow of the deceased man. In her evidence ske deposed that she lived' at Kilshaw's cottages,Burtonwood. Her husband was a.printer in, the employ of Messrs. McCorquodale and Ca. at _Newton. He was 28 years of age last birthday. She saw him alive on Saturday morning about twenty-eve iniatites to six, when he was in good health. She expected to see him ' again on Saturday at dialler tirne„ but she did not see ' him egain alive. Shosaw his dead body on Sunday morning. He oftea got a drop of drink at the week-end but never during - tile week. Mrs. Hannah Williamson,, landlady of the Wargrave Inn, said she knevr, the deceased. He came into her house, a little before eight o'clock on Saturday night, with aaother man aamed McCormick, and they went into the snug. They ordered two beers, and she took them in, but Smith only drank a small portion of his beer, but she did not see that he was intoxicated when she served him. When he got np he appeared to stag- ger. He had ooly- one gill of beer in her house. McCormick went out and left Smith in the room. Another man went out with Smith shortly afterwarth,and that was the last she saw of lsim.4—Sergeant Longworth.: Do you remeni- ber telling me on Sunday it was owing to his drunken- ness youavould not serve him; that when begot up he staggered.—Witness : Yes, he did stagger.—Sergeant Longworth : But did you not tell me it was awing to his drunkneness you would not serve him.—Witness: No, I did not.—Charles Rhodes said he was in the War- grave Inn, on. Saturday night. He left the house with Smith, and, was in the house when he came in, which would be abouthalf-paat seven with a man named Mc Cormick, He seemed to be sober when he came in. It would be about half-past eight when he left, and during that time, ha only drank a small portion of a glass of beer. He did not assist deceased across the railway cross- ing. In his.opinion Smith was quite capable of taking care himself, but the road he had to go was a dangerous one. —By Sergeant Longworth : Mrs. Williamson declined to serve him when deceased called for another glass of beer. Witness did not suggest to take him home.—Mary Derby- shire living at Burtonwood, said about a quarter-past eight, OD Saturday night, she NO as going along the canal bank, and when about 800 yards from Hay locks, she heard a plunge in the water. She hurried to the spot, and saw a man's head just above the water. She called to deceased, but he took no notice. He appeared to be standing in the water but he sank and did not rise again. Sheput a mark on the canal bank at the spot, and then went to the lock house, and reported the occurrance.— By the Sergeant: She remembered Smith's wife's sister committing suicide at nearly the same spot, about 12 months ago.—P.C. T. Bowes stationed at Newton, said Information was conveyed to the police station, by some- ' one from the lock house, and he went to the place. The last witness was at the lock house, and she pointed out the place where the man was drowned. The body was recovered about 11 o'clock the same night. The canal was seven feet deep about a yard frGm the side, and the body was four yards from the side. On the deceased he found lid. in money. There were no marks of violence and no signs a a struggle on the bank. A verdict of "Accidentally drowned," was brought in.

EXTENSION 014` CHAPEL. On Thursday evening the efficers,church members, and several of the congregation of the Primitive. Methodist Chapel, met together in the schoolroom,, and enjoyed a social tea. After the tables had been cleared, a meeting was held to receive the report on, the chapel alteration fund, and also several other, financial statements relative to church work. Tha Rev. R. Robinson presided, and called upon the secretary (Mr. T. Orraand), to read the financial' accountst,--Mr. Ormand in response said when ,the trustees considered the advisability of alien- ing the chapel, they had in the bank. .£3:l 2s. 4d. Since then they had received from membersof the congregation in donations. togetkerwith proceeds from Easter trees, sewing meetings, and tea meetings fir £B2 3s. 20., subscriptions from friends outside- the church, amounted te £77 ss. 6d..; :realised from trays begged for ths opening tea meeting, £12:23.. 6d. ; the opening services brouelat in £26 14s. 7d., the total altogether being £23085. lid. several firms ten- dered for the work, and Messrs. Kellett and Barkers' Lender : of £l3B was accepted, but with extras this amount had been increased to £lBO. The paintingand furnishing account amounted to £36 ls.,,and sundry expenses £6 13s. 4?,,d, leaving a balance of £7 13s. Sri., which had been transferred to the har- monium account, as there was a slight debt. upon that. The contractors gave the trwitees. every satisfaction, and they were well pleased with the work- manlike manner in which they had carried out their wishes. The trustees would take the opportunity of thanking all those, not only in the church but outside, who had so generously contributed towards theexten- sion fund. (Hear, hear.)—The statement was then approved, and a copy ordered to be sent to the district meeting.—Several short addresses were afterwards given, bearing principally on church work, and the, meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks..

FORMATION OF A WRAVER'S UNios.—A large number of weavers employed at the Gelborne Spinning Companys mills have become members of the Wigan and District Power-loom Weavers' Association. At a meeting held for the purpose of the inauguration, there was a good attendance, and after the local president and Mr. Smith (secretary) had addressed the meeting on union- ism, the whole of the weavers present, 130 in number, Lyn ve in their names to benome members of the associa- tion.

COUNTY OF CUES TER.—CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACTS, 1878 ec 1888.—SWINE FEVER. NTOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that at a meeting I! of the Executive Committe- of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, held at the Town Hall, Chester, on Thursday, the 7th day of May, 1891. IT WAS ORDERED that from and after the 18th day of May, 1891, the Regulations made by the Executive Com- mittee of the said Local Authority, on the 17th day of October. 1890, and the 17th day of April, 1891, SHALL BE, AND THE SAME ARE, HEREBY REVOKED. AND IT WAS FURTHER ORDERED by the said Executive Committee of the said Authority, that from and after the said 18th day of May, 1891, the movement of Swine into the District of the Local Authority of the County of Chester, from the Counties or places herein- after mentioned, shall (with the exception and for the purposes hereinafter mentioned)BE ABSOLUTELY PRO- HIBITED until this order is revoked, that ,ia to say from the Counties of Bedford Norfolk Cambridge Northampton Denbigh Salop Essex Somerset Hertford Stafford The Petty Sessional Divi- Suffolk sion of Overton in the Warwick County of Flint West Riding of York- Gloucester shire Huntington Wiltshire and from the District of any separate Local Authority situate within any of such Counties or Places. Provided 1 wars that, notwithstanding the foregoing prohibition, SWINE to be used for breeding purposes only may be moved into the district of the Local Authority of this County, from the Counties or places hereinbefore men- ticned, subject to the following regulations, that is to say :- 1. On obtaining a License from an Inspector of the Local Authority of this County, which License will only be granted on the following conditions: (a) On a declaration of the Owner of the Swine from whom they are purchased or his Agent, that the Animals have been on the premises of such Owner during the 28 days immediately preceding their removal therefrom, and that there has been no Swine Fever on such premises during the said period of 28 days. (b) On a certificate of a Veterinary Inspector of the County of Chester, or a Veterinary Inspector ap- pointed by the Local Authority of the district from which the Swine are to be moved, that such Swine are free from disease. 2. That all Swine brought into the said district under these regulations, shall not be moved from the premised of such Owner to which they are first brought for 28 days from their arrival thereat. 3. That Swine which have been moved from any of the prohibited Counties or places named therein, or from the District of any separate Local Authority situate within this County, or into any other County, SHALL NOT BE MOVED into the District of this Local Author- ity except upon a License granted under the following condition, that is to say, On a Declaration made by the Owner of the Swine or his Agent that such Swine have been on the pre- mises from which they are to be moved for 28 days immediately preceding the date thereof, and that Swine Fever has not existed on such premises during the said period of 28 days, and also that the Swine intended to be moved have not been exposed to the infection of Swine Fever during such period. 4. THAT SWINE moved into the district of this Local Authority under the foregoing License be at once isolated by the Owner thereof in this County, and kept isolated from any other swine for a period of 28 days, and shall not be moved from the premises of such Owner ' to which they are first moved for a period of 28 days front their arrival thereat. 5. That LICENSES and Declarations shall accompany the Animals therein mentioned whilst being moved,and be delivered up to the Police Officer of the County of Chester nearest to the place of their destination by the Owner or his Agent within 48 hours after their arrival thereat. REGINALD POT I'S, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Chester, 9th May, 1891. The foregoing Regulations do not restrict the move- ments of Animals by Railway through the District of the Loral Authority of this County, without untrucking. Any offence against the above Regulations is deemed an I offence against the act of 1678, which renders the offender. I liable to a penalty of not excee,ding Twenty Pounds.

THE CHARGE AGAINST MR. STOREY, M.P. • In the Queen's Bench, .London, on Tuesday, a rule to -quash the committal of Mr. Storey, M.P., on the charge of alleged perjury, at Sunderland, was made absolute, and costs were given against the individual magistrates who granted the committal. ANOTHER FACTION FIGHT. A sanguinary encounter between Parnellites and Anti- Parnellites occurred on Wednesdav night at a meeting in Limehouse, which was addressed by Mr. Parnell. Several ef the combatants were so seriously injured as te require seediest treatment. Mr. Parnell, in the course of his remarks, described the Land Purchase Bill as the great- est measure which had ever proceeded from the Imperial Parliament for the benefit of Ireland. A FATAL PRACTICAL JOKE. A lad named Frederick Riding died at Darwen, on Tuesday, from the results of an extraordinary practical joke. A fellow employe at Messrs. Potter's paper-stain- ing works remarked as Riding passed through one of the rooms, "Let's bang him." and passed a rope round his neck. At this moment the machinery started, and Rid- ing received the injuries which have resulted as stated. As. A WOMAN CHARGED WITH MURDER On Thursday an inquest was held at South Shields, on -George Dixon, moulder, who died from stabs inflicted • by a young woman named Harriet Harleigh. It appears that the parties had been living together. On Monday night some words passed between them, and the woman stabbed Dixon in the left breast in the region of the heart. The man wat; removed to the infirmary, where he died shortly after.—The jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against Harleigh. A MAN WITH EIGHT WIVES. At the Thames Police Court, London. on Thursday, a, -Jew's woman applied through an interpreter for a war- rant against a man with whom she had gone through a mock marriage, and who had thus obtained all her money. It was stated there was a regular system of mock marriages in Fast London, and that the man in lueation had married eight your'. foreign Jewesses in succession, and robbed them of their savings. The ap- plication was adjourned to allow of evidence being pro- -deiced.

The mansion is handsome. having been designed by the eminent Italian architect, Leoni. and very commodious, with exten- sive stables, coach-houses, gardens, and glass-houses. It is surrounded by lawns and pleasure grounds, woods and plan- tations, and stands in a park of about 250 acres, with three entrance lodges. The estate is compact and the shooting ex- cellent, and good hunting within easy reach. The laud is very fertile, and the farms are all well let. There are two public-houses. Several mines of coal exist under the pro- perty, and some of these are being worked within about 40 yards of the boundary. The mines and minerals, and also the timber, will be included in the sale. CRICKET. Gentlemen closed With 359, Oxford 20for 2, Lanca- shire closed with 117',, Marylebone 33'for 2 wickets. FIRE A 7 NORTHAMPTON. Yesterday morning a fire occurred at Messrs. John Phipps and Sons, furnishers and boot mercers, Gola-st: • Northampton. The damage is estimated at aboiA £15,000. COTTON MIL A BURNED' DOWN. The Bardsley Vale Cotton Mill, Ashton-undsr-Lyne, belonging to Messrs. Podgson and Grundy, was &trued by fire yesterday. The damage announts to over 2:20,000. A YOUNG LADY SHOT. A young lady, named Thomas, was fired at and struck, Ikandilo, yesterday, by a travelling actor, named Earnish, who was arrested with the revolver in his possession. NORTH BUCKS ELECTION:. The contest in North Bucks may be said to-have • nowt fairly begun. Mr. Hubbard, the Conservative candid- ate, has spoken at Olney; and Mr. Leon, 'Gladstoniac, addressed meetings in the Claydon district. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL MIL. - It is understood that the London and North-Western Railway Company, and probably one or two others- will ask to be heard against the Manchester 3hip Canal, (Money) ,Bill when it comes before the Select C6mmittee. THE MANIPUR DISASTER. 1 Blue Book on Manipur affairs, published yesterday, shows that Mr. Quinton, the murdered Commissioner; was ordered to secure the removal of Senapattilrotn the country without affording him the chance of4forcible opposition. „PEWS ATTACKED BY GREEKS. NINE JEWS KILLED. A Vienna correspondent telegraphed on Thnniday night :—ewe has been received from Corfu thate..Greek mob, excited by the orthodox clergy, yesterday stormed several !Jewish, houses and burnt two. Nine Jews were killed and two wounded. The military commander has proclaimed martial law in the island, and the governor and mayor have been removed from their posts. TERRIFIC' EXPLOSION IN A COAL MINE; SEVERAL MEN INJURED. An Ashton-under-Lyne correspondent telegraphs that a terrific explosion occurred on Thursday night at the Moss Colliery there,, by which several men were eeri- ously injured. Miners were blasting in No. 3 brow,when an explosion of.coal gas took place, throwing the men against the workings amidst falling masses of coal. One man named Worrell was injured fatally, having :his skull fractured,and a number of others were badly hurt. Fire afterwards broke otst,and much damage was caused. THE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC. The Prince of Wales passed a good night, and will soon be convalescent. On inquiry at IR* Park-lane 'early yesterday mprning it was ascertained that Mr. Gladstone had passed another good night, and that he continued to make rapid progress towards complete convalesence. The journey to Hawarden has not yet been definitely settled. The Marquis of:Exeter issuffering from an acute attack of bronchitis at Stamford, and is reported to be ins very critical condition; David Wilitinson„..aged fifteen, who was suffering from influenza, committed suicide by hanging himself at Gos- berton, near Spalding: THE' CHINESE, RIOT AT SHANGHAI. BRITISH CONSULATE WRECKED. HOUSES BURNED DOWN. SHANGHAI, THE'RSDAT.—The destruction wrought by the mob at Wahu was vridespread and serious, leaving the Catholic mission &gutted ruin. The Chinese attacked the quarters of the Custom-house officers and set them on fire. The building was soon burned to the ground. Then the people made a. stash for the British Consulate, which they reduced to a complete wreck, after looting the house from top to bottom. The Consul and his wife had fortunately been forewarned, and were able to make -their escape disguised in Chinese clothes. The Consul is, however, reported to have been wounded by the rioters. The last advices report that quiet has now been resorted to Wahu. 'YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. • HOUSE COMMONS. The Speaker tookthe chair at three o'clock. THE NORTH BUCKS. VAGANCY.—Mr. Arnold Morley.— I beg to move that the Speaker do make out his war- rant to the Clerk of the Crown to issne a new writ for the County of Bucks, northern division, in the room of Captain Edmund Hope Verney, expelled this house. The Speaker ordered the issue of the writ. Tits PERSECUTION, OF rex Jews.—Sir Julian Golds- mid asked the Under Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs whether riotsoiveretakieg place against the Jews of Corfu. Baron H. de Worms,atated that attempts were stated to have been made to fire the Jewish quarter, but hitherto fortunately without success. Her. Majesty's Minister at Athens had made representations to the Greek Government on the subject, . and the Admiral of the Mediterranean squadron had been instructed to send a ship of war to Corfu for the protection of the British Jews. A few minutes afterwards Baron H. de Worms stated that the Foreigneffice had just received a tele- ("Tam to the effect that one Jew was killed by some Greeks after the revolt. Assistance had been supplied by the Greek Gcivernment to destitute Jews suffering from starvation. IRISH LAND BILL.—Thz• House again went into Com- mittee on the Irish Land Purchase Bill.—Mr. SavroN moved an insertion in clause 18 defining the meaning of the term judicial' rent in such a manner that, in case of holdings where no judicial rent had been fixed, an aver- age might be taken which would be acceptable as the rent of the holding, although such had not been previ- ouslkr judiciallYfixed. Mr. BALFOUR moved an amend- merit providingthat. where a judicial rent had not been fixed, the annual value should be ascertained by the Land Commissioners in the manner pre- sented in the rules. After much discussion, this was agreed to. Clause 19 was also agreed to. Mr. BALFOUR said the schedules and new clauses would be taken into consideration on Thursday pext. After an angry discussion as to the day to which the House Should adjourn for the holidays, progress was reported, and the House adjourned until Thursday neat.
